For GO membrane term, heads with positive relevance and correlation with transmembrane regions are identified.
For GO catalytic activity, heads correlate with active sites and PROSITE patterns.
The method is sensitive to model parameters and provides insights beyond anecdotal evidence.
papers.limitation: The method may identify significant heads due to coincidental partial alignment of randomly initialized heads with directions in feature space that happen to correlate with sequence annotations.
papers.abstract: Motivation: We explored how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can help to shed light into the inner workings of neural networks for protein function prediction, by extending the widely used XAI method of integrated gradients such that latent representations inside of transformer models, which were finetuned to Gene Ontology term and Enzyme Commission number prediction, can be inspected too. Results: The approach enabled us to identify amino acids in the sequences that the transformers pay particular attention to, and to show that these relevant sequence parts reflect expectations from biology and chemistry, both in the embedding layer and inside of the model, where we identified transformer heads with a statistically significant correspondence of attribution maps with ground truth sequence annotations (e.g. transmembrane regions, active sites) across many proteins. Availability and Implementation: Source code can be accessed at https://github.com/markuswenzel/xai-proteins .

papers.title: Brain-optimized deep neural network models of human visual areas learn non-hierarchical representations
papers.research_question: Does hierarchical representation in deep neural networks (DNNs) improve the accuracy of predicting brain activity in human visual areas V1-V4?
papers.core_contribution: Hierarchical representations are not necessary to accurately predict human brain activity in V1-V4, and DNNs with diverse architectures (from strict serial hierarchies to multiple independent branches) can encode brain-like visual representations.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that hierarchical representations are not necessary for accurately predicting brain activity in human visual areas V1-V4, and brain-optimized DNNs can learn non-hierarchical representations while maintaining high accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Brain-optimized DNNs (GNet) predict brain activity in V1-V4 more accurately than task-optimized AlexNet for both natural and artificial stimuli.
Single-branch (GNet8j) and multi-branch (GNet8r) brain-optimized models yield similar prediction accuracy despite architectural differences.
Both single-branch and multi-branch models exhibit integration hierarchy, with receptive field sizes expanding from V1 to V4.
Only single-branch models (AlexNet and GNet8j) learn compositional and entailment hierarchies; multi-branch models (GNet8r) do not.
Hierarchical representations are not essential for accurate prediction of brain activity, as non-hierarchical models can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy.
papers.limitation: The best models leave much variance unexplained, accounting for at most 78% of explainable variance in brain activity.
future_direction: Developing new analytical tools for uncovering the function of representations encoded in different human visual areas using brain-optimized networks.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) optimized for visual tasks learn representations that align layer depth with the hierarchy of visual areas in the primate brain. One interpretation of this finding is that hierarchical representations are necessary to accurately predict brain activity in the primate visual system. To test this interpretation, we optimized DNNs to directly predict brain activity measured with fMRI in human visual areas V1-V4. We trained a single-branch DNN to predict activity in all four visual areas jointly, and a multi-branch DNN to predict each visual area independently. Although it was possible for the multi-branch DNN to learn hierarchical representations, only the single-branch DNN did so. This result shows that hierarchical representations are not necessary to accurately predict human brain activity in V1-V4, and that DNNs that encode brain-like visual representations may differ widely in their architecture, ranging from strict serial hierarchies to multiple independent branches.

papers.title: Scale-invariant feature extraction of neural network and renormalization group flow
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) and renormalization group (RG) flow, and how does the RBM learn to extract features from spin configurations?
papers.core_contribution: The unsupervised RBM trained on Ising model configurations at various temperatures generates a flow of temperature that approaches the critical point Tc, opposite to the typical RG flow, indicating the RBM learns scale-invariant features.
papers.conclusion: The RBM flow is attracted to the critical point when trained on a wide range of temperatures, and the RBM learns scale-invariant features, showing a connection to RG but with an opposite flow direction.
papers.key_findings:
For type V RBM (trained on configurations from T=0 to T=6), the temperature flow approaches the critical temperature Tc=2.27, making Tc a stable fixed point.
When the hidden layer size Nh is less than or equal to the visible layer size Nv, the flow stabilizes at Tc; for Nh > Nv, the flow eventually moves towards high temperature.
The weight matrix product WW^T reflects spin correlations, and its off-diagonal components decay similarly to spin correlations near Tc.
The eigenvalue spectrum of WW^T for type V RBM shows a gradual decrease without jumps, suggesting scale-invariant feature learning.
The RBM flow is attracted to the features it has learned during training, e.g., type H/L RBMs flow towards high/low temperatures respectively.
future_direction: Investigate the RBM flow for first-order phase transitions, e.g., in the Blume-Capel model.
Study the attractor of RBM flows for human faces to understand value judgments.
Describe the RBM flow as a stochastic process using Langevin or Fokker-Planck equations.
papers.abstract: Theoretical understanding of how a deep neural network (DNN) extracts features from input images is still unclear, but it is widely believed that the extraction is performed hierarchically through a process of coarse graining. It reminds us of the basic renormalization group (RG) concept in statistical physics. In order to explore possible relations between DNN and RG, we use the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) applied to an Ising model and construct a flow of model parameters (in particular, temperature) generated by the RBM. We show that the unsupervised RBM trained by spin configurations at various temperatures from T=0 to T=6 generates a flow along which the temperature approaches the critical value T_{c}=2.27. This behavior is the opposite of the typical RG flow of the Ising model. By analyzing various properties of the weight matrices of the trained RBM, we discuss why it flows towards T_{c} and how the RBM learns to extract features of spin configurations.

papers.title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we uncover the computational circuits in protein language models that underlie their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoMech, a framework using cross-layer transcoders to discover computational circuits in protein language models, achieving high performance recovery and enabling protein design.
papers.conclusion: ProtoMech establishes a principled framework for protein circuit tracing, revealing interpretable computational pathways and enabling effective protein design.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoMech recovers 82–89% of the original ESM2 performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks.
ProtoMech identifies compact circuits using <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy.
Steering along the discovered circuits enables high-fitness protein design, outperforming baseline methods in more than 70% of cases.
The circuits correspond to known structural and functional motifs, such as binding sites and catalytic loops.
ProtoMech provides a more accurate approximation of ESM2's computation than per-layer transcoder baselines.
papers.limitation: Full replacement models, where both attention and MLP computations are replaced, lead to substantial performance degradation due to compounding reconstruction errors.
future_direction: Developing robust full replacement models remains an active area of research.
Using a tanh loss for constraining sparsity is an interesting future direction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have emerged as powerful predictors of protein structure and function. However, the computational circuits underlying their predictions remain poorly understood. Recent mechanistic interpretability methods decompose pLM representations into interpretable features, but they treat each layer independently and thus fail to capture cross-layer computation, limiting their ability to approximate the full model. We introduce ProtoMech, a framework for discovering computational circuits in pLMs using cross-layer transcoders that learn sparse latent representations jointly across layers to capture the model's full computational circuitry. Applied to the pLM ESM2, ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of the original performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks. ProtoMech then identifies compressed circuits that use <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy, revealing correspondence with structural and functional motifs, including binding, signaling, and stability. Steering along these circuits enables high-fitness protein design, surpassing baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. These results establish ProtoMech as a principled framework for protein circuit tracing.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Antibody Language Models Using SAEs
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal interpretable features in antibody language models and be used to steer generation? How do TopK and Ordered SAEs compare in terms of interpretability and steerability?
papers.core_contribution: TopK SAEs can identify interpretable features in antibody language models but are not steerable, while Ordered SAEs can identify steerable features but with less interpretable activation patterns, suggesting Ordered SAEs are preferable for generative steering.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are effective for interpretability and steering in antibody language models, with trade-offs between interpretability and steerability between TopK and Ordered SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
TopK SAEs can reveal biologically meaningful latent features in antibody language models.
High feature-concept correlation in TopK SAEs does not guarantee causal control over generation.
Ordered SAEs impose a hierarchical structure that reliably identifies steerable features.
Ordered SAEs come at the expense of more complex and less interpretable activation patterns.
SAEs can be used to incorporate rational design principles into antibody library generation.
papers.limitation:
Lack of labelled datasets for antibodies compared to general proteins, which prevents automated feature identification and annotation.
TopK SAEs may not consistently generate monosemantic features for all concepts.
future_direction: Conduct exhaustive steering analyses to quantitatively measure the steerability of Top-K and Ordered SAE features.
Scale SAE training using more expansive, annotated datasets like FLAb to enable models to identify domain-specific abstractions.
Use SAEs to generate antibody libraries with properties such as developability and specificity.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a mechanistic interpretability technique that have been used to provide insight into learned concepts within large protein language models. Here, we employ TopK and Ordered SAEs to investigate an autoregressive antibody language model, p-IgGen, and steer its generation. We show that TopK SAEs can reveal biologically meaningful latent features, but high feature concept correlation does not guarantee causal control over generation. In contrast, Ordered SAEs impose an hierarchical structure that reliably identifies steerable features, but at the expense of more complex and less interpretable activation patterns. These findings advance the mechanistic interpretability of domain-specific protein language models and suggest that, while TopK SAEs are sufficient for mapping latent features to concepts, Ordered SAEs are preferable when precise generative steering is required.

papers.title: Mechanism-based organization of neural networks to emulate systems biology and pharmacology models
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be reorganized to mimic mechanistic models for better interpretability and performance in emulating systems biology and pharmacology models?
papers.core_contribution: By reorganizing neural network layers to mimic the structure of mechanistic models, the proposed semi-mechanistic deep learning model achieves better training rates and prediction accuracy while maintaining interpretability compared to black-box approaches.
papers.conclusion: The semi-mechanistic deep learning framework improves interpretability and performance in emulating mechanistic models, and can be expanded to other complex models in systems biology and pharmacology.
papers.key_findings:
The semi-mechanistic model has significantly lower training error and converges faster than the black-box model.
It accurately predicts the median and 95% confidence intervals of minute ventilation time courses in virtual populations.
The model reduces computational time for simulations from over 10 days to under 19 minutes for large parameter spaces.
It maintains the interpretability of mechanistic simulations by preserving the structure of underlying processes.
The approach outperforms a baseline Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR) method in prediction accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The methodology has only been tested on a simplified version of the translational opioid overdose model and needs validation on full models and other mechanistic scenarios.
No systematic comparison was performed with other data-driven models beyond PLSR.
future_direction: Expand the model to the full translational model simulations for opioid overdose.
Apply the framework to other mechanistic scenarios to confirm general applicability.
papers.abstract: Deep learning neural networks are often described as black boxes, as it is difficult to trace model outputs back to model inputs due to a lack of clarity over the internal mechanisms. This is even true for those neural networks designed to emulate mechanistic models, which simply learn a mapping between the inputs and outputs of mechanistic models, ignoring the underlying processes. Using a mechanistic model studying the pharmacological interaction between opioids and naloxone as a proof-of-concept example, we demonstrated that by reorganizing the neural networks' layers to mimic the structure of the mechanistic model, it is possible to achieve better training rates and prediction accuracy relative to the previously proposed black-box neural networks, while maintaining the interpretability of the mechanistic simulations. Our framework can be used to emulate mechanistic models in a large parameter space and offers an example on the utility of increasing the interpretability of deep learning networks.

papers.title: Representation learning of genomic sequence motifs with convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How does CNN architecture, specifically convolutional filter size and max-pooling, influence the extent that sequence motif representations are learned by first layer filters?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that CNN architecture controls whether first layer filters learn whole motif representations (localist) or partial motifs (distributed), with large max-pooling limiting hierarchical learning and encouraging interpretable filters.
papers.conclusion: Architectural design of CNNs can be used to intentionally learn interpretable representations in first layer filters, with a trade-off in performance, providing guidance for model interpretability in genomics.
papers.key_findings:
Large max-pool sizes relative to filter size encourage first layer filters to learn whole motif representations.
Small max-pool sizes allow deeper layers to assemble partial motifs into whole motifs, leading to distributed representations in first layer.
The representation learning principles generalize from synthetic sequences to in vivo genomic data.
Overparameterizing the number of first layer filters reduces the fraction that learn motifs due to optimization dynamics.
Filter size alone is not sufficient; the ability to assemble motifs in deeper layers is key.
papers.limitation:
Filter visualization does not specify the importance of filters or how they are combined for predictions.
The study uses a simplifying assumption that TF binding sites are represented by single PWM-like motifs, which may not hold in vivo.
future_direction: Quantifying the importance of filters that learn motifs.
Exploring how these principles apply to more complex regulatory codes.
papers.abstract: Although convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been applied to a variety of computational genomics problems, there remains a large gap in our understanding of how they build representations of regulatory genomic sequences. Here we perform systematic experiments on synthetic sequences to reveal how CNN architecture, specifically convolutional filter size and max-pooling, influences the extent that sequence motif representations are learned by first layer filters. We find that CNNs designed to foster hierarchical representation learning of sequence motifs-assembling partial features into whole features in deeper layers-tend to learn distributed representations, i.e. partial motifs. On the other hand, CNNs that are designed to limit the ability to hierarchically build sequence motif representations in deeper layers tend to learn more interpretable localist representations, i.e. whole motifs. We then validate that this representation learning principle established from synthetic sequences generalizes to in vivo sequences.

papers.title: Symbolic Synthesis of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be combined with symbolic programs to improve data-efficient generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces G-SSNNs, a class of neural modules that inject features from synthesized symbolic programs to improve data efficiency and generalization.
papers.conclusion: G-SSNNs improve data efficiency and generalization on a binary prediction task over Raven's Progressive Matrices and allow derivation of symbolic program semantics without manual engineering.
papers.key_findings:
G-SSNN modules modulate the data efficiency and generalization of baseline neural models, creating predictable patterns of both heightened and curtailed generalization.
Training G-SSNNs provides information about desirable semantics of symbolic programs without manual engineering, which is compact and amenable to abstraction.
future_direction: Investigate data efficient generalization and the transferability of learned symbolic representations in more complex G-SSNN designs based on more complex classes of symbolic programs.
papers.abstract: Neural networks adapt very well to distributed and continuous representations, but struggle to generalize from small amounts of data. Symbolic systems commonly achieve data efficient generalization by exploiting modularity to benefit from local and discrete features of a representation. These features allow symbolic programs to be improved one module at a time and to experience combinatorial growth in the values they can successfully process. However, it is difficult to design a component that can be used to form symbolic abstractions and which is adequately overparametrized to learn arbitrary high-dimensional transformations. I present Graph-based Symbolically Synthesized Neural Networks (G-SSNNs), a class of neural modules that operate on representations modified with synthesized symbolic programs to include a fixed set of local and discrete features. I demonstrate that the choice of injected features within a G-SSNN module modulates the data efficiency and generalization of baseline neural models, creating predictable patterns of both heightened and curtailed generalization. By training G-SSNNs, we also derive information about desirable semantics of symbolic programs without manual engineering. This information is compact and amenable to abstraction, but can also be flexibly recontextualized for other high-dimensional settings. In future work, I will investigate data efficient generalization and the transferability of learned symbolic representations in more complex G-SSNN designs based on more complex classes of symbolic programs. Experimental code and data are available at https://github.com/shlomenu/symbolically_synthesized_networks .

papers.title: Investigation of Internal Functioning of the Radial-Basis-Function Neural Network River Flow Forecasting Models
papers.research_question: Can hydrological knowledge be extracted from Radial Basis Function Neural Networks (RBFNNs) by interpreting their internal functioning, specifically by examining the responses of hidden layer neurons to understand how they represent flow components in river flow forecasting?
papers.core_contribution: The hidden neurons in an RBFNN for river flow forecasting are not arbitrary but represent specific flow components (baseflow, interflow, surface runoff), demonstrating that hydrological knowledge can be extracted from the model's internal functioning.
papers.conclusion: The RBFNN can be used as an effective flow forecasting tool, and its hidden neurons activate in a way that corresponds to hydrological flow components, suggesting that the network's internal functioning is interpretable and can extract meaningful hydrological knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The RBFNN is an effective tool for daily flow forecasting.
The activation of hidden nodes is not arbitrary; each node dominates in one of the flow domains (low, medium, high) and represents flow components resembling baseflow, interflow, and surface runoff.
The proportional contribution from each hidden neuron varies over time, reflecting dominance in specific flow ranges.
The RBFNN parameters (centers, spreads, weights) function to decompose the flow hydrograph into meaningful components.
The method provides insight into the internal functioning of RBFNNs, showing they can mimic local models corresponding to hydrological processes.
papers.limitation: The study uses a limited number of catchments, so the findings may not generalize to all catchments.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to a large number of catchments with different characteristics.
Investigate the sensitivity of the number of RBFs and network structure to represent physical processes.
papers.abstract: This paper deals with the challenging problem of hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning of artificial neural networks (ANNs) by extracting knowledge from their solutions. The neural network used in this study is based on the structure of the radial-basis-function neural network (RBFNN), which is considered as an alternative to the multilayer perceptron for solving complex modeling problems. This network consists of input, hidden, and output layers. The network is trained using the daily data of two catchments having different characteristics and from two different regions in the world. The present day and antecedent observed discharges are used as inputs to the network to forecast the flow one day ahead. A range of quantitative and qualitative techniques are used for hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning by examining the responses of the hidden layer nodes. The results of the study show that a single hidden layered RBFNN is an effective tool to forecast the daily flows and that the activation of the hidden layer nodes are far from arbitrary, but appear to represent flow components of the predicted hydrograph. The results of the study confirm that the three nodes in the hidden layer of this model effectively divide the input data space in such a way that the contribution from each node dominates in one of the flow domains—low, medium, or high—and form, in a crude manner, the base flow, interflow and surface runoff components of the hydrograph.

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret the internal representations of protein language models and steer them to generate sequences with desired features?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can be applied to protein language models to interpret their internal representations and that the identified latent features can be used to steer the model to generate protein sequences with desired structural motifs.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders provide a promising approach for interpreting and controlling protein language models, opening new avenues for protein design and engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders trained on ESM-2 activations can identify latent components associated with protein annotations such as transmembrane regions, binding sites, and zinc finger motifs.
A heuristic based on intrinsic dimension estimation can guide the selection of the transformer layer from which to extract representations for SAE training.
Intervening on specific latent components during inference can steer the model to generate protein sequences that contain desired features, such as zinc finger domains.
The sequence generation pipeline successfully produced sequences with zinc finger motifs, though it requires parameter tuning to improve success rates.
papers.limitation:
The sequence generation pipeline requires parameter fine-tuning to improve the success rate.
The features learned by the model may not directly align with manually curated dataset annotations, as latents might encode more specific or coarse-grained features.
future_direction: Extend these methods to larger models and a wider range of protein features.
Automate the parameter search for the sequence generation pipeline to improve efficiency.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancements in transformer-based language models have revolutionized natural language processing, yet understanding the internal mechanisms of these models remains a significant challenge. This paper explores the application of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to interpret the internal representations of protein language models, specifically focusing on the ESM-2 8M parameter model. By performing a statistical analysis on each latent component's relevance to distinct protein annotations, we identify potential interpretations linked to various protein characteristics, including transmembrane regions, binding sites, and specialized motifs. We then leverage these insights to guide sequence generation, shortlisting the relevant latent components that can steer the model towards desired targets such as zinc finger domains. This work contributes to the emerging field of mechanistic interpretability in biological sequence models, offering new perspectives on model steering for sequence design.

papers.title: Interpretability in Parameter Space: Minimizing Mechanistic Description Length with Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we decompose neural network parameters into faithful, minimal, and simple mechanistic components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), a method to decompose neural network parameters into mechanistic components that are faithful, minimal, and simple, optimizing for minimal description length.
papers.conclusion: APD offers a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, suggesting solutions to open problems like identifying minimal circuits in superposition and providing an architecture-agnostic framework for neural network decomposition, though challenges remain for scaling.
papers.key_findings:
APD successfully recovers ground truth mechanisms in a toy model of superposition, decomposing the weight matrix into columns corresponding to individual features.
APD identifies parameter components representing individual functions in a toy model of compressed computation, where the model computes more nonlinear functions than it has neurons.
APD learns components that represent individual functions even when they span multiple layers in a toy model of cross-layer distributed representations.
APD's components are faithful to the original parameters, minimal in number per input, and simple in terms of rank.
papers.limitation:
High computational cost due to the need for multiple forward and backward passes.
Sensitivity to hyperparameters, such as the batch top-k value and loss coefficients.
Attributions are approximated using gradients, which may not perfectly capture causal importance.
future_direction: Improving computational cost
Improving robustness to hyperparameters
Improving attributions
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. Despite recent progress toward this goal, it remains unclear how best to decompose neural network parameters into mechanistic components. We introduce Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), a method that directly decomposes a neural network's parameters into components that (i) are faithful to the parameters of the original network, (ii) require a minimal number of components to process any input, and (iii) are maximally simple. Our approach thus optimizes for a minimal length description of the network's mechanisms. We demonstrate APD's effectiveness by successfully identifying ground truth mechanisms in multiple toy experimental settings: Recovering features from superposition; separating compressed computations; and identifying cross-layer distributed representations. While challenges remain to scaling APD to non-toy models, our results suggest solutions to several open problems in mechanistic interpretability, including identifying minimal circuits in superposition, offering a conceptual foundation for 'features', and providing an architecture-agnostic framework for neural network decomposition.

papers.title: A mechanistically interpretable neural network for regulatory genomics
papers.research_question: How can we design a neural network for regulatory genomics that is both fully expressive and mechanistically interpretable, allowing motifs and their syntax to be directly readable from the model's weights and activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ARGMINN, a mechanistically interpretable neural network for regulatory genomics that directly encodes motifs and their syntax in its weights and activations, achieving full expressivity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: ARGMINN is a mechanistically interpretable architecture that successfully balances expressivity and interpretability for regulatory genomics, enabling direct motif and syntax reading, robust predictions, and interpretable sequence generation.
papers.key_findings:
ARGMINN outperforms existing methods in motif discovery, recovering more relevant motifs with fewer redundancies and extraneous motifs.
ARGMINN enables accurate motif instance calling and syntax discovery in a single forward pass, revealing biological syntax such as spacing preferences.
ARGMINN is robust to variations in GC content and adversarial attacks due to its biologically grounded design.
ARGMINN can be used for interpretable design of novel functional sequences by inserting motifs according to learned syntax.
ARGMINN demonstrates superior QTL prioritization, accurately identifying causal mutations that disrupt motif instances.
papers.limitation: The filter-overlap regularization is soft and may be ignored by the model if needed for performance, potentially allowing distributed representations.
future_direction: Extend ARGMINN to multi-task settings
Incorporate more complex biological constraints
Apply ARGMINN to other domains
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks excel in mapping genomic DNA sequences to associated readouts (e.g., protein-DNA binding). Beyond prediction, the goal of these networks is to reveal to scientists the underlying motifs (and their syntax) which drive genome regulation. Traditional methods that extract motifs from convolutional filters suffer from the uninterpretable dispersion of information across filters and layers. Other methods which rely on importance scores can be unstable and unreliable. Instead, we designed a novel mechanistically interpretable architecture for regulatory genomics, where motifs and their syntax are directly encoded and readable from the learned weights and activations. We provide theoretical and empirical evidence of our architecture's full expressivity, while still being highly interpretable. Through several experiments, we show that our architecture excels in de novo motif discovery and motif instance calling, is robust to variable sequence contexts, and enables fully interpretable generation of novel functional sequences.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of a network architecture (via intertwiner groups) relate to the symmetries in the network's internal representations of data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces intertwiner groups to connect architectural symmetries with symmetries in internal representations, and shows that for ReLU networks, the activation basis is special for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intertwiner groups connect architectural symmetries to representation symmetries, and provide a justification for focusing on activation basis in ReLU networks for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Intertwiner groups describe weight space symmetries and propagate to symmetries in internal representations.
Stitching with GReLU transformations incurs a small accuracy penalty, indicating that much of the variation between networks can be accounted for by GReLU.
GReLU-Procrustes and GReLU-CKA are effective dissimilarity measures invariant to GReLU transformations.
For ReLU networks, interpretability is higher in the activation basis than in arbitrary linear combinations, but this is not the case for networks without ReLU.
papers.limitation:
The theory does not fully account for residual connections, as noted in remark 3.6.
Stitching with GReLU does not achieve full accuracy, indicating that internal representations are not perfectly aligned by permutations and scalings.
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a fundamental tool in the exploration of a broad range of complex systems. In machine learning symmetry has been explored in both models and data. In this paper we seek to connect the symmetries arising from the architecture of a family of models with the symmetries of that family's internal representation of data. We do this by calculating a set of fundamental symmetry groups, which we call the intertwiner groups of the model. We connect intertwiner groups to a model's internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network's representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

papers.title: Neural network interpretation using descrambler groups
papers.research_question: How can inner layer signalling of fully connected neural networks be brought into a human-readable form to improve interpretability, particularly in digital signal processing and scientific computing?
papers.core_contribution: A group-theoretical method (descrambler groups) for interpreting fully connected neural networks by finding orthogonal transformations that make intermediate signals human-readable, successfully revealing sophisticated signal processing operations in a DSP network.
papers.conclusion: The descrambler group method enables interpretation of fully connected neural networks, revealing that even small networks can invent complex mathematical operations, and that reductionist understanding is possible.
papers.key_findings:
The descrambler group method can successfully interpret the inner workings of fully connected neural networks.
DEERNet spontaneously invents a bandpass filter, a notch filter, a frequency axis rectifier, frequency division multiplexing, spectral filtering regularization, and a Fourier-like transform mapping harmonics to Chebyshev polynomials.
The method reveals that even small networks can develop complex, interpretable mathematical operations during training.
The descrambling process requires defining a problem-specific interpretability metric, such as signal smoothness or diagonal dominance.
The method is applicable to fully connected layers, which are harder to interpret than convolutional layers.
papers.limitation: The method requires domain-specific expertise to recognize the functionality of descrambled weight matrices, and the descrambled matrix may still be uninterpretable to non-specialists.
future_direction: Neural networks can be mined for new knowledge, possibly discovering previously unknown mathematics.
A staged approach is recommended: first establish the role of each layer empirically, then descramble for implementation details.
papers.abstract: The lack of interpretability and trust is a much-criticized feature of deep neural networks. In fully connected nets, the signaling between inner layers is scrambled because backpropagation training does not require perceptrons to be arranged in any particular order. The result is a black box; this problem is particularly severe in scientific computing and digital signal processing (DSP), where neural nets perform abstract mathematical transformations that do not reduce to features or concepts. We present here a group-theoretical procedure that attempts to bring inner-layer signaling into a human-readable form, the assumption being that this form exists and has identifiable and quantifiable features-for example, smoothness or locality. We applied the proposed method to DEERNet (a DSP network used in electron spin resonance) and managed to descramble it. We found considerable internal sophistication: the network spontaneously invents a bandpass filter, a notch filter, a frequency axis rescaling transformation, frequency-division multiplexing, group embedding, spectral filtering regularization, and a map from harmonic functions into Chebyshev polynomials-in 10 min of unattended training from a random initial guess.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: The Molecular Structure of Thought: Mapping the Topology of Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models learn and represent effective Long Chain-of-Thought?
papers.core_contribution: The paper models Long Chain-of-Thought as a molecular structure with three bond types and introduces Mole-Syn, a method to synthesize effective Long CoT structures, improving performance and RL stability.
papers.conclusion: The molecular structure view explains how LLMs learn Long CoT, and Mole-Syn enables effective synthesis of these structures for improved reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Long CoT reasoning exhibits stable molecular-like structures formed by deep-reasoning, self-reflection, and self-exploration bonds.
Semantic isomers with compatible bond structures are crucial for effective Long CoT learning, while incompatible structures lead to instability.
Distillation from strong reasoning LLMs successfully imparts Long CoT structures, but distillation from weak instruction LLMs or human traces fails.
Mole-Syn can synthesize effective Long CoT structures by transferring behavior distributions, boosting performance across benchmarks.
Conflict between two stable molecular structures during training causes structural chaos and degrades performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail to learn effective long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning from human or non-Long-CoT LLMs imitation. To understand this, we propose that effective and learnable Long CoT trajectories feature stable molecular-like structures in unified view, which are formed by three interaction types: Deep-Reasoning (covalent-like), Self-Reflection (hydrogen-bond-like), and Self-Exploration (van der Waals-like). Analysis of distilled trajectories reveals these structures emerge from Long CoT fine-tuning, not keyword imitation. We introduce Effective Semantic Isomers and show that only bonds promoting fast entropy convergence support stable Long CoT learning, while structural competition impairs training. Drawing on these findings, we present Mole-Syn, a distribution-transfer-graph method that guides synthesis of effective Long CoT structures, boosting performance and RL stability across benchmarks.

papers.title: Integrating Evolutionary and Compositional Features with ML and DL for Robust and Interpretable Druggable Protein Prediction
papers.research_question: How can evolutionary and compositional features be integrated with machine learning and deep learning for robust and interpretable druggable protein prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hybrid feature representation combining Average Block-based PSSM and Dipeptide Composition for druggable protein prediction, achieving high accuracy with statistical validation and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid feature representation enables strong predictive performance for druggable protein prediction, with SVM and CapsBiLSTM achieving high accuracy and AUC scores, validated statistically, and providing interpretable insights into sequence descriptors.
papers.key_findings:
Hybrid features (AB-PSSM + DPC) significantly outperform individual descriptors in predicting druggable proteins.
SVM and CapsBiLSTM models achieve classification accuracies above 90% and ROC-AUC/PR-AUC scores above 95%.
Statistical tests (DeLong's test, McNemar's test, bootstrap confidence intervals) confirm the robustness and significance of the improvements.
Interpretability analyses using SHAP and t-SNE reveal biologically significant sequence descriptors influencing druggability.
The proposed framework outperforms existing machine learning and ensemble-based methods in accuracy and interpretability.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Druggable proteins are essential targets in contemporary therapeutic discovery, and their precise identification is necessary for the progression of rational drug design. Traditional biochemical screening techniques are costly, laborious, and protracted, whereas current computational models typically attain only moderate efficacy and seldom offer robust statistical validation or biological interpretability. To mitigate these limitations, we offer a hybrid computational approach that amalgamates evolutionary and compositional information by merging Average Block-based Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (AB-PSSM) characteristics with Dipeptide Composition (DPC) into a 600-dimensional representation. The hybrid feature space was assessed utilizing three machine learning algorithms (support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) alongside three deep learning architectures (CapsBiLSTM, ResCapsNetPlus, and ResNet1D) following a rigorous five-fold out-of-fold cross-validation protocol to guarantee fairness and reproducibility. A thorough assessment revealed that the hybrid attributes significantly surpassed individual descriptors, with the SVM and CapsBiLSTM classifiers attaining classification accuracies of 90% and ROC-AUC and PR-AUC values surpassing 95%. The robustness and reliability were further validated by statistical analyses, including DeLong’s test, McNemar’s test, and bootstrap confidence intervals, demonstrating that the observed enhancements were substantial and consistent. Furthermore, interpretability investigations employing SHAP feature attribution and t-SNE visualization underscored biologically significant sequence descriptors as pivotal factors influencing druggability, thus mitigating the "black box" constraint inherent in numerous deep learning methodologies. This study presents a statistically validated, interpretable, and high-performing framework for predicting druggable proteins, which outperforms current machine learning and ensemble-based methods, establishing a clear basis for future applications in precision medicine and drug discovery.

papers.title: Neural Networks Trained to Solve Differential Equations Learn General Representations
papers.research_question: How can we measure the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks? What is the generality structure of layers in neural networks trained to solve differential equations?
papers.core_contribution: We develop an efficient method using SVCCA to measure layer generality across continuously-parametrized tasks, and apply it to show that in neural networks trained to solve differential equations, the first layer is general and deeper layers are successively more specific.
papers.conclusion: We presented a method for measuring layer generality using SVCCA, found that first layers of DENNs are general and deeper layers are more specific, validated with transfer learning, and visualized the general components as generalized coordinates.
papers.key_findings:
The first hidden layer is general, and deeper layers become progressively more specific.
The SVCCA-based method agrees with transfer learning experiments but is much faster, especially for continuously-parametrized problems.
The general components of the first layer can be visualized as generalized coordinates that capture regions of interest in the input domain.
Network width affects layer generality: intrinsic dimensionality saturates with width, reproducibility increases with width, and specificity varies with width and layer depth.
Very wide networks may have training dynamics that affect convergence and generality measurements.
papers.limitation:
SVCCA is numerically unstable when correlation values are very close to each other, making component sorting ill-conditioned.
Very wide networks may have broad minima in the loss landscape, causing training to terminate before optimal convergence, potentially affecting generality measurements.
future_direction: Explore the behavior of layer generality at very large network widths.
Develop component analyses that search for closely-coupled components to improve numerical stability.
Investigate different training protocols for very wide DENNs to ensure proper convergence.
papers.abstract: We introduce a technique based on the singular vector canonical correlation analysis (SVCCA) for measuring the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks. We illustrate this method by studying generality in neural networks trained to solve parametrized boundary value problems based on the Poisson partial differential equation. We find that the first hidden layer is general, and that deeper layers are successively more specific. Next, we validate our method against an existing technique that measures layer generality using transfer learning experiments. We find excellent agreement between the two methods, and note that our method is much faster, particularly for continuously-parametrized problems. Finally, we visualize the general representations of the first layers, and interpret them as generalized coordinates over the input domain.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Comparing the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.research_question: How do different universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) encode chemical information in their latent features, and how do these encodings compare across models, training datasets, and training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically analyzes the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) using feature reconstruction errors, revealing that different models encode chemical information in distinct ways and that these differences can be quantified.
papers.conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize atomistic ML models; feature reconstruction error metrics provide a principled foundation for more transparent, interpretable, and robust model design.
papers.key_findings:
uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors.
When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol.
Fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features.
Atom-level features can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information.
Backbone features contain more information than last-layer features and are more consistent across models.
papers.abstract: The past few years have seen the development of ``universal'' machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) capable of approximating the ground-state potential energy surface across a wide range of chemical structures and compositions with reasonable accuracy. While these models differ in the architecture and the dataset used, they share the ability to compress a staggering amount of chemical information into descriptive latent features. Herein, we systematically analyze what the different uMLIPs have learned by quantitatively assessing the relative information content of their latent features with feature reconstruction errors, and observing how the trends are affected by the choice of training set and training protocol. We find that uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors. When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol of choice. We also observe that fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features. Finally, we discuss how atom-level features, which are directly output by MLIPs, can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information about the variability across the atomic environments within a given system.

papers.title: Interpretation of machine learning models using shapley values: application to compound potency and multi-target activity predictions
papers.research_question: How can Shapley values (SHAP) be used to interpret machine learning models, and how does the model-independent kernel SHAP compare to the exact tree SHAP for decision tree models? Additionally, how can SHAP be applied to interpret compound potency predictions and multi-target activity predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper evaluates and applies the SHAP methodology for interpreting machine learning models in chemoinformatics, demonstrating that kernel SHAP provides reliable approximations compared to exact tree SHAP, and shows SHAP's utility for interpreting compound potency predictions and multi-target activity predictions.
papers.conclusion: The SHAP methodology enables interpretation of ML models and their predictions, providing feature importance values for individual predictions. The kernel SHAP approach is generally applicable and yields reliable approximations compared to exact tree SHAP, shedding light on the black box nature of ML models for practical applications in drug discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Kernel SHAP and tree SHAP yield highly correlated feature importance rankings for decision tree-based models in activity and potency prediction.
SHAP analysis provides meaningful explanations for compound potency predictions and multi-target activity predictions, revealing features that drive model decisions.
SHAP helps rationalize model errors by identifying features whose absence or presence leads to incorrect predictions.
papers.limitation: SHAP-based feature prioritization identifies features that determine ML predictions, but these features may not always be responsible for specific activities.

papers.title: DeepFRI Demystified: Interpretability vs. Accuracy in AI Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How interpretable and robust is the DeepFRI model for protein function prediction, and how do different explainability methods compare in highlighting influential residues?
papers.core_contribution: The study reveals that DeepFRI's predictions prioritize conserved structural motifs over functional residues, and different explainability methods offer varying levels of granularity, highlighting trade-offs between accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DeepFRI has strengths in conserved domains but limitations in complex proteins, and interpretability methods must be chosen carefully to balance robustness and precision for biological insights.
papers.key_findings:
DeepFRI's predictions often prioritize structural motifs like beta sheets over functional residues, leading to potential misinterpretations.
GradCAM provides broad heatmaps with low sparsity, Excitation Backpropagation offers binary masks with high sparsity, and PGExplainer gives precise per-residue scores.
The model is robust to mutations, requiring over 200 mutations in some cases to cause misclassification, but this may overlook biologically significant changes.
Sparsity analysis shows that explainability methods vary significantly, with GradCAM being the least sparse and Excitation Backpropagation the most sparse.
Using an ensemble of explainability methods can highlight high-confidence residues and areas of epistemic uncertainty.
papers.limitation:
DeepFRI prioritizes structural motifs over functional residues, potentially leading to inaccurate interpretations of protein function.
The model's robustness to mutations may cause it to overlook biologically significant changes unless a large fraction of the structure is disrupted.
DeepFRI's message-passing can overlook long-range or allosteric effects in complex regulatory proteins.
future_direction: Guide experimental validation through targeted mutagenesis based on explainability results.
Fuse GCN topology with per-residue embeddings from protein language models for improved sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Machine learning technologies for protein function prediction are black box models. Despite their potential to identify key drug targets with high accuracy and accelerate therapy development, the adoption of these methods depends on verifying their findings. This study evaluates DeepFRI, a leading Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) based tool, using advanced explainability techniques (GradCAM, Excitation Backpropagation, and PGExplainer) and adversarial robustness tests. Our findings reveal that the model's predictions often prioritize conserved motifs over truly deterministic residues, complicating the identification of functional sites. Quantitative analyses show that explainability methods differ significantly in granularity, with GradCAM providing broad relevance and PGExplainer pinpointing specific active sites. These results highlight tradeoffs between accuracy and interpretability, suggesting areas for improvement in DeepFRI's architecture to enhance its trustworthiness in drug discovery and regulatory settings.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Analysis of a convolutional neural network for predicting unsteady volume wake flow fields
papers.research_question: How does a convolutional neural network system learn and predict three-dimensional unsteady wake flow dynamics in different flow regimes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a multi-scale CNN system for predicting 3D unsteady wake flow and investigates its mechanisms, showing that convolution layers integrate and transport wavenumber information to extract flow structures, and that redundant feature maps can be identified and removed to reduce model size without loss of performance.
papers.conclusion: The CNN system predicts wake flow by integrating and transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers, extracting representations of flow dynamics. Redundant feature maps can be removed based on structural similarity, significantly reducing model size without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN system predicts flow in different regimes by transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers.
Feature maps extract similar flow structures (e.g., braid shear layers and shedding vortices) across different Reynolds numbers.
Convolution layers integrate information from all input flow variables and histories, with more recent histories having larger contributions.
Redundant feature maps can be identified using structural similarity (SSIM) and removed, reducing the number of weights by 85% without affecting prediction performance.
papers.abstract: A predictive convolutional neural network is developed to predict the future of three-dimensional unsteady wake flow from past information of flow velocity and pressure. The developed network is found to be capable of predicting vortex dynamics at distinctive flow regimes with flow structures at different scales. Mechanisms of the network on predicting vortex dynamics at two distinctive flow regimes, the mode-B shedding regime and the turbulent wake regime, are investigated. Information in feature maps of the network is visualized and quantitatively assessed to investigate the encoded flow structures. A Fourier analysis is conducted to investigate the mechanisms of the network on learning fluid motions with distinctive flow scales. The transformation of information from the input to prediction layers of the network is tracked to examine how the network transforms the input information for prediction. Structural similarities among feature maps in the network are evaluated to reduce the number of feature maps containing redundant flow structures, which allows reduction of the size of the network without affecting prediction performance.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
