Finally, we analyse how the models behave with regard to biases and imbalances in the dataset.

papers.title: Bilinear MLPs enable weight-based mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: Can bilinear MLPs, which lack element-wise nonlinearities, enable weight-based mechanistic interpretability by allowing decomposition of their weights into interpretable components?
papers.core_contribution: Bilinear MLPs enable weight-based mechanistic interpretability by allowing their weights to be decomposed into interpretable components (e.g., via eigendecomposition), and they can serve as a drop-in replacement for standard MLPs with minimal performance cost.
papers.conclusion: Bilinear MLPs offer intrinsic interpretability due to their lack of element-wise nonlinearities, and weight-based interpretability is viable for understanding deep-learning models.
papers.key_findings:
Bilinear MLPs can be decomposed into interpretable eigenvectors that reveal low-rank structure across tasks.
In image classification, top eigenvectors correspond to semantically meaningful features (e.g., digit strokes, edge detectors).
The eigenvectors are consistent across training runs and model sizes, and truncating smaller eigenvalues preserves performance.
In language models, weight decomposition can identify nonlinear circuits (e.g., a sentiment negation circuit) directly from the weights.
Bilinear MLPs achieve competitive performance compared to standard MLPs (e.g., SwiGLU) when training time is constant.
papers.limitation:
Application of the methods typically relies on having a set of meaningful output directions available (e.g., from sparse autoencoders), which are dependent on an input dataset.
There are no guarantees the eigenvectors will be monosemantic, and orthogonality constraints may limit interpretability for high-rank spectra.
future_direction: Applying sparse dictionary learning approaches to decompose the bilinear tensor to relax the orthogonality constraint and find interpretable features from model weights.
papers.abstract: A mechanistic understanding of how MLPs do computation in deep neural networks remains elusive. Current interpretability work can extract features from hidden activations over an input dataset but generally cannot explain how MLP weights construct features. One challenge is that element-wise nonlinearities introduce higher-order interactions and make it difficult to trace computations through the MLP layer. In this paper, we analyze bilinear MLPs, a type of Gated Linear Unit (GLU) without any element-wise nonlinearity that nevertheless achieves competitive performance. Bilinear MLPs can be fully expressed in terms of linear operations using a third-order tensor, allowing flexible analysis of the weights. Analyzing the spectra of bilinear MLP weights using eigendecomposition reveals interpretable low-rank structure across toy tasks, image classification, and language modeling. We use this understanding to craft adversarial examples, uncover overfitting, and identify small language model circuits directly from the weights alone. Our results demonstrate that bilinear layers serve as an interpretable drop-in replacement for current activation functions and that weight-based interpretability is viable for understanding deep-learning models.

papers.title: Convolutional neural networks can identify brain interactions involved in decoding spatial auditory attention
papers.research_question: Can a convolutional neural network (CNN) be designed to learn task-specific interactions between brain regions from source-reconstructed EEG data to decode spatial auditory attention, rather than being used as a black box decoder?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretable CNN architecture that learns pairwise interactions between brain regions from source-reconstructed EEG data to decode spatial auditory attention, and demonstrates that this model identifies known important neural interactions and frequency bands.
papers.conclusion: The CNN model can effectively utilize features known to be important in auditory attention tasks, suggesting that domain knowledge-inspired CNNs applied to source-reconstructed EEG data offer a novel computational framework for studying task-relevant brain interactions.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model achieved median decoding accuracies of 77.56% (within-participant) and 65.14% (cross-participant) for spatial auditory attention.
Analysis of the model's spatial filters revealed alpha-band-dominated inter-hemisphere interactions and alpha- and beta-band dominant interactions that were hemisphere-specific or showed contrasting patterns between hemispheres.
These interactions were more pronounced in parietal and central regions for within-participant decoding, and in parietal, central, and partly frontal regions for cross-participant decoding.
Ablation analysis showed that parietal, temporal, and central brain regions are important for decoding performance.
Removing alpha and beta frequency bands from the input data significantly decreased model performance, indicating their key role.
papers.limitation:
The CNN architecture may not be deep enough to capture longer temporal structures (e.g., delta and theta frequencies), and increasing depth could lead to overfitting due to limited data.
Decoding performance varied across participants, which may be related to the relatively low number of trials per participant and the small overall number of participants.
The use of 64-channel EEG for source reconstruction may yield less precise localization compared to high-density EEG or MEG systems.
future_direction: Future research may use more data, employ data augmentation techniques, utilize more flexible CNN architectures, and/or include behavioral data to account for inter-individual heterogeneity.
Future studies may explore other architectures to adapt the model to brain dynamics, such as incorporating attention layers or graph convolutional neural networks.
Future work could develop a CNN model that integrates both stimulus information (e.g., speech envelopes) and EEG signals to decode auditory attention and study entrainment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Human listeners have the ability to direct their attention to a single speaker in a multi-talker environment. The neural correlates of selective attention can be decoded from a single trial of electroencephalography (EEG) data. In this study, leveraging the source-reconstructed and anatomically-resolved EEG data as inputs, we sought to employ CNN as an interpretable model to uncover task-specific interactions between brain regions, rather than simply to utilize it as a black box decoder. To this end, our CNN model was specifically designed to learn pairwise interaction representations for 10 cortical regions from five-second inputs. By exclusively utilizing these features for decoding, our model was able to attain a median accuracy of 77.56% for within-participant and 65.14% for cross-participant classification. Through ablation analysis together with dissecting the features of the models and applying cluster analysis, we were able to discern the presence of alpha-band-dominated inter-hemisphere interactions, as well as alpha- and beta-band dominant interactions that were either hemisphere-specific or were characterized by a contrasting pattern between the right and left hemispheres. These interactions were more pronounced in parietal and central regions for within-participant decoding, but in parietal, central, and partly frontal regions for cross-participant decoding. These findings demonstrate that our CNN model can effectively utilize features known to be important in auditory attention tasks and suggest that the application of domain knowledge inspired CNNs on source-reconstructed EEG data can offer a novel computational framework for studying task-relevant brain interactions.

papers.title: Revealing structure components of the retina by deep learning networks
papers.research_question: What types of network structure components can be revealed by CNNs when they are used to model the single retinal ganglion cell (RGC) response?
papers.core_contribution: CNNs trained to predict neural responses of single retinal ganglion cells learn convolutional filters that resemble biological subunits in the retinal circuit, suggesting CNNs can reveal structural components of neuronal circuits.
papers.conclusion: CNNs can learn interpretable parameters that correspond to biological underpinnings, and this approach can be used to reveal network structure components in neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model can predict the receptive field of retinal ganglion cells well.
The learned convolutional filters in CNN resemble the subunits in the RGC model.
For biological RGC data, the learned conv filters converge to localized subunits comparable to bipolar cells.
The features represented by these filters tile the receptive field of the RGC.
The CNN model achieves good prediction performance (CC up to 0.75) for biological RGC responses.
future_direction: Applying the approach to transfer learning
papers.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated impressive performance on visual object classification tasks. In addition, it is a useful model for predication of neuronal responses recorded in visual system. However, there is still no clear understanding of what CNNs learn in terms of visual neuronal circuits. Visualizing CNN's features to obtain possible connections to neuronscience underpinnings is not easy due to highly complex circuits from the retina to higher visual cortex. Here we address this issue by focusing on single retinal ganglion cells with a simple model and electrophysiological recordings from salamanders. By training CNNs with white noise images to predicate neural responses, we found that convolutional filters learned in the end are resembling to biological components of the retinal circuit. Features represented by these filters tile the space of conventional receptive field of retinal ganglion cells. These results suggest that CNN could be used to reveal structure components of neuronal circuits.

papers.title: Unsupervised Generative Learning and Native Explanatory Frameworks
papers.research_question: Whether native information structures emergent in unsupervised generative training can be used as an explanatory framework for learning processes in unsupervised systems, with possible extension to supervised cases.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that native concept frameworks emergent in unsupervised generative training can serve as a natural platform for explaining learning processes, based on similarity relationships in latent representations.
papers.conclusion: Native concept frameworks that emerge in unsupervised generative training can be used as a basis for explainability of learning in deep neural network models, offering a geometrical approach based on similarity relationships.
papers.key_findings:
Native density clusters are identified in the latent representation with specific characteristics like number, population, and density.
Native classifiers trained on these clusters show high accuracy (F1-score above 95%) without labeled data.
There is clear association between native clusters and external concepts, as shown in cross-population matrices.
Native classifiers can achieve good classification results for external concepts like fields, woods, and water without labeled samples.
The framework allows for explanation of learning decisions based on proximity in latent space.
future_direction: Developing methods and instruments for analyzing effective latent representations in more complex models.
Extending the framework to supervised learning cases.
Exploring environment-driven processes for associating external concepts with native clusters, similar to biological learning.
papers.abstract: A framework of native concepts emergent in unsupervised generative training under the constraints of redundancy reduction and generative accuracy was observed and investigated with an unsupervised generative neural network model and real-world image data. Characteristics of concept distributions in the latent representations were measured and possibility of effective learning with identiﬁed density structure demonstrated. We discuss the potential of using frameworks of native information clusters in the effective latent representations of learning models as a natural platform for explanation of learning processes in machine and biological systems based on the relations and criteria of native similarity that form in the process of generative learning under certain constraints. This approach can be general, intuitive and independent of speciﬁc architectures and types of data.

papers.title: Re-envisioning Euclid Galaxy Morphology: Identifying and Interpreting Features with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) efficiently identify interpretable features from pretrained neural networks for galaxy morphology, and how do they compare to PCA?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs are effective for extracting interpretable features from neural network embeddings of galaxy images, revealing morphological concepts beyond existing human-defined taxonomies and showing stronger alignment with expert labels than PCA.
papers.conclusion: Although challenges in interpretability remain, SAEs provide a powerful engine for discovering astrophysical phenomena beyond the confines of human-defined classification.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features show stronger alignment with Galaxy Zoo labels than PCA features for both supervised and self-supervised embeddings, especially beyond the top few components.
SAEs can identify interpretable morphological features outside the Galaxy Zoo decision tree, such as dust lanes in edge-on disk galaxies and elliptical galaxies with bluer companions.
The self-supervised MAE achieves superhuman reconstruction performance on masked galaxy images, indicating it extracts meaningful features.
SAE features remain interpretable and aligned with Galaxy Zoo even beyond the top 64 features, whereas PCA features become noisy and unidentifiable.
For self-supervised embeddings, SAE features are moderately predictable from Galaxy Zoo labels, suggesting they capture artifact-related information.
papers.limitation: Some SAE features remain difficult to interpret.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can efficiently identify candidate monosemantic features from pretrained neural networks for galaxy morphology. We demonstrate this on Euclid Q1 images using both supervised (Zoobot) and new self-supervised (MAE) models. Our publicly released MAE achieves superhuman image reconstruction performance. While a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the supervised model primarily identifies features already aligned with the Galaxy Zoo decision tree, SAEs can identify interpretable features outside of this framework. SAE features also show stronger alignment than PCA with Galaxy Zoo labels. Although challenges in interpretability remain, SAEs provide a powerful engine for discovering astrophysical phenomena beyond the confines of human-defined classification.

papers.title: Letters of the Alphabet: Discovering Natural Feature Sets
papers.research_question: How do hidden layers in a simple neural network represent input features, and how can natural feature sets be derived from the data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how hidden node activations in a neural network can be visualized to understand feature representation and how natural feature sets can be discovered by grouping similar inputs.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide a step-by-step blueprint for how neural networks derive natural feature sets from data, offering insights into feature representation in hidden layers.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden nodes in the network activate to specific features like vertical and horizontal bars in letter representations.
Nodes 2 and 5 are activated strongly by most letters, indicating potential overfitting or redundancy.
Natural feature sets group similarly shaped letters, such as A and H, or B, R, and P.
Adding 10% noise did not improve generalization in the natural feature sets experiment.
Heatmap visualizations effectively show which input patterns contribute to hidden node activations.
papers.limitation:
Adding 10% noise did not help the hidden nodes generalize better as expected.
Deciphering and visualizing hidden node activations took a lot of time and explanation.
future_direction: Spend more time formatting visualizations to efficiently display hidden node activations for natural feature sets.
Use algorithms to automatically determine the ideal number of hidden nodes to speed up development.
papers.abstract: Deep learning networks find intricate features in large datasets using the backpropagation algorithm. This algorithm repeatedly adjusts the network connections.' weights and examining the "hidden" nodes behavior between the input and output layer provides better insight into how neural networks create feature representations. Experiments built on each other show that activity differences computed within a layer can guide learning. A simple neural network is used, which includes a data set comprised of the alphabet letters, where each letter forms 81 input nodes comprised of 0 and 1s and a single hidden layer and an output layer. The first experiment explains how the hidden layers in this simple neural network represent the input data's features. The second experiment attempts to reverse-engineer the neural network to find the alphabet's natural feature sets. As the network interprets features, we can understand how it derives the natural feature sets for a given data. This understanding is essential to delve deeper into deep generative models, such as Boltzmann machines. Deep generative models are a class of unsupervised deep learning algorithms. The primary function of deep generative models is to find the natural feature sets for a given data set.

papers.title: Mapping Knowledge Representations to Concepts: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: How do current methods extract internal knowledge representations in a neural network and map them to human-understandable concepts? Can Deductive-Nomological (D-N) explanation taxonomy and causal types of explanations be useful in order to analyse what can be expected, and not expected, from knowledge representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a targeted review of research that aims to associate internal neural network representations with human understandable concepts, and proposes using Deductive-Nomological explanations and theories of causality as a taxonomy to understand the capabilities and limitations of such explanations.
papers.conclusion: The review raises important questions about the goal of explanations and the type of knowledge extractable from neural networks, emphasizing the need to differentiate between understanding the trained model and providing actionable decisions. It argues for involving users to emphasize contextual dependence and refocus research on the limitations of ML systems.
papers.key_findings:
Methods for extracting knowledge representations are dominated by two approaches: Feature Based Attribution (FBA) for local understanding and Internal Knowledge Representation (IKR) extraction for global understanding.
There is an ambiguity in the goal of model explainability: understanding the ML model versus providing actionable explanations in the deployment domain.
The reviewed research lacks user studies, despite heavy reliance on human abilities to compare images and infer concepts.
Explanations that aim for intervention or counterfactual reasoning rely on causal relations, but these are only valid for the ML model in isolation and not necessarily for the real-world domain.
The Deductive-Nomological explanation taxonomy is found useful for analyzing what can be expected from neural network explanations, highlighting that current methods typically aim for kind-data or model-data relations, not theory-data or entity-data relations.
papers.limitation:
The choice to use the D-N model and Overton's schematic overview delimits the type of explanations aimed for and excludes pragmatic, inductive statistical, teleological, and historical explanations.
The understanding of the concept 'concept' is not well-grounded from an ontological and epistemological perspective.
future_direction: Conducting user studies that actively involve users to emphasize contextual dependence.
Combining IKR and FBA methods in studies aiming for a global meta-perspective of model understanding.

Using scientific explanations and theories to formulate falsifiable hypotheses and evaluate how well a trained ML model models the usage domain, moving beyond the idea that more data solves the problem of induction.
papers.abstract: The success of neural networks builds to a large extent on their ability to create internal knowledge representations from real-world high-dimensional data, such as images, sound, or text. Approaches to extract and present these representations, in order to explain the neural network's decisions, is an active and multifaceted research field. To gain a deeper understanding of a central aspect of this field, we have performed a targeted review focusing on research that aims to associate internal representations with human understandable concepts. In doing this, we added a perspective on the existing research by using primarily deductive nomological explanations as a proposed taxonomy. We find this taxonomy and theories of causality, useful for understanding what can be expected, and not expected, from neural network explanations. The analysis additionally uncovers an ambiguity in the reviewed literature related to the goal of model explainability; is it understanding the ML model or, is it actionable explanations useful in the deployment domain?

papers.title: Evaluation and development of deep neural networks for RNA 5-Methyluridine classifications using autoBioSeqpy
papers.research_question: Which deep learning architecture is best suited for predicting RNA 5-methyluridine (m5U) modification sites, and how can an improved model be developed and interpreted?
papers.core_contribution: The paper performs a comparative evaluation of deep learning models for RNA m5U site classification, develops an improved CNN-BiLSTM model called Deepm5U, and demonstrates the use of interpretability techniques (LayerUMAP and DeepSHAP) to gain insights into model behavior.
papers.conclusion: Deep learning is effective for accurately predicting RNA m5U modification sites, and the use of interpretability techniques provides valuable insights into model mechanisms. The autoBioSeqpy framework facilitates the development and analysis of such models.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN-BiLSTM hybrid architecture achieved the best prediction performance for m5U site classification among the evaluated models.
Deepm5U, the developed CNN-BiLSTM model, outperformed the existing method m5UPred on benchmark datasets.
Interpretability techniques like LayerUMAP revealed how internal representations evolve to separate m5U and non-m5U sites across network layers.
DeepSHAP analysis identified nucleotide positions and features that contribute most to the model's classification decisions.
The model demonstrated robust performance in cross-cell-type and cross-sequencing-technology validations.
future_direction: Extending the strategy to facilitate the study of other RNA modifications.
papers.abstract: Post-transcriptionally RNA modifications, also known as the epitranscriptome, play crucial roles in the regulation of gene expression during development. Recently, deep learning (DL) has been employed for RNA modification site prediction and has shown promising results. However, due to the lack of relevant studies, it is unclear which DL architecture is best suited for some pyrimidine modifications, such as 5-methyluridine (m<sup>5</sup>U). To fill this knowledge gap, we first performed a comparative evaluation of various commonly used DL models for epigenetic studies with the help of autoBioSeqpy. We identified optimal architectural variations for m<sup>5</sup>U site classification, optimizing the layer depth and neuron width. Second, we used this knowledge to develop Deepm5U, an improved convolutional-recurrent neural network that accurately predicts m<sup>5</sup>U sites from RNA sequences. We successfully applied Deepm5U to transcriptomewide m<sup>5</sup>U profiling data across different sequencing technologies and cell types. Third, we showed that the techniques for interpreting deep neural networks, including LayerUMAP and DeepSHAP, can provide important insights into the internal operation and behavior of models. Overall, we offered practical guidance for the development, benchmark, and analysis of deep learning models when designing new algorithms for RNA modifications.

papers.title: Discovering and Steering Interpretable Concepts in Large Generative Music Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and interpret the internal concepts learned by autoregressive music generation models, and can we use these concepts to steer generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline using sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable concepts in autoregressive music models, and shows that these concepts can be used to steer generation.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility and potential of using sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable concepts in large music generative models, offering a scalable path towards understanding how these models represent and generate music.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can discover both familiar musical concepts (e.g., genres, instruments) and novel coherent patterns lacking clear theoretical description.
Later layers in the model encode more interpretable features on average, as measured by CLAP alignment with automatic labels.
Larger models (MusicGen-Large) produce features that are more distinctive by layer compared to smaller models (MusicGen-Small).
Automated labeling using Essentia classifiers and multimodal LLMs (Gemini) can label thousands of features at scale, with Essentia tags achieving higher human confidence.
A non-trivial fraction (15-35%) of discovered features can be used to steer model generations, altering outputs toward the intended concept.
papers.limitation: The analysis focuses on unconditional audio representations, not text-conditioned activations, which limits understanding of how prompts influence internal concepts.
future_direction: Extending the method to text-conditioned activations and multimodal interpretability.
Building a comprehensive understanding of how neural networks represent and generate music.
papers.abstract: The fidelity with which neural networks can now generate content such as music presents a scientific opportunity: these systems appear to have learned implicit theories of such content's structure through statistical learning alone. This offers a potentially new lens on theories of human-generated media. When internal representations align with traditional constructs (e.g. chord progressions in music), they show how such categories can emerge from statistical regularities; when they diverge, they expose limits of existing frameworks and patterns we may have overlooked but that nonetheless carry explanatory power. In this paper, focusing on music generators, we introduce a method for discovering interpretable concepts using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), extracting interpretable features from the residual stream of a transformer model. We make this approach scalable and evaluable using automated labeling and validation pipelines. Our results reveal both familiar musical concepts and coherent but uncodified patterns lacking clear counterparts in theory or language. As an extension, we show such concepts can be used to steer model generations. Beyond improving model transparency, our work provides an empirical tool for uncovering organizing principles that have eluded traditional methods of analysis and synthesis.

papers.title: Circuit Insights: Towards Interpretability Beyond Activations
papers.research_question: How can we move beyond activation-based interpretability by using weight-based and circuit-based analysis to understand model computations, removing dependence on explainer LLMs and datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces WeightLens and CircuitLens, two complementary methods for automated interpretability that go beyond activation analysis by using model weights and circuit-level dynamics, reducing dependence on external LLMs and datasets.
papers.conclusion: WeightLens and CircuitLens advance automated interpretability by moving beyond activations, providing more robust and scalable circuit analysis while maintaining efficiency and quality.
papers.key_findings:
WeightLens matches or exceeds activation-based methods for token-based features without needing explainer LLMs or datasets.
CircuitLens captures context-dependent features and circuit-level dynamics that activation-only methods miss.
Combining weight-based and circuit-based information improves robustness and handles polysemanticity through clustering.
Interpretability of features varies with layer depth, with early and late layers being more interpretable than middle layers.
Faithfulness scores are low across methods, suggesting individual feature interventions may not strongly affect outputs due to model redundancy.
papers.limitation:
Faithfulness is low across layers and methods, likely due to model redundancy; evaluating interventions on groups of features or entire circuits might be more trustworthy.
The validation step in WeightLens does not always succeed, as some weight-based connections are meaningful only in context and cannot be validated with single-token forward passes.
future_direction: Modifying the faithfulness metric to evaluate interventions on groups of features or entire circuits.
Exploring evaluation-guided refinement of clustering parameters and results in CircuitLens.
papers.abstract: The fields of explainable AI and mechanistic interpretability aim to uncover the internal structure of neural networks, with circuit discovery as a central tool for understanding model computations. Existing approaches, however, rely on manual inspection and remain limited to toy tasks. Automated interpretability offers scalability by analyzing isolated features and their activations, but it often misses interactions between features and depends strongly on external LLMs and dataset quality. Transcoders have recently made it possible to separate feature attributions into input-dependent and input-invariant components, providing a foundation for more systematic circuit analysis. Building on this, we propose WeightLens and CircuitLens, two complementary methods that go beyond activation-based analysis. WeightLens interprets features directly from their learned weights, removing the need for explainer models or datasets while matching or exceeding the performance of existing methods on context-independent features. CircuitLens captures how feature activations arise from interactions between components, revealing circuit-level dynamics that activation-only approaches cannot identify. Together, these methods increase interpretability robustness and enhance scalable mechanistic analysis of circuits while maintaining efficiency and quality.

papers.title: Unboxing the Black Box: Mechanistic Interpretability for Algorithmic Understanding of Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified taxonomy of mechanistic interpretability approaches, situates MI within the broader XAI landscape, and surveys key techniques and literature in the field.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems and invites new researchers into the field.
papers.key_findings:
The field of mechanistic interpretability has grown rapidly since 2020.
MI faces challenges such as superposition, spurious correlations, scalability, and evaluation problems.
MI offers opportunities for debugging, data privacy, robustness, control, human-in-the-loop, and trustworthiness.
future_direction: The need for standardized evaluation techniques.
Scaling up MI techniques to larger models.
Applying MI in real-world domains like finance and medicine.
papers.abstract: The black box nature of deep neural networks poses a significant challenge for the deployment of transparent and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) systems. With the growing presence of AI in society, it becomes increasingly important to develop methods that can explain and interpret the decisions made by these systems. To address this, mechanistic interpretability (MI) emerged as a promising and distinctive research program within the broader field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). MI is the process of studying the inner computations of neural networks and translating them into human-understandable algorithms. It encompasses reverse engineering techniques aimed at uncovering the computational algorithms implemented by neural networks. In this article, we propose a unified taxonomy of MI approaches and provide a detailed analysis of key techniques, illustrated with concrete examples and pseudo-code. We contextualize MI within the broader interpretability landscape, comparing its goals, methods, and insights to other strands of XAI. Additionally, we trace the development of MI as a research area, highlighting its conceptual roots and the accelerating pace of recent work. We argue that MI holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems -- treating models not only as tools for solving tasks, but also as systems to be studied and understood. We hope to invite new researchers into the field of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Is This Just Fantasy? Language Model Representations Reflect Human Judgments of Event Plausibility
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable)? How do these representations develop, do they reflect human categorization behavior, and what interpretable features do they correspond to?
papers.core_contribution: Language models form linear representations (modal difference vectors) that distinguish between modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable). These vectors are more diagnostic than output probabilities, emerge in an intuitive order during training, and reflect fine-grained human categorization behavior and interpretable features like event likelihood and imageability.
papers.conclusion: Language models learn internal representations of modal categories that go beyond output probabilities. These representations develop in an intuitive order and capture nuanced aspects of human categorization, offering a novel way to study world models in LMs and potentially human cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Modal difference vectors within LM hidden states reliably classify sentences by modal category, outperforming classification based on sentence probability.
Modal difference vectors develop in a consistent order: inconceivable vs. others emerges first, followed by probable vs. impossible, then probable vs. improbable, and finally improbable vs. impossible.
Projections of sentences onto modal difference vectors create a feature space that accurately models human participants' graded categorization judgments.
Projections along the impossible-inconceivable vector correlate selectively with human ratings of imageability and the presence of physical objects/places.
Preliminary steering experiments show that adding modal difference vectors to the residual stream during generation can influence the modal category of the generated text.
future_direction: Using modal difference vectors to test the intuitive theories about the world that LMs encode from text.
Using modal difference vectors to generate hypotheses about human representations of modal categories, such as the role of imagination in distinguishing impossible from inconceivable events.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are used for a diverse range of tasks, from question answering to writing fantastical stories. In order to reliably accomplish these tasks, LMs must be able to discern the modal category of a sentence (i.e., whether it describes something that is possible, impossible, completely nonsensical, etc.). However, recent studies have called into question the ability of LMs to categorize sentences according to modality (Michaelov et al., 2025; Kauf et al., 2023). In this work, we identify linear representations that discriminate between modal categories within a variety of LMs, or modal difference vectors. Analysis of modal difference vectors reveals that LMs have access to more reliable modal categorization judgments than previously reported. Furthermore, we find that modal difference vectors emerge in a consistent order as models become more competent (i.e., through training steps, layers, and parameter count). Notably, we find that modal difference vectors identified within LM activations can be used to model fine-grained human categorization behavior. This potentially provides a novel view into how human participants distinguish between modal categories, which we explore by correlating projections along modal difference vectors with human participants' ratings of interpretable features. In summary, we derive new insights into LM modal categorization using techniques from mechanistic interpretability, with the potential to inform our understanding of modal categorization in humans.

papers.title: Hierarchical Sparse Circuit Extraction from Billion-Parameter Language Models through Scalable Attribution Graph Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can sparse computational circuits be efficiently extracted from billion-parameter language models using hierarchical decomposition and attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD), a framework that reduces circuit discovery complexity from exponential to polynomial, enabling extraction of interpretable circuits from billion-parameter models with high behavioral preservation.
papers.conclusion: HAGD enables circuit extraction from large models with preserved behavior, but limitations include incomplete attention modeling, reconstruction residuals, and interpretability challenges for large circuits.
papers.key_findings:
HAGD reduces circuit discovery complexity to O(n^2 log n) and extracts circuits from models up to 70B parameters.
Behavioral preservation ranges from 82% to 97% on algorithmic tasks and 74% to 88% on natural language benchmarks.
Cross-architecture transfer shows 52%-82% structural similarity, indicating shared computational patterns.
Circuit size grows sublinearly with model parameters, but natural language tasks yield larger, less modular circuits.
The method outperforms baselines like ACDC in scalability while maintaining comparable circuit quality.
papers.limitation:
Attention circuits are not modeled, leaving significant computational pathways unanalyzed.
Reconstruction dark matter of 15-20% unexplained variance means extracted circuits are incomplete.
Validation circularity arises from using ablation experiments that assume circuit completeness.
GNN meta-model requires ground-truth circuit labels that are expensive to obtain.
Large circuits with hundreds of nodes may exceed human interpretability limits.
future_direction: Integrate attention and MLP circuit analysis.
Characterize reconstruction residuals (dark matter).
Develop label-efficient training methods for GNN meta-model.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural network computations into human-understandable algorithms, yet extracting sparse computational circuits from billion-parameter language models remains challenging due to exponential search complexity and pervasive polysemanticity. The proposed Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD) framework reduces circuit discovery complexity from O(2^n) exhaustive enumeration to O(n^2 log n) through multi-resolution abstraction hierarchies and differentiable circuit search. The methodology integrates cross-layer transcoders for monosemantic feature extraction, graph neural network meta-learning for topology prediction, and causal intervention protocols for validation. Empirical evaluation spans GPT-2 variants, Llama-7B through Llama-70B, and Pythia suite models across algorithmic tasks and natural language benchmarks. On modular arithmetic tasks, the framework achieves up to 91% behavioral preservation ($\pm$2.3\% across runs) while maintaining interpretable subgraph sizes. Cross-architecture transfer experiments suggest that discovered circuits exhibit moderate structural similarity (averaging 67%) across model families, indicating potential shared computational patterns. These results provide preliminary foundations for interpretability at larger model scales while identifying significant limitations in current attribution methodologies that require future advances.

papers.title: Sparse, guided feature connections in an Abstract Deep Network
papers.research_question: How can a deep, re-used structure of features be developed for artificial learning by combining coarse learning (evolutionary-like) with gradient descent fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Abstract Deep Network (ADN), a method that combines coarse population-based learning (similar to evolutionary algorithms) with gradient descent fine-tuning to develop a sparse, deep feature topology effective for both regular and irregular problem domains.
papers.conclusion: The ADN system provides a method for developing a sparse, deep feature topology that can find solutions in irregular domains and initialize a network for gradient descent learning, combining coarse learning processes with fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
ADN achieves accuracy comparable to benchmark SVM and optimized GBML approaches on standard UCI and Protein-Structure Prediction problems.
ADN solves the irregular 135-bit binary multiplexer problem, where gradient descent methods fail.
A convolutional implementation of ADN achieves an error rate of 0.79% on MNIST without a pre-defined topology.
The discrete ADN provides interpretable rules, while the continuous version allows gradient descent fine-tuning for improved accuracy.
The feature network developed by ADN is very sparse and deep, based on observed co-occurrences of features.
future_direction: Extension of the design to include generalization relationships ('or' operators) for increased flexibility.
papers.abstract: We present a technique for developing a network of re-used features, where the topology is formed using a coarse learning method, that allows gradient-descent fine tuning, known as an Abstract Deep Network (ADN). New features are built based on observed co-occurrences, and the network is maintained using a selection process related to evolutionary algorithms. This allows coarse ex- ploration of the problem space, effective for irregular domains, while gradient descent allows pre- cise solutions. Accuracy on standard UCI and Protein-Structure Prediction problems is comparable with benchmark SVM and optimized GBML approaches, and shows scalability for addressing large problems. The discrete implementation is symbolic, allowing interpretability, while the continuous method using fine-tuning shows improved accuracy. The binary multiplexer problem is explored, as an irregular domain that does not support gradient descent learning, showing solution to the bench- mark 135-bit problem. A convolutional implementation is demonstrated on image classification, showing an error-rate of 0.79% on the MNIST problem, without a pre-defined topology. The ADN system provides a method for developing a very sparse, deep feature topology, based on observed relationships between features, that is able to find solutions in irregular domains, and initialize a network prior to gradient descent learning.

papers.title: Structure and Representation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we find modular structure in neural networks, and does this structure have functional relevance in terms of local specialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that trained neural networks exhibit clusterability (modular structure) and that clustering can find locally specialized groups of neurons. It also shows that interpretability tools reveal shortcomings in reward models' feature representation and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation advances understanding of neural network structure and representation, and highlights the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Trained neural networks are more clusterable than randomly initialized networks.
Clustering finds groups of neurons that are important and coherent, indicating local specialization.
Interpretability tools applied to reward models show they do not adequately represent relevant features and mispredict reward out of distribution.
These tools do not reveal a clear picture of the computation the networks are performing.
There is a need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.limitation: Interpretability tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are performing.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks.
Studying the dynamics of clusterability during training.
Developing better interpretability tools for understanding generalization.
papers.abstract: Since neural networks have become dominant within the field of artificial intelligence, a sub-field of research has emerged attempting to understand their inner workings. One standard method within this sub-field has been to primarily understand neural networks as representing human-comprehensible features. Another possibility that has been less explored is to understand them as multi-step computer programs. A seeming prerequisite for this is some form of modularity: for different parts of the network to operate independently enough to be understood in isolation, and to implement distinct interpretable sub-routines.To find modular structure inside neural networks, we initially use the tools of graphical clustering. A network is clusterable in this sense if it can be divided into groups of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that a trained neural network is typically more clusterable than randomly initialized networks, and often clusterable relative to random networks with the same distribution of weights as the trained network. We investigate factors that promote clusterability, and also develop novel methods targeted at that end.For modularity to be valuable for understanding neural networks, it needs to have some sort of functional relevance.The type of functional relevance we target is local specialization of functionality. A neural network is locally specialized to the extent that parts of its computational graph can be abstractly represented as performing some comprehensible sub-task relevant to the overall task. We propose two proxies for local specialization: importance, which reflects how valuable sets of neurons are to network performance; and coherence, which reflects how consistently their neurons associate with features of the inputs. We then operationalize these proxies using techniques conventionally used to interpret individual neurons, applying them instead to groups of neurons produced by graph clustering algorithms. Our results show that clustering succeeds at finding groups of neurons that are important and coherent, although not all groups of neurons found are so.We conclude with a case study of using more standard interpretability tools, designed to understand the features being represented by directions in activation space, applying them to the analysis of neural networks trained on the reward function of the game CoinRun. Despite our networks achieving a low test loss, the application of interpretability tools shows that networks do not adequately represent relevant features and badly mispredict reward out of distribution. That said, these tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are in fact performing. This not only illustrates the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behaviour, but motivates it: if we take these networks as models of 'motivation systems' of policies trained by reinforcement learning, the conclusion is that such networks may competently pursue the wrong objectives when deployed in richer environments, indicating a need for interpretability techniques to shed light on generalization behaviour.

papers.title: NN2Poly: A polynomial representation for deep feed-forward artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: How can an explicit polynomial model be obtained to accurately represent an already trained fully-connected feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP), extending previous work limited to single hidden layers to arbitrarily deep networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces NN2Poly, a theoretical and practical method to obtain an explicit polynomial representation of a pre-trained multilayer perceptron (MLP) for regression and classification tasks, enhancing model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: NN2Poly is a promising method for obtaining polynomial representations of MLPs, providing interpretability and insights into the learned patterns, with applications to tabular data and potential for future extensions to other data types.
papers.key_findings:
NN2Poly can accurately approximate the predictions of a trained MLP with a polynomial under certain weight constraints and Taylor expansion conditions.
The method is effective for both simulated data and real-world tabular datasets (Boston Housing, Forest Covertype) in regression and classification settings.
Imposing a maximum polynomial order (Qmax) and using equivalence classes of multisets significantly improves computational efficiency.
The obtained polynomial coefficients provide interpretability, allowing insights into feature importance and interactions learned by the neural network.
The method reveals when a neural network fails to properly learn a class, as seen in the Covertype dataset where class 5 was never predicted.
papers.limitation:
The method requires synaptic potentials to be near zero for the Taylor expansion to be accurate, which may necessitate weight constraints during training.
Scalability is a challenge for high-dimensional data due to the combinatorial growth in polynomial terms and multiset partitions.
future_direction: Improve efficiency and scalability to apply the method to larger networks and higher-dimensional problems.
Extend applications to non-tabular data like images or audio.
Study the impact of different regularization techniques on the effectiveness of NN2Poly.
papers.abstract: Interpretability of neural networks and their underlying theoretical behavior remain an open field of study even after the great success of their practical applications, particularly with the emergence of deep learning. In this work, NN2Poly is proposed: a theoretical approach to obtain an explicit polynomial model that provides an accurate representation of an already trained fully-connected feed-forward artificial neural network (a multilayer perceptron or MLP). This approach extends a previous idea proposed in the literature, which was limited to single hidden layer networks, to work with arbitrarily deep MLPs in both regression and classification tasks. NN2Poly uses a Taylor expansion on the activation function, at each layer, and then applies several combinatorial properties to calculate the coefficients of the desired polynomials. Discussion is presented on the main computational challenges of this method, and the way to overcome them by imposing certain constraints during the training phase. Finally, simulation experiments as well as applications to real tabular data sets are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: CoLiDR: Concept Learning using Aggregated Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: How can disentangled generative factors be aggregated into human-understandable concepts to improve interpretability of deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CoLiDR, a method that aggregates disentangled generative factors into human-understandable concepts for interpretable concept-based modeling, achieving parity with state-of-the-art concept-based approaches.
papers.conclusion: CoLiDR unifies disentangled representation learning with concept-based explainability by aggregating generative factors into concepts, providing finer interpretability and maintaining performance.
papers.key_findings:
CoLiDR achieves task accuracy and concept error on par with concept-based models like CBM and GlanceNets.
The method effectively aggregates disentangled generative factors into human-understandable concepts.
Test-time interventions on learned concepts can fix wrongly classified samples, improving debugability.
Visual analysis using GradCAM shows that CoLiDR captures spatial concepts better than CBMs.
CoLiDR is generalizable to arbitrary numbers of concepts and generative factors across different datasets.
future_direction: Utilizing more complex disentanglement architectures like Generative Adversarial Networks.
Exploring causally related concepts instead of independent ones.
papers.abstract: Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks using concept-based models offers a promising way to explain model behavior through human-understandable concepts. A parallel line of research focuses on disentangling the data distribution into its underlying generative factors, in turn explaining the data generation process. While both directions have received extensive attention, little work has been done on explaining concepts in terms of generative factors to unify mathematically disentangled representations and human-understandable concepts as an explanation for downstream tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel method CoLiDR - which utilizes a disentangled representation learning setup for learning mutually independent generative factors and subsequently learns to aggregate the said representations into human-understandable concepts using a novel aggregation/decomposition module. Experiments are conducted on datasets with both known and unknown latent generative factors. Our method successfully aggregates disentangled generative factors into concepts while maintaining parity with state-of-the-art concept-based approaches. Quantitative and visual analysis of the learned aggregation procedure demonstrates the advantages of our work compared to commonly used concept-based models over four challenging datasets. Lastly, our work is generalizable to an arbitrary number of concepts and generative factors - making it flexible enough to be suitable for various types of data.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features and address polysemantic neurons in InceptionV1's early vision layers?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from InceptionV1, revealing missing curve detectors and decomposing polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic features.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1 and convolutional neural networks, extending their promise beyond language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn new interpretable features that were not visible when examining individual neurons.
SAEs discover additional curve detector features that fill gaps in the known family of curve detectors.
SAEs can split polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features.
papers.limitation: This paper is a very early report and does not defend the results in a systematic way.
future_direction: Investigate branch specialization and cross-branch superposition in InceptionV1 using SAEs.
papers.abstract: Recent work on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has shown promise in extracting interpretable features from neural networks and addressing challenges with polysemantic neurons caused by superposition. In this paper, we apply SAEs to the early vision layers of InceptionV1, a well-studied convolutional neural network, with a focus on curve detectors. Our results demonstrate that SAEs can uncover new interpretable features not apparent from examining individual neurons, including additional curve detectors that fill in previous gaps. We also find that SAEs can decompose some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features. These findings suggest SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1, and convolutional neural networks more generally.

papers.title: DGTN: Graph-Enhanced Transformer with Diffusive Attention Gating Mechanism for Enzyme DDG Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we accurately predict the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (∆∆G) by integrating sequence and structural information through a co-learning framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DGTN, a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network and transformer representations through a bidirectional diffusion mechanism for protein stability prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: DGTN effectively integrates 3D geometric and evolutionary sequence context through bidirectional diffusion, establishing a principled and interpretable paradigm for accurate protein stability prediction and design.
papers.key_findings:
DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance on ProTherm with Pearson correlation ρ=0.87 and RMSE=1.21 kcal/mol, outperforming existing baselines.
Ablation studies show the bidirectional diffusion mechanism contributes a 6-point gain in Pearson correlation over simple cross-modal fusion.
The model generalizes well to unseen datasets (SKEMPI, Ssym, FireProtDB), demonstrating robust learning of stability principles.
Theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to an optimal structure-aware attention matrix with a convergence rate of O(1/√T).
Attention visualization confirms the model successfully identifies spatially proximate but sequentially distant residue interactions.
papers.limitation:
Operates on a single static conformation of the wild-type protein, unable to capture dynamic or entropic contributions to stability.
Evaluates mutations in isolation and does not explicitly model epistatic (non-additive) interactions between multiple substitutions.
Training data (ProTherm) exhibits class imbalance, with certain protein families overrepresented, potentially limiting generalization.
future_direction: Incorporate ensembles of structures (from molecular dynamics or predicted distributions) to model flexibility and allostery.
Extend the architecture to jointly represent combinatorial mutations via graph-based mutation encoding or interaction-aware attention.
Improve robustness to dataset imbalance via domain-adversarial training, balanced sampling, or cross-family transfer learning.
papers.abstract: Predicting the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (DDG) is fundamental to protein engineering and drug design. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they often process sequence and structure information independently, failing to capture the intricate coupling between local structural geometry and global sequential patterns. We present DGTN (Diffused Graph-Transformer Network), a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network (GNN) weights for structural priors and transformer attention through a diffusion mechanism. Our key innovation is a bidirectional diffusion process where: (1) GNN-derived structural embeddings guide transformer attention via learnable diffusion kernels, and (2) transformer representations refine GNN message passing through attention-modulated graph updates. We provide rigorous mathematical analysis showing this co-learning scheme achieves provably better approximation bounds than independent processing. On ProTherm and SKEMPI benchmarks, DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance (Pearson Rho = 0.87, RMSE = 1.21 kcal/mol), with 6.2% improvement over best baselines. Ablation studies confirm the diffusion mechanism contributes 4.8 points to correlation. Our theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to optimal structure-sequence coupling, with convergence rate O(1/sqrt(T) ) where T is diffusion steps. This work establishes a principled framework for integrating heterogeneous protein representations through learnable diffusion.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Transformers are efficient hierarchical chemical graph learners
papers.research_question: How can we design an efficient graph transformer that reduces computational cost and captures long-range interactions in molecular graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SubFormer, a graph transformer that combines hierarchical clustering and message-passing to efficiently learn graph representations, reducing computational cost and capturing long-range interactions while being competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: SubFormer performed consistently well on standard benchmarks for predicting molecular properties from chemical structures. Visualization of the attention maps suggests the model learns chemically pertinent features. SubFormer does not suffer from over-squashing, but over-smoothing remains an issue requiring further study.
papers.key_findings:
SubFormer is competitive with state-of-the-art graph transformers on molecular property prediction benchmarks at a fraction of the computational cost.
SubFormer attention weights correspond to chemically meaningful fragments (e.g., aromatic rings, charge-transfer fragments).
SubFormer does not suffer from over-squashing because attention allows direct long-range interactions.
SubFormer exhibits limited over-smoothing compared to GAT, but still experiences over-smoothing with increasing layers.
SubFormer is more expressive than the 1-WL test for graph isomorphism.
papers.limitation: Over-smoothing remains an issue, demanding further study.
future_direction: Further study to address over-smoothing.
Refine the graph decomposition strategy to improve separation power.
papers.abstract: Transformers, adapted from natural language processing, are emerging as a leading approach for graph representation learning. Contemporary graph transformers often treat nodes or edges as separate tokens. This approach leads to computational challenges for even moderately-sized graphs due to the quadratic scaling of self-attention complexity with token count. In this paper, we introduce SubFormer, a graph transformer that operates on subgraphs that aggregate information by a message-passing mechanism. This approach reduces the number of tokens and enhances learning long-range interactions. We demonstrate SubFormer on benchmarks for predicting molecular properties from chemical structures and show that it is competitive with state-of-the-art graph transformers at a fraction of the computational cost, with training times on the order of minutes on a consumer-grade graphics card. We interpret the attention weights in terms of chemical structures. We show that SubFormer exhibits limited over-smoothing and avoids over-squashing, which is prevalent in traditional graph neural networks.

papers.title: A Detailed Study of Interpretability of Deep Neural Network based Top Taggers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural network models for top quark jet tagging, and how can interpretability methods be used to improve model design?
papers.core_contribution: The paper studies interpretability of DNN-based top taggers, uncovers pitfalls of existing XAI methods, and proposes a new model (PFIN) that improves performance through interpretability-inspired design.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes a methodological paradigm to demonstrate the usage of XAI tools for day-to-day applications of DNNs and MLPs in high energy physics, and shows how interpretability can lead to improved model design.
papers.key_findings:
Different XAI methods (∆AUC, SHAP, LRP) can produce inconsistent feature rankings, and modifying LRP to differential relevance scores (MAD) yields more consistent results.
Correlations among input features can obscure interpretability, as seen in the MB8S model.
NAP diagrams reveal sparsity in network activations and can guide model reoptimization by removing inactive layers or neurons.
The proposed PFIN model, which incorporates pairwise particle interactions, outperforms baseline models in top tagging.
Latent space embeddings in PFN capture physical jet features and show disentanglement between jet classes.
future_direction: Adapting interpretability tools for more general data types and novel architectures like graph nets and transformers
papers.abstract: Recent developments in the methods of explainable AI (XAI) allow researchers to explore the inner workings of deep neural networks (DNNs), revealing crucial information about input-output relationships and realizing how data connects with machine learning models. In this paper we explore interpretability of DNN models designed to identify jets coming from top quark decay in high energy proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We review a subset of existing top tagger models and explore different quantitative methods to identify which features play the most important roles in identifying the top jets. We also investigate how and why feature importance varies across different XAI metrics, how correlations among features impact their explainability, and how latent space representations encode information as well as correlate with physically meaningful quantities. Our studies uncover some major pitfalls of existing XAI methods and illustrate how they can be overcome to obtain consistent and meaningful interpretation of these models. We additionally illustrate the activity of hidden layers as Neural Activation Pattern (NAP) diagrams and demonstrate how they can be used to understand how DNNs relay information across the layers and how this understanding can help to make such models significantly simpler by allowing effective model reoptimization and hyperparameter tuning. These studies not only facilitate a methodological approach to interpreting models but also unveil new insights about what these models learn. Incorporating these observations into augmented model design, we propose the Particle Flow Interaction Network (PFIN) model and demonstrate how interpretability-inspired model augmentation can improve top tagging performance.

papers.title: A Spectral Theory of Neural Prediction and Alignment
papers.research_question: Why do many different deep neural networks yield similar neural predictions, and how can we differentiate among models that perform equally well at predicting neural responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a spectral theory that decomposes neural prediction error into model eigenspectra and alignment with neural data, and provides geometric measures (error mode radius Rem and dimension Dem) to interpret the error, revealing that different models can achieve similar prediction error through different geometric properties.
papers.conclusion: The spectral theory provides a framework to interpret neural prediction error and shows that geometric measures can differentiate models with similar prediction error, guiding future experiments and model design for improved neural activity prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The spectral theory accurately predicts neural prediction error for ridge regression from model activations to neural responses.
Error mode geometry (Rem and Dem) varies across models even when they have similar neural prediction error, providing additional insight into how models achieve low error.
Early model stages predict early visual areas (V1/V2) better, while later stages predict downstream areas (V4/IT) better, aligning with the hierarchical organization of the visual cortex.
Trained models have better alignment (Wi) with neural data than randomly initialized models, which is the main driver of improved prediction error.
Adversarial training improves alignment between model eigenvectors and early visual cortex activity, leading to lower prediction error in early areas.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical predictions are only accurate in the large P limit (large number of stimuli), and the tail eigenvalues of the empirical Gram matrix are often underestimated.
The results depend on the stimulus set used, which affects the model eigenspectra and thus the error mode geometry.
future_direction: Future work could consider choosing stimulus sets to maximize the difference between model eigenspectra, leading to greater differences in neural predictions.
Extending the theory to other regression methods and non-linear mappings between model activations and neural responses.
Applying the geometric measures to other domains beyond visual cortex to understand model representations more broadly.
