Our findings on molecular datasets show the potential of probing for understanding the inductive biases of graph-based models. We compare different families of models and show that transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information compared to models based on message passing. We also study the effect of different design choices such as skip connections and virtual nodes. We advocate for probing as a useful diagnostic tool for evaluating graph-based models.

papers.title: Explainable AI in drug discovery: self-interpretable graph neural network for molecular property prediction using concept whitening
papers.research_question: How can concept whitening be adapted to graph neural networks to create self-interpretable models for molecular property prediction in drug discovery, and does this improve both performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts the concept whitening (CW) interpretability method to graph neural networks, enabling self-interpretable QSAR models that align latent space axes with known molecular properties (concepts) and identify relevant structural parts of molecules for predictions.
papers.conclusion: The adaptation of concept whitening to graph neural networks provides an effective framework for building self-interpretable models in drug discovery, offering improved performance and clear insights into the molecular properties driving predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Adding concept whitening layers to GNNs improves classification performance (ROC-AUC) and interpretability on molecular property prediction tasks.
The method successfully identifies which predefined molecular properties (concepts) are most relevant for predictions at different network depths.
Two novel activation modes for CW in GNNs (weighted_topk_pool and topk_pool) are introduced and evaluated.
The choice of normalization layer (BatchNorm, InstanceNorm, LayerNorm, GraphNorm) in the base model affects the performance after adding CW layers.
The method provides both structural (via GNNExplainer) and conceptual explanations for model predictions in drug discovery.

papers.title: Interpreting GFlowNets for Drug Discovery: Extracting Actionable Insights for Medicinal Chemistry
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be adapted to structured generative models like GFlowNets to provide actionable insights for medicinal chemistry in drug discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework for GFlowNets that reveals how SynFlowNet encodes chemical properties like polarity and lipophilicity, and provides actionable insights for drug discovery through counterfactual saliency and motif analysis.
papers.conclusion: The study extends interpretability tools to GFlowNets, showing that SynFlowNet's internal representations align with chemical intuition, and suggests future directions like multi-objective analysis and direct conditioning on physicochemical properties.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based saliency with counterfactual edits identifies atom- and motif-level regions that systematically affect predicted drug-likeness (QED).
Sparse autoencoders applied to SynFlowNet embeddings reveal latent factors that correlate strongly with physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and size.
Motif probes show that functional groups like halogens and aromatic rings are encoded in a linearly decodable manner in the embeddings.
The interpretability framework links model decisions to medicinal chemistry heuristics, enabling actionable insights for molecule design.
The approach demonstrates that GFlowNets can be interpreted using adapted methods from supervised learning, extending interpretability to structured generative policies.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on QED, limiting generalization to multi-objective settings.
Disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders and motif probes impose simple structure on the latent space, which may not capture complex reward landscapes.
Gradient-based saliency is only applied to the Stop action, missing intermediate decision points.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to multi-objective settings such as synthetic accessibility or binding affinity.
Condition GFlowNets directly on physicochemical properties for more interpretable representations.
Investigate the impact of interpretability tools on downstream molecule design and compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Generative Flow Networks, or GFlowNets, offer a promising framework for molecular design, but their internal decision policies remain opaque. This limits adoption in drug discovery, where chemists require clear and interpretable rationales for proposed structures. We present an interpretability framework for SynFlowNet, a GFlowNet trained on documented chemical reactions and purchasable starting materials that generates both molecules and the synthetic routes that produce them. Our approach integrates three complementary components. Gradient based saliency combined with counterfactual perturbations identifies which atomic environments influence reward and how structural edits change molecular outcomes. Sparse autoencoders reveal axis aligned latent factors that correspond to physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and molecular size. Motif probes show that functional groups including aromatic rings and halogens are explicitly encoded and linearly decodable from the internal embeddings. Together, these results expose the chemical logic inside SynFlowNet and provide actionable and mechanistic insight that supports transparent and controllable molecular design.

papers.title: Concept Bottleneck Language Models For protein design
papers.research_question: How can we design a protein language model that is controllable, interpretable, and debuggable without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Bottleneck Language Models, a novel architecture that incorporates human-understandable concepts via a concept bottleneck layer, enabling precise control, interpretability, and debugging while maintaining performance comparable to traditional language models.
papers.conclusion: CB-pLM provides a framework for controllable, interpretable, and debuggable language models without sacrificing performance, making it particularly valuable for high-stakes domains like protein design.
papers.key_findings:
CB-pLM achieves 3x better control in terms of change in concept magnitude and 16% improvement in control accuracy compared to baselines.
CB-pLM maintains pre-training perplexity and downstream task performance comparable to traditional masked protein language models.
CB-pLM enables multi-concept interventions with high accuracy (94% control accuracy).
CB-pLM allows interpretability and debugging by inspecting the linear decoder weights, revealing concept-token relationships.
CB-pLM can generalize to unseen concept combinations, as demonstrated on ColorMNIST.
future_direction: Extending CB-LM to other domains and architectures
Adding new concepts to a trained CB-LM via fine-tuning
Generalization to new concept combinations
papers.abstract: We introduce Concept Bottleneck Protein Language Models (CB-pLM), a generative masked language model with a layer where each neuron corresponds to an interpretable concept. Our architecture offers three key benefits: i) Control: We can intervene on concept values to precisely control the properties of generated proteins, achieving a 3 times larger change in desired concept values compared to baselines. ii) Interpretability: A linear mapping between concept values and predicted tokens allows transparent analysis of the model's decision-making process. iii) Debugging: This transparency facilitates easy debugging of trained models. Our models achieve pre-training perplexity and downstream task performance comparable to traditional masked protein language models, demonstrating that interpretability does not compromise performance. While adaptable to any language model, we focus on masked protein language models due to their importance in drug discovery and the ability to validate our model's capabilities through real-world experiments and expert knowledge. We scale our CB-pLM from 24 million to 3 billion parameters, making them the largest Concept Bottleneck Models trained and the first capable of generative language modeling.

papers.title: Attribute Graphs Underlying Molecular Generative Models: Path to Learning with Limited Data
papers.research_question: How can we extract a graphical model (attribute graph) relating data attributes from the latent representations of a pre-trained generative model, and use this structure for robust prediction with limited out-of-distribution data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PerturbLearn, a method to extract an attribute graph (a DAG) from a pre-trained generative autoencoder by perturbing latent codes and observing influences on data attributes, and shows that using the Markov blanket from this graph for feature selection leads to robust prediction under distribution shifts with limited data.
papers.conclusion: The PerturbLearn framework successfully extracts a graphical model from a pre-trained generative model, and using this structure for feature selection enables more robust and generalizable predictors in scenarios with limited out-of-distribution data.
papers.key_findings:
The attribute graph derived by PerturbLearn captures latent-mediated influences among molecular attributes.
Predictors using the Markov blanket features from the PerturbLearn graph show better generalization and robustness to distribution shifts, especially when fine-tuning data is limited (e.g., n=7, 10, 25 samples).
The method is competitive with or outperforms existing causal discovery (GES, LiNGAM) and feature selection methods (Sparse Group Lasso, PPFS) in low-data regimes across multiple pharmacokinetic property prediction tasks.
The derived graphical model provides a means for sample-efficient domain adaptation and offers (partial) interpretability by identifying relevant attributes.
papers.limitation: Dependency on a pre-determined set of data attributes, which may not be comprehensive.
future_direction: Further investigation on the accordance of the derived attribute graph with domain priors.
Using only low-level and cheaply computable attributes.
Incorporating expert knowledge.
papers.abstract: Training generative models that capture rich semantics of the data and interpreting the latent representations encoded by such models are very important problems in un-/self-supervised learning. In this work, we provide a simple algorithm that relies on perturbation experiments on latent codes of a pre-trained generative autoencoder to uncover an attribute graph that is implied by the generative model. We perform perturbation experiments to check for influence of a given latent variable on a subset of attributes. Given this, we show that one can fit an effective graphical model that models a structural equation model between latent codes taken as exogenous variables and attributes taken as observed variables. One interesting aspect is that a single latent variable controls multiple overlapping subsets of attributes unlike conventional approaches that try to impose full independence. Using a pre-trained generative autoencoder trained on a large dataset of small molecules, we demonstrate that the graphical model between various molecular attributes and latent codes learned by our algorithm can be used to predict a specific property for molecules which are drawn from a different distribution. We compare prediction models trained on various feature subsets chosen by simple baselines, as well as existing causal discovery and sparse learning/feature selection methods, with the ones in the derived Markov blanket from our method. Results show empirically that the predictor that relies on our Markov blanket attributes is robust to distribution shifts when transferred or fine-tuned with a few samples from the new distribution, especially when training data is limited.

papers.title: “Amide − amine + alcohol = carboxylic acid.” chemical reactions as linear algebraic analogies in graph neural networks
papers.research_question: Do graph neural network (GNN) atom-embeddings exhibit linear algebraic analogies similar to word embeddings in NLP, and how do these analogies relate to chemical reactions and properties?
papers.core_contribution: Atom-embeddings in pretrained graph neural networks exhibit linear algebraic analogies that correspond to chemical reactions, revealing a highly structured latent space that mirrors chemical syntax.
papers.conclusion: The latent space of GNNs in chemistry is highly structured and organized according to chemical syntax, with linear analogies providing a global explanatory framework for chemical transformations and properties.
papers.key_findings:
Atom-embeddings in a pretrained GNN (SchNet) show arithmetic properties allowing linear analogies that represent valid chemical reaction formulas, similar to word analogies in NLP.
Reaction vectors (differences between reactant and product embeddings) are approximately constant for a given reaction type and are colinear for similar reactions (e.g., oxidations).
The linear analogies can be explained by a perturbational replicate model based on neighborhood chemical composition, linking the embedding structure to chemical principles.
The structured embedding space facilitates transfer learning and reveals linear relations in chemical properties like NMR chemical shifts and atomization energies.
The organization of the embedding space has two levels: substructure composition and changes to substructure, with similar changes aligning in direction.
papers.limitation:
The QM9 dataset only includes equilibrium geometries, so the reaction datasets only account for initial and product states, not mechanistic transitions.
Geometry optimization using force fields may introduce non-equilibrium geometries from the perspective of the DFT-trained model.
The replicate model is an approximation and ignores the exact layout of the graph.
future_direction: Mapping out the trajectories of reactions in the latent space to study transition states.
Studying how the global explanatory framework reduces to local explanations on a case-by-case basis.
Improving the replicate model by incorporating the exact graph layout and using the same geometry optimization as the GNN model.
papers.abstract: In deep learning methods, especially in the context of chemistry, there is an increasing urgency to uncover the hidden learning mechanisms often dubbed as "black box." In this work, we show that graph models built on computational chemical data behave similar to natural language processing (NLP) models built on text data. Crucially, we show that atom-embeddings, a.k.a atom-parsed graph neural activation patterns, exhibit arithmetic properties that represent valid reaction formulas. This is very similar to how word-embeddings can be combined to make word analogies, thus preserving the semantic meaning behind the words, as in the famous example "King" - "Man" + "Woman" = "Queen." For instance, we show how the reaction from an alcohol to a carbonyl is represented by a constant vector in the embedding space, implicitly representing "-H<sub>2</sub>." This vector is independent from the particular carbonyl reactant and alcohol product and represents a consistent chemical transformation. Other directions in the embedding space are synonymous with distinct chemical changes (ex. the tautomerization direction). In contrast to natural language processing, we can explain the observed chemical analogies using algebraic manipulations on the local chemical composition that surrounds each atom-embedding. Furthermore, the observations find applications in transfer learning, for instance in the formal structure and prediction of atomistic properties, such as <sup>1</sup>H-NMR and <sup>13</sup>C-NMR. This work is in line with the recent push for interpretable explanations to graph neural network modeling of chemistry and uncovers a latent model of chemistry that is highly structured, consistent, and analogous to chemical syntax.

papers.title: Understanding the patterns that neural networks learn from chemical spectra
papers.research_question: How does a neural network learn to classify infrared spectra of small organic molecules by functional groups, and what specific patterns (both intuitive and non-intuitive) does it use for classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a simpler 1D CNN that achieves state-of-the-art performance for functional group classification in infrared spectra and introduces a two-step explainability approach, revealing the network uses both characteristic group frequencies and non-intuitive patterns like tails and overtones.
papers.conclusion: The simplified CNN model is effective for spectral classification, and the explainability approach reveals the network uses both intuitive and non-intuitive spectral patterns, which can help assess generalization and guide future model design incorporating physics-based knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The 1D CNN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models while being significantly less complex.
The model consistently attends to the same spectral regions across different random initializations, indicating robust feature learning.
The network learns to use characteristic group frequencies (peaks) for classification, aligning with expert knowledge.
The network also uses non-intuitive patterns such as tails and anharmonic vibrations (overtones and combination bands) to improve classification certainty.
For some functional groups (e.g., nitriles), class imbalance and the presence of only one characteristic band lead to poor classification accuracy, highlighting dataset limitations.
papers.limitation:
Class imbalance leads to poor classification accuracy for rare functional groups like nitriles.
The network sometimes uses non-characteristic vibrations (e.g., C-H wags for halides) which may not generalize to new datasets.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based intuition into model design, e.g., using IR tables to initialize parameters or filters that optimally recognize peaks.
Transfer understanding from pretrained models to new datasets (potentially from different spectral regions).
papers.abstract: We train a convolutional neural network to classify functional groups from infrared spectra. With explainability methods, we show the model uses the presence and absence of peaks, at fundamental and anharmonic frequencies for accurate classification.

papers.title: BERT Learns (and Teaches) Chemistry
papers.research_question: Can attention mechanisms in BERT be used to identify important molecular substructures (functional groups) from SMILES string representations and apply these learned representations to chemical property prediction tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that BERT's attention mechanisms can identify chemically relevant functional groups from SMILES strings without domain heuristics, and that these learned representations can be applied to downstream chemical property prediction tasks.
papers.conclusion: Attention visualization in BERT provides a data-driven method to identify functional groups and important molecular substructures from SMILES strings, offering a potentially useful tool for computational chemistry despite not achieving state-of-the-art performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads, trained only on SMILES strings, learn to attend to atoms that correspond to known active reaction sites (functional groups) in molecules, even without explicit reaction data.
When fine-tuned on chemical property regression tasks (e.g., solubility), specific attention heads in BERT focus on relevant substructures (e.g., carbon chains for solubility).
Using BERT embeddings as features for graph models (GCN, GAT) on toxicity prediction tasks yields competitive but not state-of-the-art performance compared to canonical atom featurization.
Attention visualization of BERT trained on chemical data can serve as a tool for chemistry practitioners to quickly identify important substructures related to various chemical properties.
papers.limitation:
BERT embeddings did not improve upon the state of the art when used as features for graph models on toxicity prediction; the learned information appears to be a subset of that captured by canonical atom featurization.
Some molecules in the Tox21 dataset contain atoms not present in BERT's vocabulary, which may detract from performance.
Attention heads after fine-tuning on most chemical property tasks (QED, SAS) showed little change from pretraining, except for the solubility task, suggesting the fine-tuning may find a local optimum close to pretraining weights.
future_direction: Using a larger dataset of 96 million molecules from PubMed to train BERT, given that language models thrive with abundant data.
Designing a loss function that penalizes distances between embeddings of different SMILES strings representing the same molecule to force BERT to learn the inherent graphical meaning.
Further investigating the approach of analyzing chemical property-bearing molecular substructures via fine-tuning to make it a more useful tool for chemists.
papers.abstract: Modern computational organic chemistry is becoming increasingly data-driven. There remain a large number of important unsolved problems in this area such as product prediction given reactants, drug discovery, and metric-optimized molecule synthesis, but efforts to solve these problems using machine learning have also increased in recent years. In this work, we propose the use of attention to study functional groups and other property-impacting molecular substructures from a data-driven perspective, using a transformer-based model (BERT) on datasets of string representations of molecules and analyzing the behavior of its attention heads. We then apply the representations of functional groups and atoms learned by the model to tackle problems of toxicity, solubility, drug-likeness, and synthesis accessibility on smaller datasets using the learned representations as features for graph convolution and attention models on the graph structure of molecules, as well as fine-tuning of BERT. Finally, we propose the use of attention visualization as a helpful tool for chemistry practitioners and students to quickly identify important substructures in various chemical properties.

papers.title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
papers.research_question: How do the geometric and statistical properties of hidden representations evolve across layers in large transformer models, and can the intrinsic dimension profile be used to identify layers with maximal semantic content?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension profile of hidden representations in large transformers has a characteristic shape (peak, plateau, etc.), and the layers with minimal intrinsic dimension correspond to those with maximal semantic content, providing an unsupervised strategy to identify optimal layers for downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Large transformers behave like sophisticated autoencoders, with an encoding phase (expansion and compression) and a decoding phase, and the low-ID representations in the intermediate layers are semantically rich.
papers.key_findings:
Representations evolve in distinct phases: an initial expansion (high ID), a compression phase (low ID), and a decoding phase.
The ID profile shows a peak in early layers, a plateau/low-ID region in intermediate layers, and sometimes a second peak in later layers.
Semantic information (e.g., protein remote homology, image class labels) is best encoded in the low-ID regions.
The ID profile can be used in an unsupervised manner to identify layers optimal for downstream learning tasks.
The geometric evolution is consistent across transformers trained on different data modalities (protein sequences and images).
papers.limitation:
The use of average pooling to handle variable-length sequences may affect the intrinsic dimension estimates.
Differences in ID profiles between models may be attributed to data modality, training objectives, and preprocessing choices.
The analysis of NLP representations is preliminary and not as extensive as for protein and image models.
future_direction: Analyzing the similarity of representations in ID minima with those from models trained in a supervised setting.
Further investigation of the second peak in iGPT models and its relation to the decoding phase.
Extending the geometric analysis to a broader range of NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Large transformers are powerful architectures used for self-supervised data analysis across various data types, including protein sequences, images, and text. In these models, the semantic structure of the dataset emerges from a sequence of transformations between one representation and the next. We characterize the geometric and statistical properties of these representations and how they change as we move through the layers. By analyzing the intrinsic dimension (ID) and neighbor composition, we find that the representations evolve similarly in transformers trained on protein language tasks and image reconstruction tasks. In the first layers, the data manifold expands, becoming high-dimensional, and then contracts significantly in the intermediate layers. In the last part of the model, the ID remains approximately constant or forms a second shallow peak. We show that the semantic information of the dataset is better expressed at the end of the first peak, and this phenomenon can be observed across many models trained on diverse datasets. Based on our findings, we point out an explicit strategy to identify, without supervision, the layers that maximize semantic content: representations at intermediate layers corresponding to a relative minimum of the ID profile are more suitable for downstream learning tasks.

papers.title: Occupancies vs Embeddings: Internal representations of Ab Initio and Graph Probabilistic Models*
papers.research_question: To what degree does the end-to-end data-driven approach (graph neural networks) coalesce with traditional ab initio predictions of molecular behavior? Does the model contain internal characteristics of the wave function or electron density from DFT?
papers.core_contribution: This study compares atomwise representations from graph neural networks (GNNs) and ab initio density functional theory (DFT), revealing that GNN embeddings offer higher resolution and can accurately predict DFT-derived atomic occupancy values, whereas the reverse mapping is significantly less accurate.
papers.conclusion: GNN embeddings serve as a richer, more informative molecular representation than DFT-derived atomic occupancies, demonstrating the power of end-to-end statistical models to encapsulate and extend traditional quantum chemical information, though further exploration is needed regarding their robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.key_findings:
Both GNN embedding vectors and DFT-derived atomic occupancy vectors can separate and label chemical environments, but embeddings provide much higher resolution and lower classification error.
Embedding vectors can predict atomic occupancy values with high accuracy (MAE 2.5e-3, R2 0.996), but the reverse mapping from occupancies to embeddings is an order of magnitude less accurate (MAE 0.235, R2 0.379).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals qualitative similarities in the eigenvalue spectra between the two representations, but the embedding space captures more nuanced information.
The embedding representation contains more information than the occupancy representation, enabling precise mapping to occupancies but not vice versa within the same model chemistry.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) shows embeddings achieve near-perfect functional group classification, while occupancy vectors show higher error, especially for similar chemical environments.
papers.limitation: Interatomic information was omitted due to the need to respect rotational equivariance for the embeddings, and the use of Mulliken population analysis might hamper a faithful analysis of the information content in the occupancies.
future_direction: Further studies to tighten conclusions about the relationship between embeddings and electron density.
Exploration of GNN embeddings' robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical modeling has traditionally been separated into two fairly non-overlapping frameworks: the exact framework of \textit{ab initio} models and the data-driven framework of statistical models. However, recent advances in machine learning approaches have intercepted the exact \textit{ab initio} frameworks by using an \textit{end-to-end} probabilistic model of the Schr\"odinger equation in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation---from raw nuclear configurations to quantum observables such as the energy. While probabilistic modelling offers promising advancements to speed up computational predictions, the internal representation and its connection to the underlying quantum data---the wave function or electron density---which they implicitly rely on for training, remains relatively poorly understood. This study seeks to make a first comparison of the internal representation from a probabilistic end-to-end models with those from pure \textit{ab initio} frameworks such as density functional theory. We do this by comparing the internal atomwise representation of graph models, also called embeddings, to their most natural \textit{ab initio} counterpart, electron occupancy values. Our findings show that the embedding representations can be employed to transfer learn atomic occupancy values whereas the reverse mapping appears to be less accurate. We discuss the assumption that the probabilistic model could infer the existence of an underlying electron density underpinning the computational \textit{ab-initio} data.

papers.title: Multi-scale Graph Autoregressive Modeling: Molecular Property Prediction via Next Token Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the gap between graph topology preservation and scalable autoregressive training to enable decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance on molecular property prediction benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CamS bridges the gap between graph topology and autoregressive training, enabling effective molecular property prediction via next-token prediction with a standard decoder-only Transformer backbone.
papers.key_findings:
CamS-LLaMA achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and MoleculeACE benchmarks.
Multi-scale concatenation is the key driver of performance.
The causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining structural differences.
CamS provides a more nuanced structural discrimination than descriptor-based approaches like KPGT.
The method combines general-purpose robustness with fine-grained structural discriminability.
papers.limitation: Vocabulary materialization involves expensive subgraph-isomorphism matching that prohibits direct training on billion-scale corpora.
papers.abstract: We present Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via standard next-token prediction (NTP). For molecular property prediction, SMILES-based NTP scales well but lacks explicit topology, whereas graph-native masked modeling captures connectivity but risks disrupting the pivotal chemical details (e.g., activity cliffs). CamS bridges this gap by serializing molecular graphs into structure-rich causal sequences. CamS first mines data-driven connection-aware motifs. It then serializes motifs via scaffold-rooted breadth-first search (BFS) to establish a stable core-to-periphery order. Crucially, CamS enables hierarchical modeling by concatenating sequences from fine to coarse motif scales, allowing the model to condition global scaffolds on dense, uncorrupted local structural evidence. We instantiate CamS-LLaMA by pre-training a vanilla LLaMA backbone on CamS sequences. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and the activity-cliff benchmark MoleculeACE, outperforming both SMILES-based language models and strong graph baselines. Interpretability analysis confirms that our multi-scale causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining differences.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: MolReasoner: Toward Effective and Interpretable Reasoning for Molecular LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across various domains, but their ability to perform molecular reasoning remains underexplored. Existing methods mostly rely on general-purpose prompting, which lacks domain-specific molecular semantics, or fine-tuning, which faces challenges in interpretability and reasoning depth, often leading to structural and textual hallucinations. To address these issues, we introduce MolReasoner, a two-stage framework that transitions LLMs from memorization to high-fidelity chemical reasoning. In the Mol-SFT stage, knowledge-enhanced Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data provides a strong foundation, while the Mol-RL stage refines reasoning using a novel, task-adaptive reward system to mitigate hallucinations. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MolReasoner significantly outperforms a wide range of strong baselines in both molecule generation and captioning tasks. Further analyses highlight the framework's synergistic design and its ability to produce more interpretable outputs. Our work presents a principled and effective new approach for advancing high-fidelity molecular reasoning.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: GPCR-BERT: Interpreting Sequential Design of G Protein Coupled Receptors Using Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the correlation between variations in conserved motifs of GPCRs and other amino acids? Can we predict missing residues and identify key contributing amino acids?
papers.core_contribution: Developed GPCR-BERT, a fine-tuned protein language model, to interpret sequential design of GPCRs, achieving high accuracy in predicting masked residues and identifying residue correlations through attention analysis.
papers.conclusion: GPCR-BERT effectively predicts residues and distinguishes GPCR classes, providing insights into functional relationships and potential applications in mutation studies and drug development.
papers.key_findings:
GPCR-BERT achieved high accuracy (up to 100%) in predicting masked residues in conserved motifs.
The model successfully clustered GPCRs of the same class in embedding space, indicating it captures class-specific features.
Attention analysis revealed correlations between masked residues and other amino acids, some of which align with experimental mutagenesis data.
The model's predictions for CWxP motif were less accurate, likely due to smaller dataset size.
GPCR-BERT outperformed BERT and SVM on the prediction tasks, demonstrating the advantage of protein-specific pre-training.
papers.limitation: The conserved motifs are not 100% conserved (e.g., CWxP motif is only 71% conserved), so the model might not apply to GPCRs with varied versions of the motifs.
papers.abstract: With the rise of Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs) in Chemistry and Biology, new avenues for the design and understanding of therapeutics have opened up to the scientific community. Protein sequences can be modeled as language and can take advantage of recent advances in LLMs, specifically with the abundance of our access to the protein sequence datasets. In this paper, we developed the GPCR-BERT model for understanding the sequential design of G Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCRs). GPCRs are the target of over one-third of FDA-approved pharmaceuticals. However, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding the relationship between amino acid sequence, ligand selectivity, and conformational motifs (such as NPxxY, CWxP, E/DRY). By utilizing the pre-trained protein model (Prot-Bert) and fine-tuning with prediction tasks of variations in the motifs, we were able to shed light on several relationships between residues in the binding pocket and some of the conserved motifs. To achieve this, we took advantage of attention weights, and hidden states of the model that are interpreted to extract the extent of contributions of amino acids in dictating the type of masked ones. The fine-tuned models demonstrated high accuracy in predicting hidden residues within the motifs. In addition, the analysis of embedding was performed over 3D structures to elucidate the higher-order interactions within the conformations of the receptors.

papers.title: Quantum-chemical insights from interpretable atomistic neural networks
papers.research_question: How can atomistic neural networks be made interpretable to provide insights into chemical properties and underlying quantum-chemical regularities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that atomistic neural networks, through their inherent atom-wise contributions and learned embeddings, provide interpretable insights that align with chemical knowledge, enabling validation and new research avenues in quantum chemistry.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability is crucial for validating and trusting machine learning models in quantum chemistry, and the presented techniques, which yield explanations grounded in physics and chemistry, open up new venues for data-driven research in chemistry, physics, and materials science.
papers.key_findings:
Atomistic neural networks yield consistent atom-wise partitionings of energy and partial charges, which serve as local explanations.
The atom-wise energy contributions can be used to rank the stability of aromatic rings, agreeing with chemical concepts like mesomeric and inductive effects.
Local chemical potentials, derived by probing the model with a virtual atom, provide spatially resolved visualizations that reflect chemical intuition such as bond saturation and aromaticity.
Electrostatic potentials computed from latent partial charges approximate the molecular charge distribution and show excellent agreement with basic chemical reasoning.
Element embeddings learned by SchNet from crystal structures recover a structure resembling the periodic table, indicating the model infers chemical similarities from data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to measure chemical similarity of local structures.
papers.abstract: With the rise of deep neural networks for quantum chemistry applications, there is a pressing need for architectures that, beyond delivering accurate predictions of chemical properties, are readily interpretable by researchers. Here, we describe interpretation techniques for atomistic neural networks on the example of Behler-Parrinello networks as well as the end-to-end model SchNet. Both models obtain predictions of chemical properties by aggregating atom-wise contributions. These latent variables can serve as local explanations of a prediction and are obtained during training without additional cost. Due to their correspondence to well-known chemical concepts such as atomic energies and partial charges, these atom-wise explanations enable insights not only about the model but more importantly about the underlying quantum-chemical regularities. We generalize from atomistic explanations to 3d space, thus obtaining spatially resolved visualizations which further improve interpretability. Finally, we analyze learned embeddings of chemical elements that exhibit a partial ordering that resembles the order of the periodic table. As the examined neural networks show excellent agreement with chemical knowledge, the presented techniques open up new venues for data-driven research in chemistry, physics and materials science.

papers.title: ACES-GNN: can graph neural network learn to explain activity cliffs?
papers.research_question: Can Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) be trained to provide better explanations for activity cliffs (structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences) while also improving prediction accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ACES-GNN framework, which integrates explanation supervision for activity cliffs into GNN training, improving both predictive accuracy and the interpretability of molecular structure-property relationships.
papers.conclusion: ACES-GNN represents a promising direction for improving both the predictivity and interpretability of GNN models in QSAR applications, with the potential to accelerate lead optimization in drug discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ACES-GNN improves explainability (global direction) on 28 out of 30 datasets compared to unsupervised GNNs.
ACES-GNN improves prediction accuracy for activity cliff molecules, reducing RMSE_cliff.
A positive correlation exists between the improvement in prediction accuracy and the improvement in explanation quality.
The ACES framework is effective across different GNN backbones (MPNN, GIN, GAT).
Explanation supervision helps the model focus on uncommon substructures critical for activity cliffs, aligning attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations.
papers.limitation:
The ground-truth coloring relies on a fixed definition for activity cliff molecules, and some uncommon substructures between pairs may not be causative for potency changes.
The current GNN backbone does not outperform the Random Forest + ECFP combination in predictive accuracy or attribution quality across all datasets.
The validation process prioritizes minimizing RMSE during training rather than optimizing the explainability metric, so not all attributions after supervision achieve higher global direction accuracy.
future_direction: Incorporate geometric information into GNNs for further improvement.
Explore alternative gradient-based explanation techniques, such as expected gradients, to reduce potential biases.
Develop methods to identify true causal substructures in activity cliffs, enhancing explanation evaluation and guidance.
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have revolutionized molecular property prediction by leveraging graph-based representations, yet their opaque decision-making processes hinder broader adoption in drug discovery. This study introduces the Activity-Cliff-Explanation-Supervised GNN (ACES-GNN) framework, designed to simultaneously improve predictive accuracy and interpretability by integrating explanation supervision for activity cliffs (ACs) into GNN training. ACs, defined by structurally similar molecules with significant potency differences, pose challenges for traditional models due to their reliance on shared structural features. By aligning model attributions with chemist-friendly interpretations, the ACES-GNN framework bridges the gap between prediction and explanation. Validated across 30 pharmacological targets, ACES-GNN consistently enhances both predictive accuracy and attribution quality for ACs compared to unsupervised GNNs. Our results demonstrate a positive correlation between improved predictions and accurate explanations, offering a robust and adaptable framework to better understand and interpret ACs. This work underscores the potential of explanation-guided learning to advance interpretable artificial intelligence in molecular modeling and drug discovery.

papers.title: Explainability Techniques for Chemical Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Automated Neuron Labelling Enables Generative Steering and Interpretability in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we automatically label neurons in protein language models with natural language descriptions, and how can these labels be used to steer protein generation towards desired properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automated neuron labeling framework for protein language models and a neuron activation-guided steering method to generate proteins with desired biochemical and structural properties.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework for automated neuron labeling and generative steering in protein language models, enabling interpretability and control over protein generation, and suggests future directions for integration with structural validation and model pruning.
papers.key_findings:
Automated neuron labeling produces interpretable descriptions that capture diverse biochemical and structural properties of proteins.
Neuron activation-guided steering can generate proteins with targeted characteristics, such as specific molecular weight, GRAVY score, and secondary/tertiary structural motifs.
Larger PLMs capture more fine-grained protein features and show a more distributed representation of features across layers compared to smaller models.
Feature encoding follows a hierarchical pattern: sequence-derived properties peak in early layers, structural properties in middle layers, and functional properties in later layers.
Negative steering (multiplying neuron activations by negative values) can invert the effect for some features (e.g., GRAVY score) but not for others (e.g., instability index).
papers.limitation:
LLM explainer may generate oversimplified or hallucinated descriptions.
Generated proteins may not fold into viable, stable structures due to high ΔG values.
Limited to three models due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Incorporate a reinforcement learning module with structure prediction models (e.g., AlphaFold2) to improve structural viability of generated proteins.
Extend neuron labeling to more models and use multiple LLMs for more robust labels.
Explore pruning neurons based on labels to compress models while retaining performance.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) encode rich biological information, yet their internal neuron representations are poorly understood. We introduce the first automated framework for labeling every neuron in a PLM with biologically grounded natural language descriptions. Unlike prior approaches relying on sparse autoencoders or manual annotation, our method scales to hundreds of thousands of neurons, revealing individual neurons are selectively sensitive to diverse biochemical and structural properties. We then develop a novel neuron activation-guided steering method to generate proteins with desired traits, enabling convergence to target biochemical properties like molecular weight and instability index as well as secondary and tertiary structural motifs, including alpha helices and canonical Zinc Fingers. We finally show that analysis of labeled neurons in different model sizes reveals PLM scaling laws and a structured neuron space distribution.

papers.title: Attribution assignment for deep-generative sequence models enables interpretability analysis using positive-only data
papers.research_question: How can we interpret generative sequence models trained on positive-only data to extract biological insights?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces GAMA, an attribution method based on Integrated Gradients, to enable interpretability of autoregressive generative models trained on positive-only data, allowing for the extraction of biologically relevant motifs without negative examples.
papers.conclusion: GAMA provides a novel method for interpreting generative sequence models, enabling the discovery of binding motifs and enhancing trust in model-generated sequences for applications like antibody design.
papers.key_findings:
GAMA can recover implanted motifs in synthetic datasets with high accuracy, especially at high signal-to-noise ratios.
GAMA's performance is robust to the position of motifs in sequences.
For motifs with AND logic, GAMA achieves perfect retrieval at signal-to-noise ratios ≥80%.
GAMA shows significant correlation with binding affinities in synthetic antibody datasets.
In experimental antibody data, GAMA identifies key amino acid positions that partially overlap with known binding sites.
papers.limitation:
GAMA analyzes single positions within the sequence chain, limiting its ability to identify higher-order dependency patterns.
GAMA's capacity to discern motifs is constrained in environments with very low signal-to-noise ratios.
future_direction: Extending GAMA to identify higher-order dependency patterns
Applying GAMA to more complex datasets like Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire (AIRR) datasets
papers.abstract: Generative machine learning models offer a powerful framework for therapeutic design by efficiently exploring large spaces of biological sequences enriched for desirable properties. Unlike supervised learning methods, which require both positive and negative labeled data, generative models such as LSTMs can be trained solely on positively labeled sequences, for example, high-affinity antibodies. This is particularly advantageous in biological settings where negative data are scarce, unreliable, or biologically ill-defined. However, the lack of attribution methods for generative models has hindered the ability to extract interpretable biological insights from such models. To address this gap, we developed Generative Attribution Metric Analysis (GAMA), an attribution method for autoregressive generative models based on Integrated Gradients. We assessed GAMA using synthetic datasets with known ground truths to characterize its statistical behavior and validate its ability to recover biologically relevant features. We further demonstrated the utility of GAMA by applying it to experimental antibody-antigen binding data. GAMA enables model interpretability and the validation of generative sequence design strategies without the need for negative training data.

papers.title: Using attribution to decode binding mechanism in neural network models for chemistry
papers.research_question: Why do virtual screening models make the predictions they do? The paper aims to assess the influence of dataset biases on the prediction of protein binding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that uses attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) to test hypotheses about binding logic and reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, showing that models can achieve perfect accuracy while learning spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods can reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, and models can be fooled by adversarial examples despite perfect accuracy. Practitioners should analyze model predictions and not rely solely on aggregate accuracy metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on synthetic binding logics achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test sets but often have low attribution-AUC, indicating they learn spurious correlations.
Attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) can be used to identify dataset biases and construct adversarial examples that fool the model.
The attribution-AUC metric quantifies how well the model's attributions align with the hypothesized binding logic.
In the ADRB2 dataset, the model achieves perfect accuracy but very low attribution-AUC, indicating it does not learn the correct binding logic.
The framework provides a test for dataset bias given a hypothesis, indicating when models must be simplified/regularized or datasets augmented.
papers.limitation: Attributions offer a reductive view of the model's internal logic and fail to capture higher-order feature interactions.
future_direction: Further research to reveal feature interactions in the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy at classifying molecules with respect to whether they bind to specific protein targets. A key breakthrough would occur if these models could reveal the fragment pharmacophores that are causally involved in binding. Extracting chemical details of binding from the networks could enable scientific discoveries about the mechanisms of drug actions. However, doing so requires shining light into the black box that is the trained neural network model, a task that has proved difficult across many domains. Here we show how the binding mechanism learned by deep neural network models can be interrogated, using a recently described attribution method. We first work with carefully constructed synthetic datasets, in which the molecular features responsible for "binding" are fully known. We find that networks that achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test datasets still learn spurious correlations, and we are able to exploit this nonrobustness to construct adversarial examples that fool the model. This makes these models unreliable for accurately revealing information about the mechanisms of protein-ligand binding. In light of our findings, we prescribe a test that checks whether a hypothesized mechanism can be learned. If the test fails, it indicates that the model must be simplified or regularized and/or that the training dataset requires augmentation.

papers.title: Discovering symmetry invariants and conserved quantities by interpreting siamese neural networks
papers.research_question: Can Siamese Neural Networks learn symmetry invariants and conserved quantities in physical systems, and can they be interpreted to reveal these quantities without prior knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces interpretable Siamese Neural Networks to theoretical physics and shows they can learn and reveal symmetry invariants and conserved quantities without prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: SNNs are a useful tool in theoretical physics and can be interpreted to reveal physical invariants, challenging the black box nature of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
SNNs learn the spacetime interval in special relativity.
SNNs learn angular momentum and energy in central potential motion.
SNNs learn the two electromagnetic invariants (E·B and |E|^2-|B|^2).
The bottleneck layer of the SNN can be interpreted via polynomial regression to approximate the invariants.
The SNN fails to learn when the invariant is fixed, indicating it relies on that invariant.
future_direction: Upgrade polynomial regression to symbolic regression.
Combine interpretable SNNs with mathematical reasoning tools (solvers or theorem provers).
Apply to quantum error correction or particle tracking at the LHC.
papers.abstract: The authors train a Siamese neural network to decide whether two different descriptions describe the same physical object. The neural network learns to identify the objects by calculating the underlying invariants and conserved quantities.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: MolEdit: Knowledge Editing for Multimodal Molecule Language Models
papers.research_question: How to edit knowledge in multimodal molecule language models (MoLMs) to correct inaccuracies while preserving unrelated knowledge, specifically for molecule-to-caption and caption-to-molecule generation tasks.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MolEdit, a framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, and MEBench, a benchmark for evaluating such editing, addressing molecule-specific challenges of multifaceted expertise and cross-molecule interdependence.
papers.conclusion: MolEdit provides an effective framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, enabling precise knowledge updates while preserving unrelated information, and MEBench offers a comprehensive evaluation benchmark, charting a path toward safer, continuously updatable scientific foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
MolEdit outperforms fine-tuning, gradient-based (MEND), and memory-based (GRACE) baselines across Reliability, Locality, and Generality metrics on both MoMu and MolFM backbones.
MolEdit achieves up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than state-of-the-art editing baselines.
Editing molecule generation is more challenging than editing caption generation, and performance is generally better on MoMu than on MolFM.
The Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter (MEKA) effectively routes different facets of molecular knowledge to specialized experts, and the Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher (EAES) accurately activates edits only for relevant inputs.
Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component (MEKA and EAES) to MolEdit's overall performance.
papers.limitation:
Editing molecular SMILES strings is inherently more complex and abstract than editing captions, lacking explicit semantic structure.
Potential misuse of editing to amplify unsafe molecular knowledge and inadvertent propagation of dataset biases.
future_direction: Future work on editing MoLMs.
papers.abstract: Understanding and continuously refining multimodal molecular knowledge is crucial for advancing biomedicine, chemistry, and materials science. Molecule language models (MoLMs) have become powerful tools in these domains, integrating structural representations (e.g., SMILES strings, molecular graphs) with rich contextual descriptions (e.g., physicochemical properties). However, MoLMs can encode and propagate inaccuracies due to outdated web-mined training corpora or malicious manipulation, jeopardizing downstream discovery pipelines. While knowledge editing has been explored for general-domain AI, its application to MoLMs remains uncharted, presenting unique challenges due to the multifaceted and interdependent nature of molecular knowledge. In this paper, we take the first step toward MoLM editing for two critical tasks: molecule-to-caption generation and caption-to-molecule generation. To address molecule-specific challenges, we propose MolEdit, a powerful framework that enables targeted modifications while preserving unrelated molecular knowledge. MolEdit combines a Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter that routes edits to specialized experts for different molecular facets with an Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher that activates the adapters only when input closely matches the stored edits across all expertise, minimizing interference with unrelated knowledge. To systematically evaluate editing performance, we introduce MEBench, a comprehensive benchmark assessing multiple dimensions, including Reliability (accuracy of the editing), Locality (preservation of irrelevant knowledge), and Generality (robustness to reformed queries). Across extensive experiments on two popular MoLM backbones, MolEdit delivers up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than baselines while maintaining efficiency. The code is available at: https://github.com/LzyFischer/MolEdit.

papers.title: Maximum entropy methods for extracting the learned features of deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural networks and extract the features they learn from input data using maximum entropy methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a maximum entropy method for interpreting deep neural networks by sampling sequences that preserve penultimate layer activations, allowing extraction of learned features such as motifs and nucleosome positioning signals.
papers.conclusion: The maximum entropy method provides a valuable tool for interpreting deep neural networks, particularly in biological sequence analysis, and demonstrates synergy between statistical physics and machine learning for extracting subtle sequence features.
papers.key_findings:
The MaxEnt method successfully captures XOR logic learned by a simple ANN, while Saliency Map and DeepLIFT methods fail to do so.
The MaxEnt method localizes CTCF binding motifs with better agreement with conventional motif discovery tools (MEME/FIMO) than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The MaxEnt method extracts nucleosome positioning signals, including periodic GC content at 10 bp intervals, more effectively than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The method can assess the importance of global sequence features (e.g., GC content) via a feature importance score derived from the variance of MCMC samples.
Features extracted by MaxEnt (low-variance principal components) can be used for classification, as demonstrated by a nearest neighbor classifier achieving 76% accuracy.
papers.limitation: The MaxEnt method is computationally expensive compared to Saliency Map and DeepLIFT due to MCMC sampling.
papers.abstract: New architectures of multilayer artificial neural networks and new methods for training them are rapidly revolutionizing the application of machine learning in diverse fields, including business, social science, physical sciences, and biology. Interpreting deep neural networks, however, currently remains elusive, and a critical challenge lies in understanding which meaningful features a network is actually learning. We present a general method for interpreting deep neural networks and extracting network-learned features from input data. We describe our algorithm in the context of biological sequence analysis. Our approach, based on ideas from statistical physics, samples from the maximum entropy distribution over possible sequences, anchored at an input sequence and subject to constraints implied by the empirical function learned by a network. Using our framework, we demonstrate that local transcription factor binding motifs can be identified from a network trained on ChIP-seq data and that nucleosome positioning signals are indeed learned by a network trained on chemical cleavage nucleosome maps. Imposing a further constraint on the maximum entropy distribution also allows us to probe whether a network is learning global sequence features, such as the high GC content in nucleosome-rich regions. This work thus provides valuable mathematical tools for interpreting and extracting learned features from feed-forward neural networks.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
