Interpretability analyses using SHAP and t-SNE reveal biologically significant sequence descriptors influencing druggability.
The proposed framework outperforms existing machine learning and ensemble-based methods in accuracy and interpretability.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Druggable proteins are essential targets in contemporary therapeutic discovery, and their precise identification is necessary for the progression of rational drug design. Traditional biochemical screening techniques are costly, laborious, and protracted, whereas current computational models typically attain only moderate efficacy and seldom offer robust statistical validation or biological interpretability. To mitigate these limitations, we offer a hybrid computational approach that amalgamates evolutionary and compositional information by merging Average Block-based Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (AB-PSSM) characteristics with Dipeptide Composition (DPC) into a 600-dimensional representation. The hybrid feature space was assessed utilizing three machine learning algorithms (support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) alongside three deep learning architectures (CapsBiLSTM, ResCapsNetPlus, and ResNet1D) following a rigorous five-fold out-of-fold cross-validation protocol to guarantee fairness and reproducibility. A thorough assessment revealed that the hybrid attributes significantly surpassed individual descriptors, with the SVM and CapsBiLSTM classifiers attaining classification accuracies of 90% and ROC-AUC and PR-AUC values surpassing 95%. The robustness and reliability were further validated by statistical analyses, including DeLong’s test, McNemar’s test, and bootstrap confidence intervals, demonstrating that the observed enhancements were substantial and consistent. Furthermore, interpretability investigations employing SHAP feature attribution and t-SNE visualization underscored biologically significant sequence descriptors as pivotal factors influencing druggability, thus mitigating the "black box" constraint inherent in numerous deep learning methodologies. This study presents a statistically validated, interpretable, and high-performing framework for predicting druggable proteins, which outperforms current machine learning and ensemble-based methods, establishing a clear basis for future applications in precision medicine and drug discovery.

papers.title: Neural Networks Trained to Solve Differential Equations Learn General Representations
papers.research_question: How can we measure the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks? What is the generality structure of layers in neural networks trained to solve differential equations?
papers.core_contribution: We develop an efficient method using SVCCA to measure layer generality across continuously-parametrized tasks, and apply it to show that in neural networks trained to solve differential equations, the first layer is general and deeper layers are successively more specific.
papers.conclusion: We presented a method for measuring layer generality using SVCCA, found that first layers of DENNs are general and deeper layers are more specific, validated with transfer learning, and visualized the general components as generalized coordinates.
papers.key_findings:
The first hidden layer is general, and deeper layers become progressively more specific.
The SVCCA-based method agrees with transfer learning experiments but is much faster, especially for continuously-parametrized problems.
The general components of the first layer can be visualized as generalized coordinates that capture regions of interest in the input domain.
Network width affects layer generality: intrinsic dimensionality saturates with width, reproducibility increases with width, and specificity varies with width and layer depth.
Very wide networks may have training dynamics that affect convergence and generality measurements.
papers.limitation:
SVCCA is numerically unstable when correlation values are very close to each other, making component sorting ill-conditioned.
Very wide networks may have broad minima in the loss landscape, causing training to terminate before optimal convergence, potentially affecting generality measurements.
future_direction: Explore the behavior of layer generality at very large network widths.
Develop component analyses that search for closely-coupled components to improve numerical stability.
Investigate different training protocols for very wide DENNs to ensure proper convergence.
papers.abstract: We introduce a technique based on the singular vector canonical correlation analysis (SVCCA) for measuring the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks. We illustrate this method by studying generality in neural networks trained to solve parametrized boundary value problems based on the Poisson partial differential equation. We find that the first hidden layer is general, and that deeper layers are successively more specific. Next, we validate our method against an existing technique that measures layer generality using transfer learning experiments. We find excellent agreement between the two methods, and note that our method is much faster, particularly for continuously-parametrized problems. Finally, we visualize the general representations of the first layers, and interpret them as generalized coordinates over the input domain.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Comparing the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.research_question: How do different universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) encode chemical information in their latent features, and how do these encodings compare across models, training datasets, and training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically analyzes the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) using feature reconstruction errors, revealing that different models encode chemical information in distinct ways and that these differences can be quantified.
papers.conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize atomistic ML models; feature reconstruction error metrics provide a principled foundation for more transparent, interpretable, and robust model design.
papers.key_findings:
uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors.
When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol.
Fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features.
Atom-level features can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information.
Backbone features contain more information than last-layer features and are more consistent across models.
papers.abstract: The past few years have seen the development of ``universal'' machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) capable of approximating the ground-state potential energy surface across a wide range of chemical structures and compositions with reasonable accuracy. While these models differ in the architecture and the dataset used, they share the ability to compress a staggering amount of chemical information into descriptive latent features. Herein, we systematically analyze what the different uMLIPs have learned by quantitatively assessing the relative information content of their latent features with feature reconstruction errors, and observing how the trends are affected by the choice of training set and training protocol. We find that uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors. When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol of choice. We also observe that fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features. Finally, we discuss how atom-level features, which are directly output by MLIPs, can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information about the variability across the atomic environments within a given system.

papers.title: Interpretation of machine learning models using shapley values: application to compound potency and multi-target activity predictions
papers.research_question: How can Shapley values (SHAP) be used to interpret machine learning models, and how does the model-independent kernel SHAP compare to the exact tree SHAP for decision tree models? Additionally, how can SHAP be applied to interpret compound potency predictions and multi-target activity predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper evaluates and applies the SHAP methodology for interpreting machine learning models in chemoinformatics, demonstrating that kernel SHAP provides reliable approximations compared to exact tree SHAP, and shows SHAP's utility for interpreting compound potency predictions and multi-target activity predictions.
papers.conclusion: The SHAP methodology enables interpretation of ML models and their predictions, providing feature importance values for individual predictions. The kernel SHAP approach is generally applicable and yields reliable approximations compared to exact tree SHAP, shedding light on the black box nature of ML models for practical applications in drug discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Kernel SHAP and tree SHAP yield highly correlated feature importance rankings for decision tree-based models in activity and potency prediction.
SHAP analysis provides meaningful explanations for compound potency predictions and multi-target activity predictions, revealing features that drive model decisions.
SHAP helps rationalize model errors by identifying features whose absence or presence leads to incorrect predictions.
papers.limitation: SHAP-based feature prioritization identifies features that determine ML predictions, but these features may not always be responsible for specific activities.

papers.title: DeepFRI Demystified: Interpretability vs. Accuracy in AI Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How interpretable and robust is the DeepFRI model for protein function prediction, and how do different explainability methods compare in highlighting influential residues?
papers.core_contribution: The study reveals that DeepFRI's predictions prioritize conserved structural motifs over functional residues, and different explainability methods offer varying levels of granularity, highlighting trade-offs between accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DeepFRI has strengths in conserved domains but limitations in complex proteins, and interpretability methods must be chosen carefully to balance robustness and precision for biological insights.
papers.key_findings:
DeepFRI's predictions often prioritize structural motifs like beta sheets over functional residues, leading to potential misinterpretations.
GradCAM provides broad heatmaps with low sparsity, Excitation Backpropagation offers binary masks with high sparsity, and PGExplainer gives precise per-residue scores.
The model is robust to mutations, requiring over 200 mutations in some cases to cause misclassification, but this may overlook biologically significant changes.
Sparsity analysis shows that explainability methods vary significantly, with GradCAM being the least sparse and Excitation Backpropagation the most sparse.
Using an ensemble of explainability methods can highlight high-confidence residues and areas of epistemic uncertainty.
papers.limitation:
DeepFRI prioritizes structural motifs over functional residues, potentially leading to inaccurate interpretations of protein function.
The model's robustness to mutations may cause it to overlook biologically significant changes unless a large fraction of the structure is disrupted.
DeepFRI's message-passing can overlook long-range or allosteric effects in complex regulatory proteins.
future_direction: Guide experimental validation through targeted mutagenesis based on explainability results.
Fuse GCN topology with per-residue embeddings from protein language models for improved sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Machine learning technologies for protein function prediction are black box models. Despite their potential to identify key drug targets with high accuracy and accelerate therapy development, the adoption of these methods depends on verifying their findings. This study evaluates DeepFRI, a leading Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) based tool, using advanced explainability techniques (GradCAM, Excitation Backpropagation, and PGExplainer) and adversarial robustness tests. Our findings reveal that the model's predictions often prioritize conserved motifs over truly deterministic residues, complicating the identification of functional sites. Quantitative analyses show that explainability methods differ significantly in granularity, with GradCAM providing broad relevance and PGExplainer pinpointing specific active sites. These results highlight tradeoffs between accuracy and interpretability, suggesting areas for improvement in DeepFRI's architecture to enhance its trustworthiness in drug discovery and regulatory settings.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Analysis of a convolutional neural network for predicting unsteady volume wake flow fields
papers.research_question: How does a convolutional neural network system learn and predict three-dimensional unsteady wake flow dynamics in different flow regimes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a multi-scale CNN system for predicting 3D unsteady wake flow and investigates its mechanisms, showing that convolution layers integrate and transport wavenumber information to extract flow structures, and that redundant feature maps can be identified and removed to reduce model size without loss of performance.
papers.conclusion: The CNN system predicts wake flow by integrating and transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers, extracting representations of flow dynamics. Redundant feature maps can be removed based on structural similarity, significantly reducing model size without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN system predicts flow in different regimes by transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers.
Feature maps extract similar flow structures (e.g., braid shear layers and shedding vortices) across different Reynolds numbers.
Convolution layers integrate information from all input flow variables and histories, with more recent histories having larger contributions.
Redundant feature maps can be identified using structural similarity (SSIM) and removed, reducing the number of weights by 85% without affecting prediction performance.
papers.abstract: A predictive convolutional neural network is developed to predict the future of three-dimensional unsteady wake flow from past information of flow velocity and pressure. The developed network is found to be capable of predicting vortex dynamics at distinctive flow regimes with flow structures at different scales. Mechanisms of the network on predicting vortex dynamics at two distinctive flow regimes, the mode-B shedding regime and the turbulent wake regime, are investigated. Information in feature maps of the network is visualized and quantitatively assessed to investigate the encoded flow structures. A Fourier analysis is conducted to investigate the mechanisms of the network on learning fluid motions with distinctive flow scales. The transformation of information from the input to prediction layers of the network is tracked to examine how the network transforms the input information for prediction. Structural similarities among feature maps in the network are evaluated to reduce the number of feature maps containing redundant flow structures, which allows reduction of the size of the network without affecting prediction performance.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the Local Interaction Basis (LIB) method find interpretable and sparsely-interacting features in neural networks, particularly in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Local Interaction Basis (LIB), a method to transform neural network activations into a basis of computationally-relevant and sparsely-interacting features, and shows it works on toy models but not on language models.
papers.conclusion: LIB is promising on toy models but does not achieve interpretable and sparsely-interacting features on language models, likely due to the assumption of a linear non-overcomplete basis.
papers.key_findings:
LIB identifies more computationally-relevant features than PCA in modular addition and CIFAR-10 models.
LIB features interact more sparsely than PCA features in CIFAR-10 and some layers of language models.
LIB does not produce more interpretable features than PCA in language models.
Integrated gradient interaction graphs can aid circuit discovery in toy models.
LIB does not reveal modular structure in language models.
papers.limitation: LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models.
future_direction: Generalizing LIB to overcomplete bases to handle features in superposition.
Exploring other ways to average attributions over the dataset.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the behavior of neural networks by reverse-engineering their internal computations. However, current methods struggle to find clear interpretations of neural network activations because a decomposition of activations into computational features is missing. Individual neurons or model components do not cleanly correspond to distinct features or functions. We present a novel interpretability method that aims to overcome this limitation by transforming the activations of the network into a new basis - the Local Interaction Basis (LIB). LIB aims to identify computational features by removing irrelevant activations and interactions. Our method drops irrelevant activation directions and aligns the basis with the singular vectors of the Jacobian matrix between adjacent layers. It also scales features based on their importance for downstream computation, producing an interaction graph that shows all computationally-relevant features and interactions in a model. We evaluate the effectiveness of LIB on modular addition and CIFAR-10 models, finding that it identifies more computationally-relevant features that interact more sparsely, compared to principal component analysis. However, LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models. We conclude that LIB is a promising theory-driven approach for analyzing neural networks, but in its current form is not applicable to large language models.

papers.title: Robust Deep Interpretable Features for Binary Image Classification
papers.research_question: How can we find linearly separated latent representations? What implications on performance do such latent representations have? How can we interpret a model using linearly separated latent representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Deep Interpretable Features (DIF) framework, which combines deep generative models (IntroVAE) with a supervised objective based on kernel two-sample testing (ME objective) to encourage linear separation in the latent space, leading to more interpretable and robust features for binary image classification.
papers.conclusion: Combining deep generative modeling with a supervised kernel-based two-sample testing objective encourages separation between classes in the latent space, resulting in more interpretable features, improved classification performance with sparse linear models, and increased robustness to adversarial attacks.
papers.key_findings:
DIF achieves better separation in the latent space compared to vanilla IntroVAE and a logistic separation objective, as visualized via UMAP.
DIF improves classification performance with sparser L1-regularized logistic regression models and in some cases outperforms CNN classifiers on test data.
Models trained with DIF exhibit improved robustness to adversarial attacks compared to vanilla models.
DIF isolates interpretable features that correspond to meaningful visual changes (e.g., facial hair, digit width, non-organ matter in lungs).
The imposed linear structure in the latent space leads to smooth latent traversals between classes without artifacts.
papers.limitation: The results presented for the COVID-19 x-ray data are for illustration purposes and further work is needed to draw any medically relevant conclusions based on them.
papers.abstract: The problem of interpretability for binary image classification is considered through the lens of kernel two-sample tests and generative modeling. A feature extraction framework coined Deep Interpretable Features (DIF) is developed, which is used in combination with IntroVAE, a generative model capable of high-resolution image synthesis. Experimental results on a variety of datasets, including COVID-19 chest x-rays demonstrate the benefits of combining deep generative models with the ideas from kernel-based hypothesis testing in moving towards more robust interpretable deep generative models.

papers.title: Warp: a method for neural network interpretability applied to gene expression profiles
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be interpreted in the context of gene expression analysis to recover meaningful information on a sample-specific basis?
papers.core_contribution: Warping is a method for neural network interpretability that recovers sample-specific gene signatures by interpolating in input or representation space, demonstrating effectiveness on linearly and non-linearly separable datasets.
papers.conclusion: Warping shows promise as a flexible method for post-hoc interpretation of neural networks in computational biology, enabling the examination of class gene signatures with sample-specific insights.
papers.key_findings:
Warping works well on non-linearly separable datasets like XOR, allowing data points to migrate across decision boundaries.
The method provides sample-specific bias vectors, highlighting individual adjustments needed for classification changes.
In a VAE-based approach, warping recovers biologically meaningful gene expression adjustments, such as suppressing surfactant genes and boosting kidney-specific genes to change phenotype classification.
papers.limitation:
Linear interpolation assumes the data manifold is continuous in input space, which may lead to adversarial examples.
Reconstruction blurriness caused by the variational autoencoder encoding.
future_direction: Determine how destructive warps are to other gene signatures within samples.
Overcome reconstruction blurriness caused by the VAE encoding.
papers.abstract: We show a proof of principle for warping, a method to interpret the inner working of neural networks in the context of gene expression analysis. Warping is an efficient way to gain insight to the inner workings of neural nets and make them more interpretable. We demonstrate the ability of warping to recover meaningful information for a given class on a samplespecific individual basis. We found warping works well in both linearly and nonlinearly separable datasets. These encouraging results show that warping has a potential to be the answer to neural networks interpretability in computational biology.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Words ? Exploring framework for hidden state reasoning
papers.research_question: Can reasoning in a continuous latent space, as opposed to the language space, lead to more efficient and effective reasoning in LLMs, particularly for tasks requiring planning and search?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Coconut, a method for reasoning in a continuous latent space by feeding the last hidden state back as the next input embedding, which enables emergent tree search behavior and improves reasoning efficiency and accuracy on certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in latent space leads to advanced emergent behaviors like BFS, and Coconut enhances LLM performance across reasoning tasks, with potential for future scaling and research.
papers.key_findings:
Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require planning and search (ProsQA).
Continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, enabling a breadth-first search (BFS) pattern.
Coconut provides a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency (fewer tokens) compared to CoT.
The multi-stage training curriculum is crucial for learning latent reasoning; without it, performance drops.
Increasing the number of continuous thoughts per reasoning step (c) can improve performance up to a point.
papers.limitation:
Training requires a multi-stage curriculum; without it, performance drops significantly.
Larger models (Llama) show less pronounced gains, possibly due to extensive language-focused pre-training.
Training efficiency is challenging due to sequential forward passes, limiting parallelism.
future_direction: Refine and scale latent reasoning to pretraining for better generalization.
Combine iCoT and Coconut for improved training.
Develop better strategies for learning reasoning in latent space without supervision from language reasoning chains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically constrained to reason in the language space, where they express the reasoning process through a chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems. However, the language space may not always be optimal for reasoning. Most word tokens primarily ensure textual coherence and are not essential for reasoning, while some critical tokens require complex planning and pose challenges to LLMs. To explore the potential of reasoning beyond language, we introduce a new paradigm called Coconut (Chain of Continuous Thought). Coconut utilizes the last hidden state of the LLM as a representation of the reasoning state, termed "continuous thought." Instead of decoding this state into words, we feed it back to the model as the next input embedding directly in the continuous space. This latent reasoning paradigm enables an advanced reasoning pattern, where continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, allowing the model to perform a breadth-first search (BFS) rather than committing prematurely to a single deterministic path as in CoT. Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require substantial search during planning and achieves a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: The Computational Complexity of Circuit Discovery for Inner Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the computational complexity of circuit discovery queries for inner interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a complexity analysis of circuit discovery queries, showing that many are intractable (NP-hard, Σp2-hard, etc.), but also identifies tractable relaxations such as quasi-minimal circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuit discovery for inner interpretability is computationally challenging, but identifies tractable relaxations and provides a framework for understanding the complexity of interpretability queries.
papers.key_findings:
Many circuit discovery queries (e.g., sufficient circuit, circuit ablation) are NP-hard or Σp2-hard.
Some queries remain fixed-parameter intractable (W[1]-hard) even when parameterizing by model depth or other features.
Some queries are inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes.
There is a formal separation between local and global query complexity, which helps explain interpretability illusions.
Quasi-minimal circuit queries are tractable (PTIME) and retain useful affordances for description and control.
future_direction: Empirical and formal characterization of learned weights to inform average-case analyses.
Exploring more parameters for fixed-parameter tractability in circuit discovery queries.
Designing queries that rely on mid-level abstractions to bridge circuits and human-intelligible algorithms.
papers.abstract: Many proposed applications of neural networks in machine learning, cognitive/brain science, and society hinge on the feasibility of inner interpretability via circuit discovery. This calls for empirical and theoretical explorations of viable algorithmic options. Despite advances in the design and testing of heuristics, there are concerns about their scalability and faithfulness at a time when we lack understanding of the complexity properties of the problems they are deployed to solve. To address this, we study circuit discovery with classical and parameterized computational complexity theory: (1) we describe a conceptual scaffolding to reason about circuit finding queries in terms of affordances for description, explanation, prediction and control; (2) we formalize a comprehensive set of queries for mechanistic explanation, and propose a formal framework for their analysis; (3) we use it to settle the complexity of many query variants and relaxations of practical interest on multi-layer perceptrons. Our findings reveal a challenging complexity landscape. Many queries are intractable, remain fixed-parameter intractable relative to model/circuit features, and inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes. To navigate this landscape, we prove there exist transformations to tackle some of these hard problems with better-understood heuristics, and prove the tractability or fixed-parameter tractability of more modest queries which retain useful affordances. This framework allows us to understand the scope and limits of interpretability queries, explore viable options, and compare their resource demands on existing and future architectures.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Low-$N$ Protein Function Prediction and Design
papers.research_question: How effective are sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for protein function prediction and design in low-data (low-N) regimes?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a compact and biologically meaningful latent space that improves low-N fitness prediction and enables effective protein design via latent steering, outperforming ESM2 baselines.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a powerful tool for low-N protein function prediction and design, expanding the biologist's toolkit for resource-constrained applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform ESM2 baselines in 58% of fitness extrapolation tasks with as few as 24 training sequences.
SAEs design top-fitness variants in 83% of cases via latent steering, compared to designing with ESM2 alone.
The sparse latent space of SAEs encodes biologically interpretable motifs and compresses relevant information, reducing overfitting in low-N regimes.
Analysis of steered variants reveals that SAEs activate latents corresponding to known biological motifs such as active sites, allosteric sites, and epistatic sites.
SAE performance is influenced by the number of available multiple sequence alignment (MSA) sequences for training.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to a set of proteins; it could be extended to other proteins with clinically relevant functions such as antibiotic resistance and viral replication.
SAE performance is strongly influenced by the number of MSA sequences available for training; strategies are needed for robust training when MSAs are shallow.
Protein engineering experiments rely on in-silico fitness models; wet lab validation is necessary to verify function.
Designed variants are constrained to a maximum of five mutations away from the wildtype; beyond this radius, designing highly-functional sequences is difficult with a single predictive latent.
In-silico evaluation tools become less reliable the further away variants are from the wildtype.
future_direction: Extend evaluation to other proteins with clinically relevant functions.
Explore strategies for robust SAE training when multiple sequence alignments are shallow or unavailable.
Couple SAE steering with physics-based tools like Rosetta to jointly optimize for both function and stability.
papers.abstract: Predicting protein function from amino acid sequence remains a central challenge in data-scarce (low-$N$) regimes, limiting machine learning-guided protein design when only small amounts of assay-labeled sequence-function data are available. Protein language models (pLMs) have advanced the field by providing evolutionary-informed embeddings and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have enabled decomposition of these embeddings into interpretable latent variables that capture structural and functional features. However, the effectiveness of SAEs for low-$N$ function prediction and protein design has not been systematically studied. Herein, we evaluate SAEs trained on fine-tuned ESM2 embeddings across diverse fitness extrapolation and protein engineering tasks. We show that SAEs, with as few as 24 sequences, consistently outperform or compete with their ESM2 baselines in fitness prediction, indicating that their sparse latent space encodes compact and biologically meaningful representations that generalize more effectively from limited data. Moreover, steering predictive latents exploits biological motifs in pLM representations, yielding top-fitness variants in 83% of cases compared to designing with ESM2 alone.

papers.title: Studying Cross-cluster Modularity in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of training neural networks to be modular using a clusterability loss on interpretability, such as task specialization and circuit size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a clusterability measure and loss function to train neural networks to be modular. Shows that modular models do not exhibit more task specialization but have smaller circuits, aiding interpretability.
papers.conclusion: A simple regularizer can split neural network layers into non-interacting modules, but these modules do not yield expected interpretability benefits like task specialization. However, modularity improves circuit size and search space without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models are not modular; clusters are highly enmeshed.
Training with clusterability loss effectively increases modularity in models.
Modular models do not show increased task specialization compared to non-modular models.
Modular models have smaller effective circuits, reducing circuit size.
Theoretical analysis indicates modularity simplifies function spaces and reduces the number of features.
papers.limitation: The modularity metric does not lead to clear interpretability benefits such as task specialization.
future_direction: Investigate alternative regularizers for interpretability benefits.
Build an automated subtask detection mechanism.
papers.abstract: An approach to improve neural network interpretability is via clusterability, i.e., splitting a model into disjoint clusters that can be studied independently. We define a measure for clusterability and show that pre-trained models form highly enmeshed clusters via spectral graph clustering. We thus train models to be more modular using a "clusterability loss" function that encourages the formation of non-interacting clusters. We then investigate the emerging properties of these highly clustered models. We find our trained clustered models do not exhibit more task specialization, but do form smaller circuits. We investigate CNNs trained on MNIST and CIFAR, small transformers trained on modular addition, and GPT-2 and Pythia on the Wiki dataset, and Gemma on a Chemistry dataset. This investigation shows what to expect from clustered models.

papers.title: Patterning: The Dual of Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the dual problem to interpretability? The paper introduces patterning as the dual: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data leads to it.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces patterning as the dual of interpretability, using susceptibilities to derive data interventions that steer internal structure formation in neural networks, demonstrated in small language models and a synthetic task.
papers.conclusion: Patterning provides a principled approach to steering generalization by inverting the susceptibility relationship, with potential applications to AI alignment and control of internal structure.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting training data along the second principal susceptibility direction can accelerate or delay the formation of the induction circuit.
In the parentheses balancing task, patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution.
Susceptibility-guided interventions produce predictable changes in internal structures.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use small models (3M parameters) and simple tasks.
Susceptibility estimation is computationally expensive.
Focus on one-off interventions made at the start of training, not online control.
Theoretical framework assumes infinitesimal perturbations, while practical interventions are finite; understanding when the linear approximation breaks down is important.
Connection between observables and downstream behavior (e.g., safety properties) requires further study.
future_direction: Develop online control (adjusting data distribution dynamically during training).
Scale to larger models and more efficient methods.
Study the connection to safety properties and AI alignment applications.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how neural networks generalize beyond their training data by reverse-engineering their internal structures. We introduce patterning as the dual problem: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data produces it. Our approach is based on susceptibilities, which measure how posterior expectation values of observables respond to infinitesimal shifts in the data distribution. Inverting this linear response relationship yields the data intervention that steers the model toward a target internal configuration. We demonstrate patterning in a small language model, showing that re-weighting training data along principal susceptibility directions can accelerate or delay the formation of structure, such as the induction circuit. In a synthetic parentheses balancing task where multiple algorithms achieve perfect training accuracy, we show that patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution. These results establish that the same mathematical framework used to read internal structure can be inverted to write it.

papers.title: Tensor Product Decomposition Networks: Uncovering Representations of Structure Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode compositional symbolic structure in their vector representations, and do they use tensor product representations?
papers.core_contribution: TPDNs show that RNNs can learn structured representations similar to tensor product representations for artificial tasks, but for real-world NLP tasks, representations are less structured, approximated by bag-of-words, suggesting training tasks may not induce robust structural representations.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on structure-sensitive tasks learn representations well approximated by tensor-product representations, but sentence encoders for NLP tasks show less structure, approximated by bag-of-words.
papers.key_findings:
TPDNs can closely approximate RNN representations for digit sequence copying tasks, indicating structured encoding.
Linear RNNs use bidirectional role schemes, while tree RNNs use tree position roles for representation.
For natural language processing models like InferSent and Skip-thought, representations are well approximated by bag-of-words, showing limited structure.
The nature of learned representations is related to the RNN's structure and the training task.
Training tasks influence whether networks discover structured or unstructured representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an analysis technique for understanding compositional structure present in the vector representations used by neural networks. The inner workings of neural networks are notoriously difficult to understand, and in particular it is far from clear how they manage to perform remarkably well on tasks that depend on compositional structure even though they use continuous vector representations with no obvious compositional structure. Using our analysis technique, we show that the representations of these models can be closely approximated by Tensor Product Representations, a type of interpretable structure that lends significant insight into the workings of these hard-to-interpret models.

papers.title: The Representational Status of Deep Learning Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether deep learning models are representational in a relational sense and to what extent they are semantically decomposable.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that deep learning models are representational in a relational sense, but they are minimally semantically decomposable (holistic) models, and there is no evidence that they encode locally decomposable representations of their targets.
papers.conclusion: Deep learning models are best conceived as holistic representational models, and interpreting them as locally decomposable is epistemically risky.
papers.key_findings:
Deep learning models are representational in a relational sense (they have real targets).
Deep learning models are not locally semantically decomposable; their representational capacity is global/holistic.
Opacity blocks a full assessment of the representational status of deep learning models.
Attempts to interpret deep learning models as locally decomposable are underdetermined and unfalsifiable.
The degree of idealization of a deep learning model cannot be evaluated due to opacity.
future_direction: Future analysis on situating deep learning models in the wider class of holistic models.
Exploring how deep learning models can be leveraged for scientific discovery without relying on local decomposability.
papers.abstract: This paper aims to clarify the representational status of Deep Learning Models (DLMs). While commonly referred to as 'representations', what this entails is ambiguous due to a conflation of functional and relational conceptions of representation. This paper argues that while DLMs represent their targets in a relational sense, in general, we have no good reason to believe that DLMs encode locally semantically decomposable representations of their targets. That is, the representational capacity these models have is largely global, rather than decomposable into stable, local subrepresentations. This result has immediate implications for explainable AI (XAI) and directs attention toward exploring the global relational nature of deep learning representations and their relationship both to models more generally to understand their potential role in future scientific inquiry.

papers.title: Interpretable and Explainable Machine Learning for Materials Science and Chemistry
papers.research_question: How can interpretability and explainability techniques be applied to machine learning models in materials science and chemistry to improve scientific discovery, build trust, and unveil correlations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper summarizes applications of interpretability and explainability techniques for materials science and chemistry, discussing how these techniques can improve scientific studies by providing insights beyond predictive power, building trust, and revealing unexpected correlations.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable machine learning is crucial for realizing the true potential of ML in materials science, and human experts who embrace interpretable ML will replace those who do not.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability in scientific machine learning involves trade-offs between explainability, completeness, and scientific validity (correctness).
Intrinsically interpretable models (e.g., linear models, decision trees) offer direct interpretations but may lack correctness for complex phenomena.
Extrinsic interpretation methods (e.g., SHAP, salience maps, attention mechanisms) can provide insights for complex models like deep neural networks.
Interpretability techniques can generate scientific hypotheses and guide experiments, but they require careful validation to avoid over-interpretation and confusion with causation.
Future directions include integrating uncertainty estimates into explanations and combining machine learning with causal inference for more robust insights.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability methods may lead to over-interpretation, especially when searching for physical explanations, and can be misled by shortcut learning or unrealistic feature combinations.
Explanations from machine learning models do not have strong causal guarantees and are susceptible to confounding effects, requiring secondary confirmation by experiments or simulation.
There is a trade-off between interpretability, completeness, and correctness in model explanations, meaning no single explanation may fully capture the model's operation and physical reality.
future_direction: Integrating uncertainty estimates into model explanations to improve confidence in insights.
Combining machine learning with causal inference to uncover cause-and-effect relationships from materials data.
Using advanced methods like autoencoders and sparse regression to directly extract physical knowledge from noisy experimental data.
papers.abstract:
While the uptake of data-driven approaches for materials science and
chemistry is at an exciting, early stage, to realise the true potential of
machine learning models for successful scientific discovery, they must have
qualities beyond purely predictive power. The predictions and inner workings of
models should provide a certain degree of explainability by human experts,
permitting the identification of potential model issues or limitations,
building trust on model predictions and unveiling unexpected correlations that
may lead to scientific insights. In this work, we summarize applications of
interpretability and explainability techniques for materials science and
chemistry and discuss how these techniques can improve the outcome of
scientific studies. We discuss various challenges for interpretable machine
learning in materials science and, more broadly, in scientific settings. In
particular, we emphasize the risks of inferring causation or reaching
generalization by purely interpreting machine learning models and the need of
uncertainty estimates for model explanations. Finally, we showcase a number of
exciting developments in other fields that could benefit interpretability in
material science and chemistry problems.

papers.title: Language Ranker: A Metric for Quantifying LLM Performance Across High and Low-Resource Languages
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the performance of LLMs across different languages, especially low-resource ones, using internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Language Ranker, an intrinsic metric that benchmarks and ranks languages based on LLM performance by comparing internal representations to an English baseline, revealing performance disparities between high and low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: Language Ranker effectively quantifies LLM performance across languages, showing that high-resource languages perform better and are more evenly distributed in embedding space, and that performance correlates with training data proportion.
papers.key_findings:
High-resource languages exhibit higher similarity scores with English, indicating better performance, while low-resource languages show lower similarity scores.
There is a strong correlation between LLM performance in a language and the proportion of that language in the pre-training corpus.
High-resource languages are more evenly distributed in the embedding space, while low-resource languages cluster narrowly.
The proposed cosine similarity metric correlates with performance on reasoning tasks (ARC and MMLU).
Different LLMs show consistent language performance rankings, as measured by rank correlation.
future_direction: Design more comprehensive benchmarks to measure LLM capabilities in different languages.
Develop nuanced evaluation metrics that capture syntactic and semantic understanding across language families.
Apply Language Ranker insights to guide the development of more balanced multilingual training datasets and inform architectural improvements.
papers.abstract: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on extensive text corpora, which are often unevenly distributed across languages. This imbalance results in LLMs performing significantly better on high-resource languages like English, German, and French, while their capabilities in low-resource languages remain inadequate. Currently, there is a lack of quantitative methods to evaluate the performance of LLMs in these low-resource languages. To address this gap, we propose the Language Ranker, an intrinsic metric designed to benchmark and rank languages based on LLM performance using internal representations. By comparing the LLM's internal representation of various languages against a baseline derived from English, we can assess the model's multilingual capabilities in a robust and language-agnostic manner. Our analysis reveals that high-resource languages exhibit higher similarity scores with English, demonstrating superior performance, while low-resource languages show lower similarity scores, underscoring the effectiveness of our metric in assessing language-specific capabilities. Besides, the experiments show that there is a strong correlation between the LLM’s performance in different languages and the proportion of those languages in its pre-training corpus. These insights underscore the efficacy of the Language Ranker as a tool for evaluating LLM performance across different languages, particularly those with limited resources.

papers.title: Analysis of Atomistic Representations Using Weighted Skip-Connections
papers.research_question: How do weighted skip-connections help in understanding the relative importance of interaction blocks in SchNet for property prediction, and how does this depend on chemical composition and configurational degrees of freedom?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sc-SchNet, a modified SchNet architecture with weighted skip-connections, enabling analysis of the relative importance of interaction blocks for property prediction, revealing dependencies on molecular structure and dataset.
papers.conclusion: sc-SchNet enables interpretable analysis of atomistic representations, showing that contribution weights vary with dataset and molecular structure, providing insights into model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
sc-SchNet performs similarly to SchNet on energy and force prediction tasks.
During training on QM9, contribution weights shift from early layers to later layers as the model learns.
For MD17 trajectories, atom type embeddings have constant contribution due to fixed chemical composition.
Higher interaction blocks are more important for larger and more flexible molecules like salicylic acid and aspirin.
The relative weighting of interaction blocks depends on the chemical composition and configurational degrees of freedom of the molecules.
future_direction: Investigate if interaction coefficients encode information on locality of different molecular properties.
Explore relation to fundamental modes of molecular motion in the context of the MD17 molecules.
papers.abstract: In this work, we extend the SchNet architecture by using weighted skip connections to assemble the final representation. This enables us to study the relative importance of each interaction block for property prediction. We demonstrate on both the QM9 and MD17 dataset that their relative weighting depends strongly on the chemical composition and configurational degrees of freedom of the molecules which opens the path towards a more detailed understanding of machine learning models for molecules.

papers.title: Visualizing a neural network that develops quantum perturbation theory
papers.research_question: Whether neural networks, when trained on data from a quantum scattering problem, can develop the same perturbation theory structure as derived by human physicists.
papers.core_contribution: The neural network develops perturbation theory order by order when trained to predict scattering lengths from potentials, and this understanding inspires an empirical formula that works beyond perturbative regimes.
papers.conclusion: The neural network develops perturbation theory order by order, providing a positive answer that machines can discover the same physical laws as humans, and this understanding can shed light on more sophisticated problems.
papers.key_findings:
For shallow potentials, neurons in the first hidden layer approximate the first-order Born approximation, computing the integral of the potential.
For deeper potentials, additional neurons appear that approximate the second-order Born approximation, corresponding to eigenvectors of the kernel matrix.
The network sequentially develops perturbation theory as potential depth increases, mirroring human-derived physics.
Reducing the first hidden layer to one neuron still yields accurate predictions, leading to an empirical formula for scattering lengths.
The empirical formula works well even beyond the weakly interacting regime, outperforming the second-order Born approximation.
future_direction: Generalize the formalism to more complicated quantum few-body and many-body problems.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the question whether the empirical fitting of data by neural networks can yield the same structure of physical laws, we apply neural networks to a quantum-mechanical two-body scattering problem with short-range potentials---a problem that by itself plays an important role in many branches of physics. After training, the neural network can accurately predict $s$-wave scattering length, which governs the low-energy scattering physics. By visualizing the neural network, we show that it develops perturbation theory order by order when the potential depth increases, without solving the Schr\"odinger equation or obtaining the wave function explicitly. The result provides an important benchmark to the machine-assisted physics research or even automated machine learning physics laws.

papers.title: An Investigation of Interpretability Techniques for Deep Learning in Predictive Process Analytics
papers.research_question: Do patients with specific types of cancer have a targeted set of medical activities associated with them? What explainability mechanisms are appropriate for understanding predictions in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This paper applies interpretability techniques (autoencoders and LIME) to deep learning and random forest models on medical event logs, providing insights into cancer prediction and model decisions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques like autoencoders and LIME can provide meaningful insights into model predictions for medical event logs, aiding in understanding and trust.
papers.key_findings:
