A seeming prerequisite for this is some form of modularity: for different parts of the network to operate independently enough to be understood in isolation, and to implement distinct interpretable sub-routines.To find modular structure inside neural networks, we initially use the tools of graphical clustering. A network is clusterable in this sense if it can be divided into groups of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that a trained neural network is typically more clusterable than randomly initialized networks, and often clusterable relative to random networks with the same distribution of weights as the trained network. We investigate factors that promote clusterability, and also develop novel methods targeted at that end.For modularity to be valuable for understanding neural networks, it needs to have some sort of functional relevance.The type of functional relevance we target is local specialization of functionality. A neural network is locally specialized to the extent that parts of its computational graph can be abstractly represented as performing some comprehensible sub-task relevant to the overall task. We propose two proxies for local specialization: importance, which reflects how valuable sets of neurons are to network performance; and coherence, which reflects how consistently their neurons associate with features of the inputs. We then operationalize these proxies using techniques conventionally used to interpret individual neurons, applying them instead to groups of neurons produced by graph clustering algorithms. Our results show that clustering succeeds at finding groups of neurons that are important and coherent, although not all groups of neurons found are so.We conclude with a case study of using more standard interpretability tools, designed to understand the features being represented by directions in activation space, applying them to the analysis of neural networks trained on the reward function of the game CoinRun. Despite our networks achieving a low test loss, the application of interpretability tools shows that networks do not adequately represent relevant features and badly mispredict reward out of distribution. That said, these tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are in fact performing. This not only illustrates the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behaviour, but motivates it: if we take these networks as models of 'motivation systems' of policies trained by reinforcement learning, the conclusion is that such networks may competently pursue the wrong objectives when deployed in richer environments, indicating a need for interpretability techniques to shed light on generalization behaviour.

papers.title: NN2Poly: A polynomial representation for deep feed-forward artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: How can an explicit polynomial model be obtained to accurately represent an already trained fully-connected feed-forward artificial neural network (MLP), extending previous work limited to single hidden layers to arbitrarily deep networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces NN2Poly, a theoretical and practical method to obtain an explicit polynomial representation of a pre-trained multilayer perceptron (MLP) for regression and classification tasks, enhancing model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: NN2Poly is a promising method for obtaining polynomial representations of MLPs, providing interpretability and insights into the learned patterns, with applications to tabular data and potential for future extensions to other data types.
papers.key_findings:
NN2Poly can accurately approximate the predictions of a trained MLP with a polynomial under certain weight constraints and Taylor expansion conditions.
The method is effective for both simulated data and real-world tabular datasets (Boston Housing, Forest Covertype) in regression and classification settings.
Imposing a maximum polynomial order (Qmax) and using equivalence classes of multisets significantly improves computational efficiency.
The obtained polynomial coefficients provide interpretability, allowing insights into feature importance and interactions learned by the neural network.
The method reveals when a neural network fails to properly learn a class, as seen in the Covertype dataset where class 5 was never predicted.
papers.limitation:
The method requires synaptic potentials to be near zero for the Taylor expansion to be accurate, which may necessitate weight constraints during training.
Scalability is a challenge for high-dimensional data due to the combinatorial growth in polynomial terms and multiset partitions.
future_direction: Improve efficiency and scalability to apply the method to larger networks and higher-dimensional problems.
Extend applications to non-tabular data like images or audio.
Study the impact of different regularization techniques on the effectiveness of NN2Poly.
papers.abstract: Interpretability of neural networks and their underlying theoretical behavior remain an open field of study even after the great success of their practical applications, particularly with the emergence of deep learning. In this work, NN2Poly is proposed: a theoretical approach to obtain an explicit polynomial model that provides an accurate representation of an already trained fully-connected feed-forward artificial neural network (a multilayer perceptron or MLP). This approach extends a previous idea proposed in the literature, which was limited to single hidden layer networks, to work with arbitrarily deep MLPs in both regression and classification tasks. NN2Poly uses a Taylor expansion on the activation function, at each layer, and then applies several combinatorial properties to calculate the coefficients of the desired polynomials. Discussion is presented on the main computational challenges of this method, and the way to overcome them by imposing certain constraints during the training phase. Finally, simulation experiments as well as applications to real tabular data sets are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: CoLiDR: Concept Learning using Aggregated Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: How can disentangled generative factors be aggregated into human-understandable concepts to improve interpretability of deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CoLiDR, a method that aggregates disentangled generative factors into human-understandable concepts for interpretable concept-based modeling, achieving parity with state-of-the-art concept-based approaches.
papers.conclusion: CoLiDR unifies disentangled representation learning with concept-based explainability by aggregating generative factors into concepts, providing finer interpretability and maintaining performance.
papers.key_findings:
CoLiDR achieves task accuracy and concept error on par with concept-based models like CBM and GlanceNets.
The method effectively aggregates disentangled generative factors into human-understandable concepts.
Test-time interventions on learned concepts can fix wrongly classified samples, improving debugability.
Visual analysis using GradCAM shows that CoLiDR captures spatial concepts better than CBMs.
CoLiDR is generalizable to arbitrary numbers of concepts and generative factors across different datasets.
future_direction: Utilizing more complex disentanglement architectures like Generative Adversarial Networks.
Exploring causally related concepts instead of independent ones.
papers.abstract: Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks using concept-based models offers a promising way to explain model behavior through human-understandable concepts. A parallel line of research focuses on disentangling the data distribution into its underlying generative factors, in turn explaining the data generation process. While both directions have received extensive attention, little work has been done on explaining concepts in terms of generative factors to unify mathematically disentangled representations and human-understandable concepts as an explanation for downstream tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel method CoLiDR - which utilizes a disentangled representation learning setup for learning mutually independent generative factors and subsequently learns to aggregate the said representations into human-understandable concepts using a novel aggregation/decomposition module. Experiments are conducted on datasets with both known and unknown latent generative factors. Our method successfully aggregates disentangled generative factors into concepts while maintaining parity with state-of-the-art concept-based approaches. Quantitative and visual analysis of the learned aggregation procedure demonstrates the advantages of our work compared to commonly used concept-based models over four challenging datasets. Lastly, our work is generalizable to an arbitrary number of concepts and generative factors - making it flexible enough to be suitable for various types of data.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features and address polysemantic neurons in InceptionV1's early vision layers?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from InceptionV1, revealing missing curve detectors and decomposing polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic features.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1 and convolutional neural networks, extending their promise beyond language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn new interpretable features that were not visible when examining individual neurons.
SAEs discover additional curve detector features that fill gaps in the known family of curve detectors.
SAEs can split polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features.
papers.limitation: This paper is a very early report and does not defend the results in a systematic way.
future_direction: Investigate branch specialization and cross-branch superposition in InceptionV1 using SAEs.
papers.abstract: Recent work on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has shown promise in extracting interpretable features from neural networks and addressing challenges with polysemantic neurons caused by superposition. In this paper, we apply SAEs to the early vision layers of InceptionV1, a well-studied convolutional neural network, with a focus on curve detectors. Our results demonstrate that SAEs can uncover new interpretable features not apparent from examining individual neurons, including additional curve detectors that fill in previous gaps. We also find that SAEs can decompose some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features. These findings suggest SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1, and convolutional neural networks more generally.

papers.title: DGTN: Graph-Enhanced Transformer with Diffusive Attention Gating Mechanism for Enzyme DDG Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we accurately predict the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (∆∆G) by integrating sequence and structural information through a co-learning framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DGTN, a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network and transformer representations through a bidirectional diffusion mechanism for protein stability prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: DGTN effectively integrates 3D geometric and evolutionary sequence context through bidirectional diffusion, establishing a principled and interpretable paradigm for accurate protein stability prediction and design.
papers.key_findings:
DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance on ProTherm with Pearson correlation ρ=0.87 and RMSE=1.21 kcal/mol, outperforming existing baselines.
Ablation studies show the bidirectional diffusion mechanism contributes a 6-point gain in Pearson correlation over simple cross-modal fusion.
The model generalizes well to unseen datasets (SKEMPI, Ssym, FireProtDB), demonstrating robust learning of stability principles.
Theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to an optimal structure-aware attention matrix with a convergence rate of O(1/√T).
Attention visualization confirms the model successfully identifies spatially proximate but sequentially distant residue interactions.
papers.limitation:
Operates on a single static conformation of the wild-type protein, unable to capture dynamic or entropic contributions to stability.
Evaluates mutations in isolation and does not explicitly model epistatic (non-additive) interactions between multiple substitutions.
Training data (ProTherm) exhibits class imbalance, with certain protein families overrepresented, potentially limiting generalization.
future_direction: Incorporate ensembles of structures (from molecular dynamics or predicted distributions) to model flexibility and allostery.
Extend the architecture to jointly represent combinatorial mutations via graph-based mutation encoding or interaction-aware attention.
Improve robustness to dataset imbalance via domain-adversarial training, balanced sampling, or cross-family transfer learning.
papers.abstract: Predicting the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (DDG) is fundamental to protein engineering and drug design. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they often process sequence and structure information independently, failing to capture the intricate coupling between local structural geometry and global sequential patterns. We present DGTN (Diffused Graph-Transformer Network), a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network (GNN) weights for structural priors and transformer attention through a diffusion mechanism. Our key innovation is a bidirectional diffusion process where: (1) GNN-derived structural embeddings guide transformer attention via learnable diffusion kernels, and (2) transformer representations refine GNN message passing through attention-modulated graph updates. We provide rigorous mathematical analysis showing this co-learning scheme achieves provably better approximation bounds than independent processing. On ProTherm and SKEMPI benchmarks, DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance (Pearson Rho = 0.87, RMSE = 1.21 kcal/mol), with 6.2% improvement over best baselines. Ablation studies confirm the diffusion mechanism contributes 4.8 points to correlation. Our theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to optimal structure-sequence coupling, with convergence rate O(1/sqrt(T) ) where T is diffusion steps. This work establishes a principled framework for integrating heterogeneous protein representations through learnable diffusion.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Transformers are efficient hierarchical chemical graph learners
papers.research_question: How can we design an efficient graph transformer that reduces computational cost and captures long-range interactions in molecular graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SubFormer, a graph transformer that combines hierarchical clustering and message-passing to efficiently learn graph representations, reducing computational cost and capturing long-range interactions while being competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: SubFormer performed consistently well on standard benchmarks for predicting molecular properties from chemical structures. Visualization of the attention maps suggests the model learns chemically pertinent features. SubFormer does not suffer from over-squashing, but over-smoothing remains an issue requiring further study.
papers.key_findings:
SubFormer is competitive with state-of-the-art graph transformers on molecular property prediction benchmarks at a fraction of the computational cost.
SubFormer attention weights correspond to chemically meaningful fragments (e.g., aromatic rings, charge-transfer fragments).
SubFormer does not suffer from over-squashing because attention allows direct long-range interactions.
SubFormer exhibits limited over-smoothing compared to GAT, but still experiences over-smoothing with increasing layers.
SubFormer is more expressive than the 1-WL test for graph isomorphism.
papers.limitation: Over-smoothing remains an issue, demanding further study.
future_direction: Further study to address over-smoothing.
Refine the graph decomposition strategy to improve separation power.
papers.abstract: Transformers, adapted from natural language processing, are emerging as a leading approach for graph representation learning. Contemporary graph transformers often treat nodes or edges as separate tokens. This approach leads to computational challenges for even moderately-sized graphs due to the quadratic scaling of self-attention complexity with token count. In this paper, we introduce SubFormer, a graph transformer that operates on subgraphs that aggregate information by a message-passing mechanism. This approach reduces the number of tokens and enhances learning long-range interactions. We demonstrate SubFormer on benchmarks for predicting molecular properties from chemical structures and show that it is competitive with state-of-the-art graph transformers at a fraction of the computational cost, with training times on the order of minutes on a consumer-grade graphics card. We interpret the attention weights in terms of chemical structures. We show that SubFormer exhibits limited over-smoothing and avoids over-squashing, which is prevalent in traditional graph neural networks.

papers.title: A Detailed Study of Interpretability of Deep Neural Network based Top Taggers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural network models for top quark jet tagging, and how can interpretability methods be used to improve model design?
papers.core_contribution: The paper studies interpretability of DNN-based top taggers, uncovers pitfalls of existing XAI methods, and proposes a new model (PFIN) that improves performance through interpretability-inspired design.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes a methodological paradigm to demonstrate the usage of XAI tools for day-to-day applications of DNNs and MLPs in high energy physics, and shows how interpretability can lead to improved model design.
papers.key_findings:
Different XAI methods (∆AUC, SHAP, LRP) can produce inconsistent feature rankings, and modifying LRP to differential relevance scores (MAD) yields more consistent results.
Correlations among input features can obscure interpretability, as seen in the MB8S model.
NAP diagrams reveal sparsity in network activations and can guide model reoptimization by removing inactive layers or neurons.
The proposed PFIN model, which incorporates pairwise particle interactions, outperforms baseline models in top tagging.
Latent space embeddings in PFN capture physical jet features and show disentanglement between jet classes.
future_direction: Adapting interpretability tools for more general data types and novel architectures like graph nets and transformers
papers.abstract: Recent developments in the methods of explainable AI (XAI) allow researchers to explore the inner workings of deep neural networks (DNNs), revealing crucial information about input-output relationships and realizing how data connects with machine learning models. In this paper we explore interpretability of DNN models designed to identify jets coming from top quark decay in high energy proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We review a subset of existing top tagger models and explore different quantitative methods to identify which features play the most important roles in identifying the top jets. We also investigate how and why feature importance varies across different XAI metrics, how correlations among features impact their explainability, and how latent space representations encode information as well as correlate with physically meaningful quantities. Our studies uncover some major pitfalls of existing XAI methods and illustrate how they can be overcome to obtain consistent and meaningful interpretation of these models. We additionally illustrate the activity of hidden layers as Neural Activation Pattern (NAP) diagrams and demonstrate how they can be used to understand how DNNs relay information across the layers and how this understanding can help to make such models significantly simpler by allowing effective model reoptimization and hyperparameter tuning. These studies not only facilitate a methodological approach to interpreting models but also unveil new insights about what these models learn. Incorporating these observations into augmented model design, we propose the Particle Flow Interaction Network (PFIN) model and demonstrate how interpretability-inspired model augmentation can improve top tagging performance.

papers.title: A Spectral Theory of Neural Prediction and Alignment
papers.research_question: Why do many different deep neural networks yield similar neural predictions, and how can we differentiate among models that perform equally well at predicting neural responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a spectral theory that decomposes neural prediction error into model eigenspectra and alignment with neural data, and provides geometric measures (error mode radius Rem and dimension Dem) to interpret the error, revealing that different models can achieve similar prediction error through different geometric properties.
papers.conclusion: The spectral theory provides a framework to interpret neural prediction error and shows that geometric measures can differentiate models with similar prediction error, guiding future experiments and model design for improved neural activity prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The spectral theory accurately predicts neural prediction error for ridge regression from model activations to neural responses.
Error mode geometry (Rem and Dem) varies across models even when they have similar neural prediction error, providing additional insight into how models achieve low error.
Early model stages predict early visual areas (V1/V2) better, while later stages predict downstream areas (V4/IT) better, aligning with the hierarchical organization of the visual cortex.
Trained models have better alignment (Wi) with neural data than randomly initialized models, which is the main driver of improved prediction error.
Adversarial training improves alignment between model eigenvectors and early visual cortex activity, leading to lower prediction error in early areas.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical predictions are only accurate in the large P limit (large number of stimuli), and the tail eigenvalues of the empirical Gram matrix are often underestimated.
The results depend on the stimulus set used, which affects the model eigenspectra and thus the error mode geometry.
future_direction: Future work could consider choosing stimulus sets to maximize the difference between model eigenspectra, leading to greater differences in neural predictions.
Extending the theory to other regression methods and non-linear mappings between model activations and neural responses.
Applying the geometric measures to other domains beyond visual cortex to understand model representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: The representations of neural networks are often compared to those of biological systems by performing regression between the neural network responses and those measured from biological systems. Many different state-of-the-art deep neural networks yield similar neural predictions, but it remains unclear how to differentiate among models that perform equally well at predicting neural responses. To gain insight into this, we use a recent theoretical framework that relates the generalization error from regression to the spectral properties of the model and the target. We apply this theory to the case of regression between model activations and neural responses and decompose the neural prediction error in terms of the model eigenspectra, alignment of model eigenvectors and neural responses, and the training set size. Using this decomposition, we introduce geometrical measures to interpret the neural prediction error. We test a large number of deep neural networks that predict visual cortical activity and show that there are multiple types of geometries that result in low neural prediction error as measured via regression. The work demonstrates that carefully decomposing representational metrics can provide interpretability of how models are capturing neural activity and points the way towards improved models of neural activity.

papers.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied to dense text embeddings to extract interpretable features and enable fine-grained control over semantic search?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can effectively disentangle semantic concepts in dense text embeddings, enabling interpretable features that can be used to precisely steer semantic search.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable features from dense text embeddings, enabling enhanced control and understanding in semantic search applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn interpretable features from dense embeddings with high Pearson correlation in automated labeling.
Feature families can be identified through graph-based clustering, representing related concepts at different abstraction levels.
SAE features can be used to intervene on embeddings for fine-grained control in semantic search.
Scaling laws show power-law relationships between SAE performance and model parameters like number of latents and compute.
Features exhibit splitting and recurrence across different SAE capacities, with some universal features appearing across models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in extracting interpretable features from complex neural networks. We present one of the first applications of SAEs to dense text embeddings from large language models, demonstrating their effectiveness in disentangling semantic concepts. By training SAEs on embeddings of over 420,000 scientific paper abstracts from computer science and astronomy, we show that the resulting sparse representations maintain semantic fidelity while offering interpretability. We analyse these learned features, exploring their behaviour across different model capacities and introducing a novel method for identifying ``feature families'' that represent related concepts at varying levels of abstraction. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we show how these interpretable features can be used to precisely steer semantic search, allowing for fine-grained control over query semantics. This work bridges the gap between the semantic richness of dense embeddings and the interpretability of sparse representations. We open source our embeddings, trained sparse autoencoders, and interpreted features, as well as a web app for exploring them.

papers.title: Interpretable Embeddings of Speech Enhance and Explain Brain Encoding Performance of Audio Models
papers.research_question: What drives the alignment between speech foundation models and brain responses? Is it due to non-linear uninterpretable representations or simpler interpretable features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the alignment of speech foundation models with brain responses is largely due to their ability to encode interpretable speech features, and augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features improves brain encoding performance and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest a principled approach to building more interpretable, accurate, and efficient encoding models of the brain by augmenting speech foundation model embeddings with interpretable features.
papers.key_findings:
Most of the neural variance captured by speech foundation models (SFMs) can be attributed to interpretable features.
SFMs exhibit a systematic trade-off between encoding of brain-relevant low-level and high-level features across layers.
SFMs learn brain-relevant semantic information that cannot be explained by lower-level speech features, with this capacity increasing with model size and context length.
Augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features consistently improves encoding performance across all layers and mitigates the trade-off between low-level and high-level feature encoding.
The trade-off between precision and temporal windows of acoustic information encoded by SFMs is architecture-dependent (e.g., Whisper and WavLM shift from fine-grained detail to broader integration, while HuBERT's acoustic representations degrade).
papers.abstract: Speech foundation models (SFMs) are increasingly hailed as powerful computational models of human speech perception. However, since their representations are inherently black-box, it remains unclear what drives their alignment with brain responses. To remedy this, we built linear encoding models from six interpretable feature families: mel-spectrogram, Gabor filter bank features, speech presence, phonetic, syntactic, and semantic features, and contextualized embeddings from three state-of-the-art SFMs (Whisper, HuBERT, WavLM), quantifying electrocorticography (ECoG) response variance shared between feature classes. Variance-partitioning analyses revealed several key insights: First, the SFMs' alignment with the brain can be mostly explained by their ability to learn and encode simple interpretable speech features. Second, SFMs exhibit a systematic trade-off between encoding of brain-relevant low-level and high-level features across layers. Finally, our results show that SFMs learn brain-relevant semantics which cannot be explained by lower-level speech features, with this capacity increasing with model size and context length. Together, our findings suggest a principled approach to build more interpretable, accurate, and efficient encoding models of the brain by augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features.

papers.title: Rewire-then-Probe: A Contrastive Recipe for Probing Biomedical Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to effectively probe biomedical knowledge from pre-trained language models, addressing domain-specific challenges such as multi-token entities and vocabulary bias.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces MedLAMA, a biomedical knowledge probing benchmark, and Contrastive-Probe, a self-supervised method that improves probing performance by rewiring PLMs without using probing data.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents MedLAMA and Contrastive-Probe, showing that PLMs can be rewired to better probe biomedical knowledge, though evaluation criteria may underestimate their capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Existing probing methods achieve less than 3% acc@10 on MedLAMA due to challenges like multi-token answers.
Contrastive-Probe improves acc@10 to 24% by rewiring PLMs with self-supervised contrastive learning.
Different PLMs perform better on different types of relational knowledge, reflecting their training corpora.
Transformer layers encode different types of information, with optimal probing performance varying by relation and layer.
Human evaluation reveals that UMLS does not cover all factual knowledge, suggesting PLMs encode richer information than benchmarked.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty in early stopping due to different optimal training steps for different models and datasets.
Performance variance with different contrastive tuning corpora and random seeds.
future_direction: Integrating encoding space and input space optimization for better probing.
Improving the stability of Contrastive-Probe and investigating its nature.
Exploring layer-wise and relation-wise training for knowledge infusion.
papers.abstract: Knowledge probing is crucial for understanding the knowledge transfer mechanism behind the pre-trained language models (PLMs). Despite the growing progress of probing knowledge for PLMs in the general domain, specialised areas such as biomedical domain are vastly under-explored. To catalyse the research in this direction, we release a well-curated biomedical knowledge probing benchmark, MedLAMA, which is constructed based on the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) Metathesaurus. We test a wide spectrum of state-of-the-art PLMs and probing approaches on our benchmark, reaching at most 3% of acc@10. While highlighting various sources of domain-specific challenges that amount to this underwhelming performance, we illustrate that the underlying PLMs have a higher potential for probing tasks. To achieve this, we propose Contrastive-Probe, a novel self-supervised contrastive probing approach, that adjusts the underlying PLMs without using any probing data. While Contrastive-Probe pushes the acc@10 to 28%, the performance gap still remains notable. Our human expert evaluation suggests that the probing performance of our Contrastive-Probe is still under-estimated as UMLS still does not include the full spectrum of factual knowledge. We hope MedLAMA and Contrastive-Probe facilitate further developments of more suited probing techniques for this domain.

papers.title: Learning local discrete features in explainable-by-design convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design a convolutional neural network that is both high-performance and explainable by using a lateral inhibition mechanism to learn local discrete features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ExplaiNet, an explainable-by-design CNN that uses a lateral inhibition layer to learn local discrete feature vectors, enabling high accuracy and providing explanations via a probabilistic graph and motif discovery.
papers.conclusion: The ExplaiNet framework breaks the performance-explainability trade-off by introducing an explainable-by-design CNN that retains or surpasses baseline performance while providing causal explanations based on discrete feature motifs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed ExplaiNet model achieves comparable or better performance than baseline ResNet and DenseNet architectures on tiny image datasets while providing explanations.
The lateral inhibition layer amplifies gradients of winner neurons, leading to ordered activations and the formation of local discrete feature vectors.
Feature motif discovery using the EXTREME algorithm reduces the vocabulary of local discrete features, providing concise explanations.
The explainer probabilistic graph can infer causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs.
Experiments show that the explainer can sometimes correctly classify samples that the neural predictor misclassifies, suggesting potential for ensemble use or adversarial sample detection.
papers.limitation:
Further research on regularization aspects of the lateral inhibition function is required to investigate the magnitude of weights and activations during training.
Experiments are limited to tiny image datasets due to computational resources; the method has not been tested on medium-resolution images or high numbers of classes.
future_direction: Investigate the proper amount of weight decay and restriction of input values for positively monotonic gradient amplification in the lateral inhibition function.
Scale up the method to train models on medium-resolution images, high number of classes, and with millions of parameters.
Adjust the EXTREME algorithm to support custom numeric system bases, making the conversion to the quaternary system optional.
papers.abstract: Our proposed framework attempts to break the trade-off between performance and explainability by introducing an explainable-by-design convolutional neural network (CNN) based on the lateral inhibition mechanism. The ExplaiNet model consists of the predictor, that is a high-accuracy CNN with residual or dense skip connections, and the explainer probabilistic graph that expresses the spatial interactions of the network neurons. The value on each graph node is a local discrete feature (LDF) vector, a patch descriptor that represents the indices of antagonistic neurons ordered by the strength of their activations, which are learned with gradient descent. Using LDFs as sequences we can increase the conciseness of explanations by repurposing EXTREME, an EM-based sequence motif discovery method that is typically used in molecular biology. Having a discrete feature motif matrix for each one of intermediate image representations, instead of a continuous activation tensor, allows us to leverage the inherent explainability of Bayesian networks. By collecting observations and directly calculating probabilities, we can explain causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs. Moreover, experiments on various tiny image benchmark datasets confirm that our predictor ensures the same level of performance as the baseline architecture for a given count of parameters and/or layers. Our novel method shows promise to exceed this performance while providing an additional stream of explanations. In the solved MNIST classification task, it reaches a comparable to the state-of-the-art performance for single models, using standard training setup and 0.75 million parameters.

papers.title: Invertible Neural Networks for Understanding Semantics of Invariances of CNN Representations
papers.research_question: How can we understand the semantic concepts and invariances learned by deep neural networks (specifically CNNs) by recovering the invariances and translating the representations into an interpretable form without modifying the original model?
papers.core_contribution: An invertible neural network (INN) approach that recovers the invariances a deep model has learned and bijectively translates the model representation and its invariances into a semantically accessible encoding without compromising the original model's performance.
papers.conclusion: The invertible approach provides a powerful, post-hoc diagnostic pipeline for explaining deep representations by recovering invariances and enabling semantic interpretation without retraining the model.
papers.key_findings:
The method visualizes representations and their invariances without artifacts, outperforming existing network inversion methods.
Analysis of FaceNet shows that invariances (e.g., to pose) increase with layer depth, while some features (e.g., glasses) remain identity-relevant across layers.
The approach can quantify how much of a semantic concept (e.g., texture vs. shape) is captured by a model's representation, revealing biases like texture bias in ImageNet-trained CNNs.
Semantic modifications in the interpretable space correctly alter the original representation and can be visualized, enabling diagnostic probing of model sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Abstract To tackle increasingly complex tasks, it has become an essential ability of neural networks to learn abstract representations. These task-specific representations and, particularly, the invariances they capture turn neural networks into black-box models that lack interpretability. To open such a black box, it is, therefore, crucial to uncover the different semantic concepts a model has learned as well as those that it has learned to be invariant to. We present an approach based on invertible neural networks (INNs) that (i) recovers the task-specific, learned invariances by disentangling the remaining factor of variation in the data and that (ii) invertibly transforms these recovered invariances combined with the model representation into an equally expressive one with accessible semantic concepts. As a consequence, neural network representations become understandable by providing the means to (i) expose their semantic meaning, (ii) semantically modify a representation, and (iii) visualize individual learned semantic concepts and invariances. Our invertible approach significantly extends the abilities to understand black-box models by enabling post hoc interpretations of state-of-the-art networks without compromising their performance. Our implementation is available at https://compvis.github.io/invariances/ .

papers.title: SkinCon: A skin disease dataset densely annotated by domain experts for fine-grained model debugging and analysis
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SkinCon, a skin disease dataset densely annotated by dermatologists with 48 clinical concepts applicable across multiple diseases, and demonstrates its utility for explaining model mistakes and building interpretable concept bottleneck models.
papers.conclusion: SkinCon addresses the need for densely annotated medical datasets to enable interpretability and fine-grained error analysis in healthcare AI, providing a foundation for developing and validating concept-based methods in dermatology.
papers.key_findings:
The SkinCon dataset provides the first medical dataset with dense concept annotations that are broadly applicable across multiple disease processes, not just a single diagnosis.
Using SkinCon concepts, Conceptual Counterfactual Explanations (CCE) can generate human-understandable explanations for model misclassifications in skin disease diagnosis.
Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck Models (PCBMs) built with SkinCon concepts can match or exceed the performance of the original black-box model while providing interpretability.
The concept importance weights from the PCBM align with some clinical knowledge (e.g., Ulcer, Telangiectasia, Black predict malignancy) but also reveal potential biases (e.g., Scar predicts benign, though cancers can appear near scars).
The dataset enables fine-grained error analysis and slice discovery for dermatology AI models, addressing the need for interpretability in high-risk settings.
papers.limitation:
The dataset does not cover all dermatological diseases and is imbalanced in its concept representation due to real-world disease prevalence.
The dataset lacks patient demographic information (sex, gender, race, age), limiting fine-grained error analysis across protected classes.
The Fitzpatrick skin tone scale used may not have enough granularity to capture the full range of human skin diversity.
future_direction: Expand the size and scope of the dataset by densely labeling additional skin disease images.
papers.abstract: For the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in high-risk settings, such as healthcare, methods that provide interpretability/explainability or allow fine-grained error analysis are critical. Many recent methods for interpretability/explainability and fine-grained error analysis use concepts, which are meta-labels that are semantically meaningful to humans. However, there are only a few datasets that include concept-level meta-labels and most of these meta-labels are relevant for natural images that do not require domain expertise. Densely annotated datasets in medicine focused on meta-labels that are relevant to a single disease such as melanoma. In dermatology, skin disease is described using an established clinical lexicon that allows clinicians to describe physical exam findings to one another. To provide a medical dataset densely annotated by domain experts with annotations useful across multiple disease processes, we developed SkinCon: a skin disease dataset densely annotated by dermatologists. SkinCon includes 3230 images from the Fitzpatrick 17k dataset densely annotated with 48 clinical concepts, 22 of which have at least 50 images representing the concept. The concepts used were chosen by two dermatologists considering the clinical descriptor terms used to describe skin lesions. Examples include "plaque", "scale", and "erosion". The same concepts were also used to label 656 skin disease images from the Diverse Dermatology Images dataset, providing an additional external dataset with diverse skin tone representations. We review the potential applications for the SkinCon dataset, such as probing models, concept-based explanations, and concept bottlenecks. Furthermore, we use SkinCon to demonstrate two of these use cases: debugging mistakes of an existing dermatology AI model with concepts and developing interpretable models with post-hoc concept bottleneck models.

papers.title: GENNI: Visualising the Geometry of Equivalences for Neural Network Identifiability
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently identify and visualize the subspace of functionally equivalent parameters (symmetries) in neural networks to study identifiability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GENNI, an efficient optimization-based method to identify and visualize the subspace of functionally equivalent parameters (symmetries) in neural networks, aiding the study of identifiability.
papers.conclusion: GENNI is a scalable method for visualizing equivalence classes of neural network parameters, which can be used to study identifiability and inform initialization techniques.
papers.key_findings:
GENNI can efficiently find and visualize equivalence classes in neural network parameter spaces.
For a simple ReLU network, the visualized equivalence class shows shapes consistent with scaling and permutation symmetries.
For LeNet, the equivalence class exhibits a large connected region with low loss, indicating many symmetries.
The method scales to high-dimensional networks like LeNet (60,000 parameters).
Visualizations via UMAP can reveal topological properties like connectedness even in higher dimensions.
papers.limitation:
Visualization becomes computationally infeasible for high-dimensional hyperplanes (m > 7).
UMAP visualizations in higher dimensions are less interpretable.
The method currently visualizes only a single equivalence class, not the entire quotient set.
future_direction: Develop a guide to deduce symmetries from visualizations for specific architectures.
Explore the quotient space of equivalence classes.
Apply GENNI to understand meta-learning and transfer learning.
papers.abstract: We propose an efficient algorithm to visualise symmetries in neural networks. Typically, models are defined with respect to a parameter space, where non-equal parameters can produce the same input-output map. Our proposed method, GENNI, allows us to efficiently identify parameters that are functionally equivalent and then visualise the subspace of the resulting equivalence class. By doing so, we are now able to better explore questions surrounding identifiability, with applications to optimisation and generalizability, for commonly used or newly developed neural network architectures.

papers.title: Video Prediction of Dynamic Physical Simulations With Pixel-Space Spatiotemporal Transformers
papers.research_question: This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts, focusing on causal modelling of physical simulations over time.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a simple, interpretable pure transformer model (PSViT) for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction in pixel-space, which extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% compared to existing latent-space approaches.
papers.conclusion: The presented simple, interpretable pure transformer for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction extends the horizon for physically accurate predictions while maintaining competitive performance on standard video quality metrics, highlighting the benefits of a straightforward end-to-end approach.
papers.key_findings:
The PSViT model achieves increased temporal accuracy in predicting PDE-driven video sequences compared to existing approaches, as measured by an object tracking metric.
The model maintains competitive performance on standard video quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR).
Interpretability experiments identify network regions that encode information useful for estimating PDE simulation parameters via probing.
The learned encoding of underlying physics generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters.
The model's performance is evaluated on several physics simulation datasets and common video prediction benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
For three of the simulation datasets increasing PSViT model size has minimal impact on performance over time.
For stochastic video-generation results on BAIR, the approach falls short compared to latent space models.
Object shapes, although positioned accurately, can distort over time, particularly when rotation is involved.
By performing end-to-end training, the model doesn't benefit from the large-scale pretrained image encoders/decoders often employed by latent space models.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated metrics for evaluating physical accuracy, moving beyond current object-based pixel distance methods.
Training larger models on higher-resolution datasets featuring increased visual fidelity and physical complexity.
papers.abstract: Inspired by the performance and scalability of autoregressive large language models (LLMs), transformer-based models have seen recent success in the visual domain. This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts. Focusing on causal modeling of physical simulations over time; a common shortcoming of existing video-generative approaches, we attempt to isolate spatiotemporal reasoning via physical object tracking metrics and unsupervised training on physical simulation datasets. We introduce a simple yet effective pure transformer model for autoregressive video prediction, utilizing continuous pixel-space representations for video prediction. Without the need for complex training strategies or latent feature-learning components, our approach significantly extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% when compared with existing latent-space approaches, while maintaining comparable performance on common video quality metrics. In addition, we conduct interpretability experiments to identify network regions that encode information useful to perform accurate estimations of PDE simulation parameters via probing models, and find that this generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters. This work serves as a platform for further attention-based spatiotemporal modeling of videos via a simple, parameter efficient, and interpretable approach.

papers.title: Clustering units in neural networks: upstream vs downstream information
papers.research_question: How can we define and quantify modularity in neural networks? The paper investigates this by comparing upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity between hidden units.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that dropout increases modularity by making hidden units redundant, and that upstream and downstream definitions of functional similarity yield different clusters, indicating a misalignment between input-driven and output-driven neural representations.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that upstream and downstream ways of thinking about neural representations are not necessarily aligned, which has implications for representation learning and the definition of modularity.
papers.key_findings:
Dropout dramatically increases modularity, contrary to the initial hypothesis that it would decrease modularity.
L2 regularization also increases modularity, while L1 regularization has a more modest effect.
Upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity agree within their families but disagree across families, leading to different cluster assignments.
The redundancy-inducing effect of dropout increases the clusterability of units.
Training increases cluster-similarity among upstream methods but not downstream methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to feedforward networks on MNIST, which may not have a meaningful modular solution.
Pairwise independence does not guarantee groupwise independence, which could be a limitation of the method.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks trained on more structured data, and to recurrent networks.
Evaluating the effect of maximizing modularity during training to see if it leads to performance benefits.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that some form of "modular" structure in artificial neural networks should be useful for learning, compositionality, and generalization. However, defining and quantifying modularity remains an open problem. We cast the problem of detecting functional modules into the problem of detecting clusters of similar-functioning units. This begs the question of what makes two units functionally similar. For this, we consider two broad families of methods: those that define similarity based on how units respond to structured variations in inputs ("upstream"), and those based on how variations in hidden unit activations affect outputs ("downstream"). We conduct an empirical study quantifying modularity of hidden layer representations of simple feedforward, fully connected networks, across a range of hyperparameters. For each model, we quantify pairwise associations between hidden units in each layer using a variety of both upstream and downstream measures, then cluster them by maximizing their "modularity score" using established tools from network science. We find two surprising results: first, dropout dramatically increased modularity, while other forms of weight regularization had more modest effects. Second, although we observe that there is usually good agreement about clusters within both upstream methods and downstream methods, there is little agreement about the cluster assignments across these two families of methods. This has important implications for representation-learning, as it suggests that finding modular representations that reflect structure in inputs (e.g. disentanglement) may be a distinct goal from learning modular representations that reflect structure in outputs (e.g. compositionality).

papers.title: Insights on representational similarity in neural networks with\n canonical correlation
papers.research_question: How can we compare neural network representations and how do they evolve over time?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces projection weighted CCA, an improved method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that generalizing networks converge to more similar representations than memorizing networks, wider networks converge to more similar solutions, and RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence during training.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates the utility of projection weighted CCA for analyzing neural network representations, revealing insights about convergence and similarity in CNNs and RNNs.
papers.key_findings:
Networks that generalize converge to more similar representations than those that memorize.
Wider networks converge to more similar solutions than narrower networks.
Networks with identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters of solutions.
RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence over the course of training.
RNN hidden states vary nonlinearly across sequence timesteps.
future_direction: Examine what is unique about directions preserved across networks trained with different initializations.
Explore whether the insight that similar solutions lead to higher generalization could be used as a regularizer.
Investigate which aspects of RNN representations are stable over time and which vary.
papers.abstract:
Comparing different neural network representations and determining how
representations evolve over time remain challenging open questions in our
understanding of the function of neural networks. Comparing representations in
neural networks is fundamentally difficult as the structure of representations
varies greatly, even across groups of networks trained on identical tasks, and
over the course of training. Here, we develop projection weighted CCA
(Canonical Correlation Analysis) as a tool for understanding neural networks,
building off of SVCCA, a recently proposed method (Raghu et al., 2017). We
first improve the core method, showing how to differentiate between signal and
noise, and then apply this technique to compare across a group of CNNs,
demonstrating that networks which generalize converge to more similar
representations than networks which memorize, that wider networks converge to
more similar solutions than narrow networks, and that trained networks with
identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters
with diverse representations. We also investigate the representational dynamics
of RNNs, across both training and sequential timesteps, finding that RNNs
converge in a bottom-up pattern over the course of training and that the hidden
state is highly variable over the course of a sequence, even when accounting
for linear transforms. Together, these results provide new insights into the
function of CNNs and RNNs, and demonstrate the utility of using CCA to
understand representations.

papers.title: Using Causal Analysis for Conceptual Deep Learning Explanation
papers.research_question: How to provide clinically relevant explanations for deep learning models in healthcare by associating hidden units with concepts and using causal analysis to ensure influence.
papers.core_contribution: A framework for explaining black-box models using clinically relevant concepts and causal mediation analysis to ensure concepts causally influence the model's decisions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides global explanations for black-box models in terms of clinically relevant concepts that are causally influencing the model's decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Concept classifiers using sparse logistic regression achieve high recall, indicating effective association of hidden units with concepts.
Hidden units act as visual concept detectors, localizing radiographic features without explicit concept supervision during training.
Causal mediation analysis via counterfactual interventions ranks concepts based on indirect effect, with top-ranked concepts being clinically consistent.
The indirect effect is highest in middle layers (dense-block 3), showing their role in mediating decisions.
A decision tree surrogate function provides interpretable global explanations using the top-ranked concepts.
future_direction: Extend concept definition to include a broader set of clinical metrics.

papers.title: Explaining the Behavior of Black-Box Prediction Algorithms with Causal Learning
papers.research_question: How can we provide causal explanations for black-box prediction models in terms of interpretable macro-level features, especially in the presence of unmeasured confounding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal discovery-based approach (using algorithms like FCI) to explain black-box model predictions in terms of interpretable macro-level features, which can handle unmeasured confounding and distinguish causal features from spurious associations.
papers.conclusion: Causal discovery methods provide a promising approach for explaining black-box models by identifying causal determinants of predictions in terms of interpretable features, advancing towards more trustworthy AI.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies stable causal macro-features for bird classification (e.g., Wing Shape, Wing Pattern) and pneumonia detection (e.g., Atelectasis, Infiltration).
Existing pixel-level explanation methods (LIME, SHAP) are less informative for these tasks as they do not map to interpretable high-level features.
Causal discovery can reveal unmeasured confounding among observed macro-level variables, which is crucial for valid causal explanation.
papers.limitation:
Requires annotated data with interpretable macro-level features, which may not always be available.
Assumes causal sufficiency among the observed variables (though allows unmeasured confounding among them).
Causal discovery algorithms can be computationally expensive and sensitive to statistical errors in independence tests.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other data modalities like text and time series.
Automate the extraction of interpretable features from unannotated data.
Incorporate interventional data when available to improve causal discovery.
papers.abstract: Causal approaches to post-hoc explainability for black-box prediction models (e.g., deep neural networks trained on image pixel data) have become increasingly popular. However, existing approaches have two important shortcomings: (i) the "explanatory units" are micro-level inputs into the relevant prediction model, e.g., image pixels, rather than interpretable macro-level features that are more useful for understanding how to possibly change the algorithm's behavior, and (ii) existing approaches assume there exists no unmeasured confounding between features and target model predictions, which fails to hold when the explanatory units are macro-level variables. Our focus is on the important setting where the analyst has no access to the inner workings of the target prediction algorithm, rather only the ability to query the output of the model in response to a particular input. To provide causal explanations in such a setting, we propose to learn causal graphical representations that allow for arbitrary unmeasured confounding among features. We demonstrate the resulting graph can differentiate between interpretable features that causally influence model predictions versus those that are merely associated with model predictions due to confounding. Our approach is motivated by a counterfactual theory of causal explanation wherein good explanations point to factors that are "difference-makers" in an interventionist sense.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Capturing the Development of Internal Representations in a High-Performing Deep Network for Sleep Stage Classification
papers.research_question: How does the ability to differentiate sleep stages develop across the layers of a deep convolutional neural network, and how can this be quantified using visualization and kernel alignment methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a deep convolutional neural network for sleep stage classification that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, and introduces a max-pooling CKA approach to quantify the development of sleep stage specialization and differentiation across network layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a high-accuracy CNN for sleep stage classification and demonstrates through t-SNE and max-pooling CKA that sleep stage specialization and differentiation abilities increase monotonically with network layer depth.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN achieves 84.50% accuracy on sleep stage classification, exceeding human inter-scorer agreement of 82.6%.
Including wake data before and after sleep improves performance on wake epochs, but mid-sleep wake epochs are harder to classify.
Visualization with t-SNE shows increasing class separation with layer depth.
Max-pooling CKA provides quantitative measures that validate t-SNE and show monotonic improvement in stage specialization and differentiation with depth.
The network's internal representations gradually develop sleep stage differentiation, with partial differentiation even in shallow layers.
papers.limitation:
Performance is weakest on the under-represented sleep stage S1, and oversampling did not significantly improve it.
Models with more input channels may require more data to achieve optimal generalization compared to single-channel models.
future_direction: Investigating the use of CKA with nonlinear kernels.
Applying the proposed techniques to alternative network types such as recurrent neural networks.
Simultaneous and complementary use of CKA-based quantification and activation maximization approaches.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep neural networks can provide accurate automated classification of human sleep signals into sleep stages that enables more effective diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders. We develop a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) that attains state-of-the-art sleep stage classification performance on input data consisting of human sleep EEG and EOG signals. Nested cross-validation is used for optimal model selection and reliable estimation of out-of-sample classification performance. The resulting network attains a classification accuracy of $$84.50 \pm 0.13\%$$ <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mml:mrow> <mml:mn>84.50</mml:mn> <mml:mo>±</mml:mo> <mml:mn>0.13</mml:mn> <mml:mo>%</mml:mo> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> ; its performance exceeds human expert inter-scorer agreement, even on single-channel EEG input data, therefore providing more objective and consistent labeling than human experts demonstrate as a group. We focus on analyzing the learned internal data representations of our network, with the aim of understanding the development of class differentiation ability across the layers of processing units, as a function of layer depth. We approach this problem visually, using t-Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), and propose a pooling variant of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) that provides an objective quantitative measure of the development of sleep stage specialization and differentiation with layer depth. The results reveal a monotonic progression of both of these sleep stage modeling abilities as layer depth increases.

papers.title: Topological Data Analysis of Neural Network Layer Representations
papers.research_question: How are topological features preserved within the internal representations of neural network layers?
papers.core_contribution: Early neural network layer representations approximate homeomorphisms and preserve topological features of the input data, but deeper layers significantly alter the topology. Networks with bijective activation functions (Tanh) preserve topological features longer than those with non-bijective functions (ReLU).
papers.conclusion: Topological analysis can provide insight into how neural networks represent data, and activation functions affect topology preservation, but the study is preliminary and not conclusive.
papers.key_findings:
Early layer representations approximate homeomorphisms and preserve topological features of the input data.
Deeper layer representations have topology markedly different from the original data, possibly due to repeated application of non-homeomorphic layers.
Persistent homology has difficulty computing topological features from deeper layer representations due to noise.
Networks with bijective activation functions (Tanh) preserve topological features longer than those with non-bijective functions (ReLU).
The network may be isolating relevant topological features for classification and excising superfluous features.
papers.limitation:
The study is preliminary and not conclusive.
Noise in clusterings disrupts persistent homology.
Only one topology (modified torus) was tested.
future_direction: Testing neural networks on more varied topologies.
Using alternative clustering algorithms to reduce noise disruption in persistent homology.
